references.title: Federated Learning: A Survey on Enabling Technologies, Protocols, and Applications
references.abstract: This paper provides a comprehensive study of Federated Learning (FL) with an emphasis on enabling software and hardware platforms, protocols, real-life applications and use-cases. FL can be applicable to multiple domains but applying it to different industries has its own set of obstacles. FL is known as collaborative learning, where algorithm(s) get trained across multiple devices or servers with decentralized data samples without having to exchange the actual data. This approach is radically different from other more established techniques such as getting the data samples uploaded to servers or having data in some form of distributed infrastructure. FL on the other hand generates more robust models without sharing data, leading to privacy-preserved solutions with higher security and access privileges to data. references.abstract: Abstract The adoption of immersive virtual reality (I-VR) as a pedagogical method in education has challenged the conceptual definition of what constitutes a learning environment. High fidelity graphics and immersive content using head-mounted-displays (HMD) have allowed students to explore complex subjects in a way that traditional teaching methods cannot. Despite this, research focusing on learning outcomes, intervention characteristics, and assessment measures associated with I-VR use has been sparse. To explore this, the current systematic review examined experimental studies published since 2013, where quantitative learning outcomes using HMD based I-VR were compared with less immersive pedagogical methods such as desktop computers and slideshows. references.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) generally and machine learning (ML) specifically demonstrate impressive practical success in many different application domains, e.g. in autonomous driving, speech recognition, or recommender systems. Deep learning approaches, trained on extremely large data sets or using reinforcement learning methods have even exceeded human performance in visual tasks, particularly on playing games such as Atari, or mastering the game of Go. Even in the medical domain there are remarkable results. The central problem of such models is that they are regarded as black-box models and even if we understand the underlying mathematical principles, they lack an explicit declarative knowledge representation, hence have difficulty in generating the underlying explanatory structures. references.title: A review of machine learning applications in wildfire science and management
references.abstract: Artificial intelligence has been applied in wildfire science and management since the 1990s, with early applications including neural networks and expert systems. Since then, the field has rapidly progressed congruently with the wide adoption of machine learning (ML) methods in the environmental sciences. Here, we present a scoping review of ML applications in wildfire science and management. Our overall objective is to improve awareness of ML methods among wildfire researchers and managers, as well as illustrate the diverse and challenging range of problems in wildfire science available to ML data scientists. To that end, we first present an overview of popular ML approaches used in wildfire science to date and then review the use of ML in wildfire science as broadly categorized into six problem domains, including (i) fuels characterization, fire detection, and mapping; (ii) fire weather and climate change; (iii) fire occurrence, susceptibility, and risk; (iv) fire behavior prediction

references.abstract: The ontogeny of large-scale functional organization of the human brain is not well understood. Here we use network analysis of intrinsic functional connectivity to characterize the organization of brain networks in 23 children (ages 7-9 y) and 22 young-adults (ages 19-22 y). Comparison of network properties, including path-length, clustering-coefficient, hierarchy, and regional connectivity, revealed that although children and young-adults' brains have similar "small-world" organization at the global level, they differ significantly in hierarchical organization and interregional connectivity. We found that subcortical areas were more strongly connected with primary sensory, association, and paralimbic areas in children, whereas young-adults showed stronger cortico-cortical connectivity between paralimbic, limbic, and association areas. references.abstract: As the smart city applications are moving from conceptual models to development phase, smart transportation is one of smart cities applications and it is gaining ground nowadays. Electric Vehicles (EVs) are considered one of the major pillars of smart transportation applications. EVs are ever growing in popularity due to their potential contribution in reducing dependency on fossil fuels and greenhouse gas emissions. However, large-scale deployment of EV charging stations poses multiple challenges to the power grid and public infrastructure. To overcome the issue of prolonged charging time, the simple solution of deploying more charging stations to increase charging capacity does not work due to the strain on power grids and physical space limitations. Therefore, researchers have focused on developing smart scheduling algorithms to manage the demand for public charging using modeling and optimization. references.title: Clickstream Data Yields High-Resolution Maps of Science
references.abstract: BACKGROUND: Intricate maps of science have been created from citation data to visualize the structure of scientific activity. However, most scientific publications are now accessed online. Scholarly web portals record detailed log data at a scale that exceeds the number of all existing citations combined. Such log data is recorded immediately upon publication and keeps track of the sequences of user requests (clickstreams) that are issued by a variety of users across many different domains. Given these advantages of log datasets over citation data, we investigate whether they can produce high-resolution, more current maps of science. METHODOLOGY: Over the course of 2007 and 2008, we collected nearly 1 billion user interactions recorded by the scholarly web portals of some of the most significant publishers, aggregators and institutional consortia. references.authors: Hugo Storm, Kathy Baylis, Thomas Heckelei
references.title: Machine learning in agricultural and applied economics
references.abstract: Abstract This review presents machine learning (ML) approaches from an applied economist’s perspective. We first introduce the key ML methods drawing connections to econometric practice. We then identify current limitations of the econometric and simulation model toolbox in applied economics and explore potential solutions afforded by ML. We dive into cases such as inflexible functional forms, unstructured data sources and large numbers of explanatory variables in both prediction and causal analysis, and highlight the challenges of complex simulation models. Finally, we argue that economists have a vital role in addressing the shortcomings of ML when used for quantitative economic analysis.

references.title: A Comprehensive Review on Synergy of Multi-Modal Data and AI Technologies in Medical Diagnosis
references.abstract: Disease diagnosis represents a critical and arduous endeavor within the medical field. Artificial intelligence (AI) techniques, spanning from machine learning and deep learning to large model paradigms, stand poised to significantly augment physicians in rendering more evidence-based decisions, thus presenting a pioneering solution for clinical practice. Traditionally, the amalgamation of diverse medical data modalities (e.g., image, text, speech, genetic data, physiological signals) is imperative to facilitate a comprehensive disease analysis, a topic of burgeoning interest among both researchers and clinicians in recent times. Hence, there exists a pressing need to synthesize the latest strides in multi-modal data and AI technologies in the realm of medical diagnosis. references.authors: Seoyon Yang, Min Cheol Chang
references.title: Poststroke Pain
references.abstract: Pain is common but often underrecognized after stroke. Poststroke pain (PSP) hinders recovery, impairs quality of life, and is associated with the psychological state of patients with stroke. The most common subtypes of PSP include central PSP, complex regional pain syndrome, shoulder pain, spasticity-related pain, and headache. The pathophysiologies of these PSP subtypes are not yet clearly understood, and PSP is refractory to conventional treatment in many patients. However, recent studies have proposed potential pathophysiologies of PSP subtypes, which may help prioritize therapies that target specific mechanisms.

Following PRISMA principles adapted for mechanistic synthesis, two reviewers searched PubMed, Scopus, Google Scholar, ResearchGate and Cochrane from January 2000 to May 2025 using "MRI/fMRI" AND "burnout". After duplicate removal and multi-stage screening, 17 clinical studies met predefined inclusion criteria (English language, MRI outcomes, validated burnout diagnosis). In total, ≈1365 participants were scanned, 880 with clinically significant burnout and 470 controls. references.abstract: Prescription opioid misuse and addiction among chronic pain patients are emerging public health concerns of considerable significance. Estimates suggest that more than 10% of chronic pain patients misuse opioid analgesics, and the number of fatalities related to nonmedical or inappropriate use of prescription opioids is climbing. Because the prevalence and adverse consequences of this threat are increasing, there is a pressing need for research that identifies the biobehavioral risk chain linking chronic pain, opioid analgesia, and addictive behaviors. To that end, the current manuscript draws upon current neuropsychopharmacologic research to provide a conceptual framework of the downward spiral leading to prescription opioid misuse and addiction among chronic pain patients receiving opioid analgesic pharmacotherapy. references.title: International Expert Consensus Document on Takotsubo Syndrome (Part I): Clinical Characteristics, Diagnostic Criteria, and Pathophysiology
references.abstract: Takotsubo syndrome (TTS) is a poorly recognized heart disease that was initially regarded as a benign condition. Recently, it has been shown that TTS may be associated with severe clinical complications including death and that its prevalence is probably underestimated. Since current guidelines on TTS are lacking, it appears timely and important to provide an expert consensus statement on TTS. The clinical expert consensus document part I summarizes the current state of knowledge on clinical presentation and characteristics of TTS and agrees on controversies surrounding TTS such as nomenclature, different TTS types, role of coronary artery disease, and etiology. This consensus also proposes new diagnostic criteria based on current knowledge to improve diagnostic accuracy.

references.abstract: Early detection of cardiovascular dysfunctions directly caused by acute ischemic stroke (AIS) has become paramount. Researchers now generally agree on the existence of a bidirectional interaction between the brain and the heart. In support of this theory, AIS patients are extremely vulnerable to severe cardiac complications. Sympathetic hyperactivity, hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis, the immune and inflammatory responses, and gut dysbiosis have been identified as the main pathological mechanisms involved in brain-heart axis dysregulation after AIS. Moreover, evidence has confirmed that the main causes of mortality after AIS include heart attack, congestive heart failure, hemodynamic instability, left ventricular systolic dysfunction, diastolic dysfunction, arrhythmias, electrocardiographic anomalies, and cardiac arrest, all of which are more or less associated with poor outcomes and death. references.authors: Sylvia Biso, Supakanya Wongrakpanich, Akanksha Agrawal
references.title: A Review of Neurogenic Stunned Myocardium
references.abstract: Neurologic stunned myocardium (NSM) is a phenomenon where neurologic events give rise to cardiac abnormalities. Neurologic events like stroke and seizures cause sympathetic storm and autonomic dysregulation that result in myocardial injury. The clinical presentation can involve troponin elevation, left ventricular dysfunction, and ECG changes. These findings are similar to Takotsubo cardiomyopathy and acute coronary syndrome. It is difficult to distinguish NSM from acute coronary syndrome based on clinical presentation alone. Because of this difficulty, a patient with NSM who is at high risk for coronary heart disease may undergo cardiac catheterization to rule out coronary artery disease. The objective of this review of literature is to enhance physician's awareness of NSM and its features to help tailor management according to the patient's clinical profile.

references.title: Sudden death: Neurogenic causes, prediction and prevention
references.abstract: Sudden death is a major health problem all over the world. The most common causes of sudden death are cardiac but there are also other causes such as neurological conditions (stroke, epileptic attacks and brain trauma), drugs, catecholamine toxicity, etc. A common feature of all these diverse pathologies underlying sudden death is the imbalance of the autonomic nervous system control of the cardiovascular system. This paper reviews different pathologies underlying sudden death with emphasis on the autonomic nervous system contribution, possibilities of early diagnosis and prognosis of sudden death using various clinical markers including autonomic markers (heart rate variability and baroreflex sensitivity), present possibilities of management and promising prevention by electrical neuromodulation.

references.abstract: Previous studies have established the importance of the insular cortex and temporal lobe in cardiovascular autonomic modulation. Some investigators, based on the results of cortical stimulation response, functional imaging, EEG recordings of seizures, and lesional studies, have suggested that cardiac sympathetic and parasympathetic function may be lateralized, with sympathetic representation lateralized to the right insula, and parasympathetic, to the left. These studies have suggested that ictal bradycardia is most commonly a manifestation of activation of the left temporal and insular cortex. However, the evidence for this is inconsistent. We sought to assess critically the predictable value of ictal bradycardia for seizure localization and lateralization. PhysioNet.coverage: MIMIC-IV includes tens of thousands of ICU patients with diagnosis codes; PhysioNet hosts stroke-adjacent HRV datasets
PhysioNet.how: MIMIC-IV can be filtered for stroke patients (ICD codes I63/I64) to extract ECG-derived HRV metrics and compare distributions against non-stroke controls. PhysioNet's 'Autonomic Aging' and 'Normal Sinus Rhythm' databases provide healthy baselines. Statistical distribution comparison (KL divergence, MMD) between stroke and healthy HRV feature spaces is directly computable. Limitation: lesion location/laterality not systematically recorded in MIMIC-IV.

NHANES.coverage: 50K+ participants per cycle; stroke history captured via questionnaire
NHANES.how: NHANES cycles (1999-2004 included HRV from 24-hr Holter monitoring) allow comparison of HRV metrics between self-reported stroke survivors and healthy controls. Can test whether stroke survivors occupy a statistically distinct HRV distribution. Limitation: no lesion location data, no EDA, cross-sectional only.

OpenNeuro.coverage: 900+ datasets; some include stroke patient neuroimaging
OpenNeuro.how: OpenNeuro contains stroke neuroimaging datasets (e.g., ds004169 stroke lesion atlas) but rarely co-registers autonomic physiological signals. Could provide lesion location data to cross-reference with external autonomic datasets, but cannot directly test the autonomic disruption claim alone.

DEAP.how: DEAP provides the healthy-population multimodal physiological + affective label baseline against which stroke patient distributions can be compared. Critically, DEAP involves minimal motor effort (passive viewing), so it represents the 'clean' affect-physiology mapping that c3 claims breaks down in stroke rehabilitation. Can be used to train a healthy-population classifier and then characterize its expected failure modes when applied to a motor+autonomic-confounded population. Cannot directly test the three-way confound — no stroke patients, no motor effort condition.

proposed.title: Systematic HRV Distribution Shift in Subacute-to-Chronic Stroke vs. Age-Sex-Matched Controls: A Multi-Site Cross-Sectional Study with Computational Pre-Validation
proposed.hypothesis_to_test: Stroke survivors in subacute (2–12 weeks) and chronic (>6 months) rehabilitation phases exhibit HRV distributions shifted relative to age-sex-matched healthy controls, with Bhattacharyya distance > 0.1 and Cohen's d > 0.3 for at least two of four metrics (SDNN, RMSSD, HF power, LF/HF ratio), and this shift is large enough to produce systematic bias when healthy-population-trained affective classifiers are applied to stroke patients.
proposed.method: Phase 1 (Computational Pilot, 3 months): Extract 5-minute resting HRV epochs from MIMIC-IV-ECG for ICD-10 coded ischemic (I63) and hemorrhagic (I60, I61) stroke admissions (estimated n=800–1,200) and age-sex-matched non-stroke controls from the same database. Compute SDNN, RMSSD, HF power, and LF/HF ratio. Calculate Bhattacharyya distance, Kullback-Leibler divergence, Cohen's d, and Mann-Whitney U statistics for each metric. Cross-validate against NHANES participants with self-reported stroke history vs. no stroke history. Phase 2 (Prospective Clinical Study, 18 months): Recruit 120 stroke survivors (60 subacute, 60 chronic) from inpatient and outpatient rehabilitation units at 2–3 sites, plus 120 age-sex-matched healthy controls. Record 24-hour Holter ECG and 5-minute laboratory resting ECG. Apply a commercially available healthy-population-trained affective HRV classifier (e.g., Empatica E4 SDK or comparable validated system) to both groups during standardized emotional stimuli (IAPS images, validated for stroke populations). Measure classifier output (arousal/valence estimates) and compare against ground truth from behavioral ratings and facial action coding. Compute distributional overlap metrics and classifier bias indices (systematic over/under-estimation of arousal).
measurements: SDNN (ms) — 5-minute and 24-hour epochs
RMSSD (ms) — 5-minute and 24-hour epochs
HF power (ms²) — spectral analysis 0.15–0.4 Hz
LF/HF ratio — spectral analysis
Bhattacharyya distance between stroke and control distributions for each metric
Kullback-Leibler divergence for each metric
Cohen's d effect sizes
Mann-Whitney U p-values with Bonferroni correction
Healthy-population classifier arousal/valence output in stroke vs. control during IAPS stimuli
Classifier bias index: mean signed error (classifier estimate minus behavioral ground truth)
Lesion location (insular vs. non-insular) from clinical MRI reports
Time post-stroke (days)
Stroke severity (NIHSS at enrollment)
Autonomic medications (beta-blockers, antihypertensives) as covariates
proposed.what_makes_it_audacious: Despite decades of post-stroke cardiac autonomic literature, nobody has explicitly framed the distribution shift as a classifier bias problem — connecting the autonomic neurology literature to the affective computing literature. The assumption being challenged is that HRV-based affective classifiers trained on healthy populations are 'good enough' for clinical stroke populations. This experiment makes that assumption empirically testable and quantifies the bias magnitude for the first time. The computational pilot using MIMIC-IV-ECG can be run immediately with existing data before a single patient is recruited.
proposed.expected_if_true: Bhattacharyya distance > 0.1 for SDNN and RMSSD; Cohen's d > 0.5 (medium effect); healthy-population classifier systematically overestimates arousal in stroke patients by >1 SD on a normalized scale; insular lesion subgroup shows largest distributional shift.
proposed.expected_if_false: Bhattacharyya distances < 0.05 across all metrics, indicating negligible distributional shift. This would be a landmark null finding: it would mean post-stroke autonomic changes are not large enough to bias HRV-based affective classifiers, substantially simplifying the clinical translation problem and redirecting research toward other confounds (motor artifact, medication). Still highly publishable as a reassurance study for the affective computing field.
required_expertise: HRV signal processing and spectral analysis
Affective computing and physiological classifier design

data_availability.computational_proxy: Yes — MIMIC-IV-ECG (PhysioNet) contains ECG waveforms with ICD-10 codes; NHANES 2011–2014 contains HRV variables and self-reported stroke history. Estimated stroke cases in MIMIC-IV-ECG: 800–1,500. NHANES stroke-positive participants: ~400–600 with HRV data.
data_availability.pilot_feasibility: Full computational pilot is runnable in 2–4 weeks with Python (neurokit2, scipy). Pilot answers: does the distributional shift exist at population level? Full experiment additionally answers: does the shift bias affective classifiers in real-time, and does lesion location moderate the effect?

proposed.title: Lateralized Autonomic Asymmetry in Acute-to-Subacute Stroke: Right vs. Left Hemispheric Lesion Effects on HRV and Baroreflex Sensitivity
proposed.hypothesis_to_test: Right hemispheric stroke produces greater sympathetic hyperactivation (elevated LF/HF ratio, reduced baroreflex sensitivity) than left hemispheric stroke of matched volume, consistent with right-hemispheric predominance in cardiac sympathetic control, with the lateralization effect surviving adjustment for lesion volume and NIHSS severity.
proposed.method: Retrospective-prospective hybrid design. Phase 1 (Retrospective): Query MIMIC-IV-ECG for patients with acute ischemic stroke (I63) who have both ECG data and available imaging reports. Use NLP extraction (scispaCy) on radiology reports to classify lesions as right-hemispheric, left-hemispheric, bilateral, or brainstem/cerebellar. Extract HRV metrics from the first 24-hour ECG epoch post-admission. Phase 2 (Prospective): Recruit 80 subacute stroke patients (40 right-hemisphere, 40 left-hemisphere, confirmed by MRI DWI with lesion volume quantified via FSL or FreeSurfer lesion tools) at 2 stroke rehabilitation centers. Record 24-hour Holter ECG at weeks 2, 6, and 12 post-stroke. Measure baroreflex sensitivity (BRS) using the sequence method from continuous beat-to-beat blood pressure (Finapres or Task Force Monitor) and simultaneous ECG. Compute time-domain HRV (SDNN, RMSSD), frequency-domain HRV (LF, HF, LF/HF), and BRS. Use linear mixed models with hemisphere (right/left) × time interaction, covarying for lesion volume, NIHSS, age, sex, and autonomic medications.
measurements: SDNN, RMSSD (ms) at weeks 2, 6, 12
LF power, HF power, LF/HF ratio at each timepoint
Baroreflex sensitivity (ms/mmHg) via sequence method
Lesion hemisphere (right/left/bilateral) from MRI DWI
Lesion volume (cm³) from FSL FAST segmentation
Insular cortex involvement (binary, from MRI report NLP)
NIHSS score at enrollment and each timepoint
24-hour mean heart rate and heart rate variability
QTc interval (surrogate for sympathetic cardiac influence)
Plasma catecholamines (norepinephrine, epinephrine) at week 2 in prospective arm
Autonomic medication inventory (beta-blockers, ACE inhibitors, etc.)
proposed.what_makes_it_audacious: The hemispheric lateralization hypothesis (Oppenheimer, Sander, Naver) has been discussed theoretically for 30 years but never tested with the statistical rigor and sample sizes needed to survive covariate adjustment for lesion volume. The assumption being challenged is that 'hemisphere' is the relevant unit — it may be that insular involvement, not hemisphere per se, drives the autonomic asymmetry. This experiment can dissociate those two explanations. The MIMIC-IV retrospective arm can be run immediately as a computational pilot.
proposed.expected_if_true: Right-hemisphere stroke patients show LF/HF ratio elevated by ≥0.5 units and BRS reduced by ≥3 ms/mmHg relative to left-hemisphere patients at week 2, with the difference attenuating but remaining significant at week 12. Insular involvement moderates the effect.
proposed.expected_if_false: No significant hemisphere × HRV interaction after covarying for lesion volume and NIHSS. This would suggest that lesion size and severity, not lateralization, drive post-stroke autonomic derangement — a finding that would redirect clinical monitoring protocols away from hemisphere-based risk stratification toward severity-based approaches, with major implications for post-stroke cardiac monitoring guidelines.

data_availability.computational_proxy: MIMIC-IV-ECG with ICD-10 I63 codes and radiology NLP extraction. Estimated n=500–900 with usable ECG and imaging reports. GTEx does not apply. The retrospective MIMIC arm can test the lateralization hypothesis at population scale before prospective recruitment. Pilot answers: is there a signal in administrative data? Full experiment additionally answers: does BRS (not just HRV) show lateralization, and does it persist longitudinally?

proposed.title: Signal Space Overlap Between Insular Stroke Autonomic Activation and Emotional Arousal: A Within-Subject Dissociation Experiment
proposed.hypothesis_to_test: In stroke patients with insular cortex involvement, resting-state EDA and HRV signals occupy the same multivariate signal space as emotional arousal signals in healthy controls, creating a systematic signal identity confound that is quantifiably more severe than in non-insular stroke patients or healthy controls.
proposed.method: Three-group cross-sectional study: (A) insular stroke patients (MRI-confirmed insular involvement, n=30), (B) non-insular stroke patients (matched volume, no insular involvement, n=30), (C) age-sex-matched healthy controls (n=30). All participants undergo a standardized 90-minute protocol: (1) 10-minute resting baseline; (2) emotionally neutral cognitive task (digit span); (3) standardized emotional arousal induction (validated film clips: neutral, positive, negative, high-arousal); (4) second resting baseline. Simultaneously record ECG (HRV), EDA (wrist-worn), and facial EMG (zygomaticus, corrugator). Extract EDA features (SCR amplitude, SCL, SCR frequency), HRV features (SDNN, RMSSD, LF/HF), and facial EMG features. Train a Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) on healthy control emotional arousal data (high-arousal vs. low-arousal states). Apply this GMM to the resting-state data of insular stroke patients, non-insular stroke patients, and healthy controls. Quantify what fraction of resting-state samples from each group fall within the high-arousal cluster of the healthy-control GMM. Use Mahalanobis distance to quantify signal space overlap between resting stroke physiology and healthy-control arousal states.
measurements: EDA: skin conductance level (SCL, µS), SCR amplitude (µS), SCR frequency (events/min)
HRV: SDNN, RMSSD, LF power, HF power, LF/HF ratio
Facial EMG: zygomaticus and corrugator mean amplitude during emotion clips
Mahalanobis distance from each participant's resting-state feature vector to healthy-control high-arousal GMM centroid
Fraction of resting-state windows classified as 'high arousal' by healthy-control GMM
Insular lesion volume (cm³) and laterality from MRI
Plasma norepinephrine at rest (sympathetic tone biomarker)
Self-reported arousal during rest (Visual Analogue Scale — adapted for aphasia)
NIHSS and Barthel Index
Classifier confusion matrix: healthy-population arousal classifier applied to all three groups
proposed.what_makes_it_audacious: Nobody has directly measured whether the autonomic signal produced by insular stroke damage is geometrically indistinguishable from emotional arousal in the feature space used by affective classifiers. The insular cortex literature and the affective computing literature have never been brought into the same experiment. The assumption being challenged is that 'resting state' is a clean baseline in stroke patients — this experiment tests whether insular damage makes the resting state physiologically mimic arousal, making affective computing fundamentally ambiguous in this population.
proposed.expected_if_true: Insular stroke patients' resting-state EDA/HRV vectors fall within the healthy-control high-arousal GMM cluster at a rate ≥3× higher than healthy controls' resting state (e.g., 45% vs. 15% of windows classified as high-arousal). Mahalanobis distance from insular stroke resting state to healthy-control arousal centroid is significantly smaller than from non-insular stroke or healthy control resting state.
proposed.expected_if_false: Insular stroke resting-state signals are not closer to the healthy-control arousal cluster than non-insular stroke or healthy control resting signals. This would mean the signal identity problem is not insular-lesion-specific, suggesting the confound is a general post-stroke phenomenon rather than an insular-specific one — redirecting intervention design toward stroke-wide rather than lesion-targeted calibration strategies.
required_expertise: Psychophysiology (EDA, HRV, facial EMG recording and analysis)
Affective computing and machine learning (GMM, Mahalanobis distance)

data_availability.computational_proxy: Partial — DEAP dataset contains EDA/HRV during emotional stimuli in healthy controls and can be used to build the reference GMM. MIMIC-IV-ECG can provide resting HRV distributions for stroke patients. However, the critical within-subject dissociation (resting stroke physiology vs. emotional arousal in the same individuals) requires the prospective study. Pilot: build healthy-control arousal GMM from DEAP, then project MIMIC-IV stroke resting HRV into that space to estimate overlap — runnable in 2–3 weeks.

proposed.title: Muscle Synergy Stability Under Autonomic Perturbation in Stroke vs. Healthy Adults: Testing the Stroke-Robust Motor Effort Channel Hypothesis
proposed.hypothesis_to_test: EMG-derived muscle synergy weights (W matrix from NMF decomposition) are significantly less sensitive to autonomic state fluctuations (induced by sympathetic activation) than raw EMG amplitude in stroke patients with spasticity, providing a more stable motor effort signal that can be partially dissociated from autonomic confounds.
proposed.method: Within-subject crossover experiment in three groups: (A) chronic stroke with spasticity (Modified Ashworth Scale 1–3, n=25), (B) chronic stroke without spasticity (MAS 0, n=25), (C) age-matched healthy controls (n=25). Each participant completes two sessions (counterbalanced): (1) sympathetic activation condition: cold pressor test (hand in 4°C water for 90 seconds) followed immediately by a standardized upper-limb reaching task; (2) autonomic baseline condition: thermoneutral hand immersion followed by the same reaching task. During the reaching task, record 8-channel surface EMG from upper limb muscles (biceps, triceps, anterior/posterior deltoid, pectoralis major, infraspinatus, flexor carpi radialis, extensor carpi radialis). Extract: (a) raw EMG amplitude (RMS per channel), (b) muscle synergy weights (W) and activation coefficients (H) via non-negative matrix factorization (NMF, r=3–5 synergies). Measure HRV and EDA continuously to confirm sympathetic activation during cold pressor. Primary outcome: intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) of synergy weights W between cold-pressor and baseline conditions (high ICC = stable synergy structure despite autonomic perturbation). Secondary outcome: ICC of raw EMG amplitude between conditions. Test whether ICC(W) > ICC(raw EMG) in stroke patients specifically.
measurements: 8-channel surface EMG RMS amplitude per muscle per condition
NMF synergy weights W (muscle × synergy matrix) per condition
NMF activation coefficients H per condition
Synergy weight ICC between cold-pressor and baseline conditions
Raw EMG amplitude ICC between cold-pressor and baseline conditions
Number of synergies (r) explaining ≥90% variance per condition
Synergy similarity index (cosine similarity of W matrices between conditions)
HRV metrics (SDNN, LF/HF) confirming sympathetic activation during cold pressor
EDA (SCL) confirming sympathetic activation
Modified Ashworth Scale score per muscle group
Spasticity-related EMG artifact index (co-contraction ratio at rest)
Reaching task kinematics (wrist trajectory smoothness via accelerometer)
Time post-stroke and NIHSS
proposed.what_makes_it_audacious: The synergy literature and the autonomic physiology literature have never been crossed. The assumption being challenged is that muscle synergies are 'motor primitives' independent of autonomic state — nobody has tested whether sympathetic activation destabilizes synergy structure, and nobody has tested this specifically in the stroke spasticity context where both motor and autonomic signals are simultaneously degraded. The Cheung (2009) synergy merging finding implies stroke changes synergy structure, but the question of whether the remaining synergies are autonomic-state-stable has never been asked.
proposed.expected_if_true: Synergy weight ICC(W) ≥ 0.85 across cold-pressor vs. baseline in all groups; raw EMG amplitude ICC ≤ 0.65 in stroke-with-spasticity group. The gap between ICC(W) and ICC(raw EMG) is largest in the spasticity group, confirming synergy decomposition as a stroke-robust motor effort channel.
proposed.expected_if_false: ICC(W) and ICC(raw EMG) are not significantly different, or synergy weights are MORE destabilized by autonomic perturbation in stroke patients than in healthy controls. This would mean synergy decomposition does not provide autonomic robustness in stroke — a critical negative finding that would rule out the proposed multi-modal framework's motor channel and redirect the field toward alternative motor effort proxies (e.g., kinematic-only measures).
required_expertise: Motor control neuroscience (muscle synergy analysis, NMF)

data_availability.computational_proxy: Partial — NinaPro database contains multi-channel EMG from stroke and healthy subjects during hand/arm movements. PhysioNet contains some combined EMG+HRV datasets. However, the critical manipulation (sympathetic activation via cold pressor during motor task) requires prospective data collection. Pilot: use NinaPro stroke data to compare synergy weight stability across sessions (test-retest as a proxy for perturbation stability) before running the cold-pressor experiment.

proposed.title: Longitudinal HRV Trajectory Mapping in Stroke Rehabilitation: Non-Monotonic Recovery and Within-Patient Drift Quantification
proposed.hypothesis_to_test: HRV recovery trajectories in stroke survivors across 6 months of rehabilitation are non-monotonic (exhibiting at least one inflection point), with within-patient HRV baseline drift exceeding the between-session variability of healthy controls by a factor of ≥2, rendering static healthy-population classifier baselines clinically inadequate across rehabilitation timescales.
proposed.method: Prospective longitudinal cohort study: 80 subacute stroke survivors (NIHSS 4–20 at enrollment, 2–4 weeks post-stroke) recruited from 2 inpatient rehabilitation units. Participants wear a medical-grade wearable ECG monitor (e.g., Holter patch, Zio XT or equivalent) continuously for the first 2 weeks of each measurement month, at months 1, 2, 3, and 6 post-stroke. Additionally, 40 age-sex-matched healthy controls wear the same monitor at months 1 and 6 (to quantify healthy-population between-occasion variability). Extract daily HRV metrics (SDNN, RMSSD, HF power, LF/HF) from each 24-hour epoch. Fit individual-level growth curve models (multilevel spline regression) to each patient's HRV trajectory. Test for non-monotonicity by comparing linear vs. quadratic vs. cubic spline fits using AIC. Quantify within-patient drift as the standard deviation of daily RMSSD across the 6-month period. Compare within-patient drift magnitude to between-session variability in healthy controls. Apply a static healthy-population-trained HRV affective classifier (trained on month-1 data) to month-6 data and measure classification accuracy degradation as a function of individual drift magnitude.
measurements: Daily SDNN, RMSSD (ms) from 24-hour Holter epochs at months 1–6
Daily HF power, LF power, LF/HF ratio
Individual-level HRV trajectory shape (linear vs. non-monotonic, AIC comparison)
Within-patient RMSSD standard deviation across 6 months
Between-session RMSSD variability in healthy controls (months 1 vs. 6)
Drift ratio: within-patient stroke SD / healthy-control between-occasion SD
Static classifier accuracy at month 6 vs. month 1 (trained on month-1 data)
Functional Independence Measure (FIM) at each timepoint
NIHSS at each timepoint
Depression screening (PHQ-9 or VAMS for aphasic patients) at each timepoint
Autonomic medication changes across the study period
Rehabilitation intensity (therapy hours per week) as moderator
proposed.what_makes_it_audacious: Longitudinal HRV studies in stroke exist, but none have framed the trajectory as a concept drift problem for affective classifiers. The assumption being challenged is that HRV-based classifiers calibrated at one timepoint remain valid across rehabilitation. This experiment directly quantifies how fast a classifier 'expires' in stroke patients and whether non-monotonic trajectories (e.g., initial improvement followed by plateau or decline) make static calibration fundamentally inadequate. The concept drift framing is entirely novel in the stroke rehabilitation context.
proposed.expected_if_true: ≥60% of patients show non-monotonic HRV trajectories (quadratic or cubic fit preferred over linear by AIC); within-patient RMSSD SD across 6 months exceeds healthy-control between-occasion SD by ≥2×; static classifier accuracy degrades by ≥15 percentage points from month 1 to month 6, with degradation magnitude correlating with individual drift (r > 0.4).
proposed.expected_if_false: HRV trajectories are predominantly monotonic (linear recovery); within-patient drift is comparable to healthy-control between-occasion variability; static classifier accuracy does not significantly degrade across 6 months. This would be a reassuring finding for the field — it would mean that a single calibration session is sufficient for 6-month deployment, substantially reducing the clinical burden of adaptive systems.
required_expertise: HRV signal processing and longitudinal analysis
Growth curve modeling and multilevel statistics
Wearable sensor deployment in clinical populations

data_availability.computational_proxy: MIMIC-IV-ECG contains serial ECG recordings for some stroke patients during hospitalization (days 1–14), enabling a short-term trajectory pilot. UK Biobank contains longitudinal HRV data in a general population (not stroke-specific) for healthy-control drift benchmarking. Pilot: extract MIMIC-IV serial HRV from stroke admissions to characterize short-term (days 1–14) trajectory shape before committing to 6-month prospective study. Answers: is non-monotonicity present in the acute phase? Full study answers: does it persist across rehabilitation timescales?

proposed.title: Hierarchical Ground Truth Acquisition for Affective State in Aphasic Stroke Patients: Validating Multi-Modal Behavioral Proxies Against Aphasia-Compatible Self-Report
proposed.hypothesis_to_test: A hierarchical ground-truth acquisition strategy combining aphasia-compatible self-report (Visual Analogue Mood Scale), observer-rated facial action coding (FACS), and behavioral proxies (engagement duration, task withdrawal) produces internally consistent affective state labels in stroke patients with aphasia, with inter-rater reliability κ > 0.6 and convergent validity r > 0.5 between VAMS and FACS-derived affect ratings.
proposed.method: Cross-sectional validation study in 60 stroke patients stratified by aphasia severity (20 no aphasia, 20 mild-moderate aphasia [WAB-R AQ 50–93], 20 severe aphasia [WAB-R AQ < 50]) and 20 healthy controls. Each participant undergoes a 60-minute standardized session: (1) baseline rest; (2) positive emotional induction (personally meaningful photographs, music); (3) frustration induction (unsolvable puzzle adapted for motor impairment); (4) recovery rest. Ground truth is acquired simultaneously via: (a) VAMS (self-report, administered with pointing response for aphasic patients); (b) Stroke Aphasic Depression Questionnaire (SADQ, observer-rated); (c) FACS coding of video-recorded facial expressions by two certified FACS coders blind to condition; (d) behavioral proxies (task engagement duration, withdrawal attempts, vocalizations coded for valence). Physiological signals (ECG, EDA, wrist PPG) are recorded throughout. Primary analyses: (1) inter-rater reliability between FACS coders (Cohen's κ); (2) convergent validity between VAMS and FACS ratings (Pearson r, stratified by aphasia severity); (3) temporal alignment analysis: do behavioral proxies (event-level) correlate with session-level VAMS ratings? (4) test whether physiological signals predict FACS-coded affect better than VAMS in severe aphasia.
measurements: VAMS scores (0–100 mm) for happiness, sadness, anxiety, anger at each condition
SADQ total score and subscale scores
FACS action unit frequencies and intensities per 30-second epoch (two independent coders)
Inter-rater reliability: Cohen's κ for FACS affect categories
Convergent validity: Pearson r between VAMS and FACS-derived affect ratings
Behavioral proxies: task engagement duration (seconds), withdrawal attempts (count), vocalization valence codes
Temporal alignment: correlation between event-level behavioral proxies and session-level VAMS
WAB-R Aphasia Quotient (aphasia severity)
ECG-derived HRV metrics per condition
EDA (SCL, SCR) per condition
Wrist PPG-derived HRV per condition
Classifier performance: physiological signal prediction of FACS vs. VAMS labels, stratified by aphasia severity
proposed.what_makes_it_audacious: Affective computing validation studies universally rely on self-report ground truth, which is unavailable or unreliable in severe aphasia — yet no study has systematically validated a hierarchical multi-modal ground truth strategy specifically for this population. The assumption being challenged is that ground truth acquisition is a solved problem. This experiment tests whether FACS and behavioral proxies can substitute for self-report in severe aphasia, and whether the substitution introduces systematic bias. The temporal scale mismatch (event-level proxies vs. session-level ratings) is a methodological problem that has never been formally characterized.
proposed.expected_if_true: FACS-VAMS convergent validity r > 0.6 in no-aphasia and mild-aphasia groups; r remains > 0.4 in severe aphasia; inter-rater FACS κ > 0.7; behavioral proxies correlate with session-level VAMS at r > 0.5 in no-aphasia group but decline to r < 0.3 in severe aphasia, quantifying the temporal mismatch problem.
proposed.expected_if_false: FACS-VAMS convergent validity r < 0.3 even in no-aphasia group, or inter-rater FACS κ < 0.5. This would indicate that FACS coding is not a valid substitute for self-report even in non-aphasic stroke patients — a finding that would fundamentally challenge the feasibility of affective computing validation in stroke rehabilitation and redirect the field toward purely physiological or caregiver-report approaches.

data_availability.computational_proxy: Limited — DEAP and MAHNOB-HCI contain FACS + physiological data in healthy subjects and can be used to benchmark FACS-physiology relationships before the stroke study. No public dataset contains FACS + VAMS + aphasia severity in stroke patients. Pilot: use DEAP to establish expected FACS-HRV correlations in healthy subjects as a reference benchmark, then compare against stroke patient data to quantify degradation.

proposed.title: Prospective Validation of Adaptive vs. Static Affective Classifiers in Stroke Rehabilitation: First Benchmark Study
proposed.hypothesis_to_test: Within-subject adaptive affective classifiers (initialized with stroke-specific Bayesian priors and updated with session-level ground truth) achieve ≥15 percentage points higher classification accuracy than healthy-population transfer baselines in stroke rehabilitation patients, with the accuracy gap increasing as a function of time post-stroke and autonomic drift magnitude.
proposed.method: Randomized crossover trial (classifier comparison, not treatment randomization): 50 chronic stroke patients (≥6 months post-stroke, NIHSS 2–15) enrolled in outpatient rehabilitation. Each patient attends 8 weekly sessions. At each session, ECG, EDA, and wrist PPG are recorded during a standardized 45-minute protocol including rest, cognitive tasks, and motor rehabilitation exercises. Ground truth affective labels are acquired using the hierarchical strategy validated in the c6 experiment (VAMS + FACS for non-aphasic; FACS + behavioral proxies for aphasic). Two classifier systems are compared within each patient (counterbalanced order, sessions 1–4 vs. 5–8): (A) Static transfer baseline: healthy-population-trained classifier (trained on DEAP/MAHNOB-HCI, no patient-specific adaptation); (B) Adaptive classifier: Bayesian logistic regression initialized with stroke-cohort priors (derived from the c1 and c5 experiments) and updated online using session-level ground truth labels via variational Bayes. Primary outcome: classification accuracy (F1 score for arousal high/low, valence positive/negative) per session per classifier. Secondary outcomes: accuracy trajectory across sessions (does adaptive classifier improve over time?), accuracy stratified by hemiparesis severity (mild-moderate MAS 0–1 vs. severe MAS 2–3), and accuracy as a function of individual autonomic drift magnitude.
measurements: F1 score for arousal classification (high/low) per session per classifier
F1 score for valence classification (positive/negative) per session per classifier
Accuracy trajectory across 8 sessions (learning curve for adaptive classifier)
Classifier accuracy stratified by hemiparesis severity (MAS score)
Classifier accuracy stratified by aphasia presence/absence
Individual autonomic drift magnitude (RMSSD SD across 8 sessions) as moderator
Bayesian prior update magnitude per session (quantifying how much the adaptive classifier changes)
Confusion matrix: false positive rate for high-arousal classification in stroke patients
Ground truth label quality: FACS inter-rater κ per session
NIHSS, FIM, and Barthel Index at enrollment
Time post-stroke
Sensor configuration feasibility: data completeness rates for ECG, EDA, PPG across sessions
proposed.what_makes_it_audacious: This is the first prospective benchmark study of affective classifier performance in stroke rehabilitation — the entire empirical foundation for this field does not yet exist. The assumption being challenged is that transfer learning from healthy populations is 'good enough' for clinical deployment. This experiment produces the first empirical answer to that question and establishes the performance floor and ceiling for the field. Even if the adaptive classifier does not outperform the static baseline, the benchmark data (accuracy, confusion matrices, drift-accuracy relationships) will define the field's starting point for the next decade.
proposed.expected_if_true: Adaptive classifier achieves F1 ≥ 0.70 by session 4; static transfer baseline achieves F1 ≤ 0.55 throughout; accuracy gap ≥ 0.15 F1 units; gap is larger in patients with higher autonomic drift (r > 0.4 between drift magnitude and accuracy gap); accuracy gap is larger in severe hemiparesis (MAS 2–3) than mild (MAS 0–1).
proposed.expected_if_false: Adaptive and static classifiers achieve similar F1 scores (difference < 0.05), or both perform near chance (F1 < 0.55). The former would suggest that stroke-specific adaptation is unnecessary — healthy-population models transfer adequately — a finding that would dramatically simplify clinical deployment. The latter would indicate that affective classification from HRV/EDA is fundamentally infeasible in stroke rehabilitation, redirecting the field toward alternative modalities (facial, vocal, kinematic).
required_expertise: Affective computing and machine learning (Bayesian adaptive classifiers, online learning)
Biostatistics (mixed models, F1 score trajectory analysis)

data_availability.computational_proxy: DEAP and MAHNOB-HCI provide healthy-population training data for the static transfer baseline. MIMIC-IV-ECG provides stroke-population HRV distributions for Bayesian prior initialization. The adaptive classifier architecture can be prototyped and tested on DEAP data (simulating concept drift by training on one subject subset and testing on another) before deployment. Pilot answers: does the Bayesian adaptation algorithm converge in a reasonable number of sessions? Full study answers: does it outperform static transfer in real stroke patients with real ground truth.

feasibility.experiment_title: Systematic HRV Distribution Shift in Subacute-to-Chronic Stroke vs. Age-Sex-Matched Controls: A Multi-Site Cross-Sectional Study with Computational Pre-Validation

required: 24-hour Holter ECG monitors (minimum 10 units for rolling recruitment)
Laboratory-grade ECG acquisition system (5-minute resting recordings)
IAPS image display system (calibrated monitor, standardized viewing distance)
Facial action coding system or automated FACS software (e.g., iMotions, OpenFace)
Empatica E4 or comparable wrist-worn physiological sensor with SDK access
Secure clinical data server for multi-site data aggregation
High-performance computing access for MIMIC-IV-ECG BigQuery queries and HRV batch processing
equipment.availability: All equipment is commercially available and present in most clinical research cardiology or rehabilitation medicine labs. Holter monitors are standard clinical equipment. IAPS license requires institutional application but is routinely granted. BigQuery access to MIMIC-IV-ECG requires PhysioNet credentialing (free, ~1 week turnaround). No exotic or custom hardware required.
equipment.cost_estimate: Phase 1 computational pilot: ~$500–2,000 (cloud compute for BigQuery, analyst time). Phase 2 clinical study: $150,000–350,000 total (Holter monitors $5,000–15,000, participant compensation $30,000–60,000, research coordinator salaries dominate, multi-site coordination overhead, affective computing software licenses $5,000–20,000). Total grant budget: $200,000–400,000 over 2 years.

required: HRV signal processing specialist (neurokit2/Python or MATLAB HRV toolbox proficiency)
Stroke rehabilitation physician or neurologist (patient eligibility, NIHSS scoring)
Clinical research coordinator with IRB/consent experience in stroke populations
Affective computing researcher familiar with IAPS paradigms and physiological classifiers
Biostatistician with distributional comparison methods expertise (Bhattacharyya, KL divergence)
Neuroimaging reader for lesion localization from clinical MRI reports
Data engineer for MIMIC-IV BigQuery extraction and NHANES linkage
expertise.rarity: This specific combination is uncommon but achievable. Cardiac autonomic neurology labs exist at most academic medical centers. The affective computing + stroke rehabilitation crossover is rare — perhaps 15–30 labs globally have all components. However, the experiment can be assembled from collaborators across departments (neurology + biomedical engineering + psychology) without requiring a single lab to have all expertise. The computational pilot requires only HRV signal processing and biostatistics skills, available at hundreds of institutions.

sample.type: Phase 1: Retrospective EHR/waveform cohort from MIMIC-IV-ECG (hospitalized patients with ICD-10 stroke codes I60, I61, I63) and NHANES participants with self-reported stroke history. Phase 2: Prospective recruitment of stroke survivors in subacute (2–12 weeks post-stroke) and chronic (>6 months post-stroke) rehabilitation phases from inpatient and outpatient rehabilitation units, plus age-sex-matched healthy community controls.
sample.size: Phase 1: Estimated 800–1,500 stroke cases in MIMIC-IV-ECG with extractable ECG waveforms; 400–600 NHANES stroke-positive participants with HRV variables. Controls matched 1:1 from same databases. Phase 2: 120 stroke survivors (60 subacute, 60 chronic) + 120 matched controls = 240 total. Power justification: with Cohen's d = 0.5 (medium effect, conservative estimate), alpha = 0.05, power = 0.80, two-sample t-test requires n = 64 per group; 60 per subgroup provides adequate power with Bonferroni correction across 4 HRV metrics requiring d ≈ 0.6 per metric. Attrition buffer of 20% already factored into 60-per-subgroup target.
sample.ethical_concerns: Phase 1 is retrospective de-identified data — MIMIC-IV and NHANES are both publicly available under data use agreements, minimal IRB burden (likely exempt or expedited review). Phase 2 requires full IRB approval: stroke patients are a vulnerable population with potential cognitive and communication impairments affecting consent capacity. Surrogate consent procedures may be needed for subacute patients. IAPS stimuli include emotionally negative images — distress monitoring protocol required. Exclusion criteria must address post-stroke depression, aphasia severity, and cardiac devices (pacemakers invalidate HRV). Multi-site coordination requires IRB reliance agreements. These are manageable but non-trivial ethical requirements.

feasibility.timeline: Month 1–3: IRB submissions, MIMIC-IV credentialing, NHANES data download, Phase 1 computational pilot execution. Month 4–6: Phase 1 analysis complete, manuscript drafted, Phase 2 site setup and staff training. Month 7–24: Phase 2 prospective recruitment and data collection (18-month window for 240 participants across 2–3 sites). Month 25–30: Phase 2 analysis, classifier bias quantification, manuscript preparation. Total: approximately 30 months from funding to submitted results. Realistically 3 years to publication.
simplification_options: Run Phase 1 computational pilot only as a standalone publication: MIMIC-IV-ECG + NHANES analysis answers the primary distributional shift question with no patient recruitment, no IRB burden beyond data use agreements, and can be completed in 2–4 months. This is publishable independently and de-risks the full study.

Replace 24-hour Holter with 5-minute resting ECG only: reduces equipment cost and participant burden substantially, still captures SDNN, RMSSD, HF power, LF/HF for the primary hypothesis. Loses circadian HRV information but preserves core distributional comparison.

Drop the affective classifier validation component (Phase 2 IAPS paradigm) and focus solely on HRV distributional characterization: simpler design, faster IRB approval, no need for affective computing expertise or IAPS license. Answers whether the shift exists; defers the classifier bias question to a follow-up study.

Single-site design with 80 participants (40 stroke, 40 controls) to establish proof-of-concept before multi-site expansion: reduces coordination overhead and cost by ~50%, still adequately powered for d = 0.6.

Use wrist-worn consumer devices (Empatica E4, Polar H10) instead of clinical Holter monitors for the chronic outpatient group: reduces equipment cost and enables remote data collection, though signal quality is lower and requires validation against clinical ECG in a subset.
killer_risks: MIMIC-IV-ECG recording duration problem: MIMIC-IV-ECG contains 10-second diagnostic ECGs, not 5-minute recordings. Frequency-domain HRV (HF power, LF/HF ratio) requires minimum 2–5 minutes of stationary RR intervals. This makes the computational pilot's spectral HRV analysis unreliable or impossible from MIMIC-IV-ECG alone. Time-domain metrics (SDNN, RMSSD) from 10-second recordings are non-standard and not comparable to clinical 5-minute norms. This is a fundamental methodological constraint that must be addressed upfront.

NHANES HRV data limitations: NHANES HRV examination data (available in 2011–2014 cycles) uses a specific 2-minute resting ECG protocol with its own normative values. Self-reported stroke history in NHANES has low sensitivity and does not capture stroke timing (subacute vs. chronic) or severity. The NHANES proxy is weaker than the proposal implies.

Medication confounding: Beta-blockers and antihypertensives are nearly universal in post-stroke patients and profoundly suppress HRV. If the distributional shift is primarily medication-driven rather than neurological, the finding is clinically real but mechanistically different from autonomic dysregulation. Disentangling this requires large enough subgroups of medication-free or medication-naive patients, which may be impossible in stroke populations.

Cognitive and communication impairments in subacute stroke patients: Aphasia, neglect, and cognitive deficits may prevent reliable behavioral ratings of IAPS stimuli (the ground truth for classifier bias assessment). If ground truth is unreliable, the classifier bias index is uninterpretable. The study may need to exclude patients with significant aphasia, which biases the sample toward milder strokes.

Affective classifier access and reproducibility: Commercial affective HRV classifiers (Empatica SDK) may not be publicly documented, may change between software versions, and may not be independently replicable. If the classifier is a black box, the bias index cannot be decomposed or generalized. The study should pre-register the specific classifier version and algorithm.

Selection bias in rehabilitation recruitment: Patients enrolled in rehabilitation programs are systematically healthier and less severely affected than the full stroke population. The distributional shift may be underestimated relative to acute or severely affected patients.

Heterogeneity of stroke: Ischemic vs. hemorrhagic, cortical vs. subcortical, insular vs. non-insular lesions have very different autonomic profiles. With n=60 per subgroup, there is insufficient power to test lesion-location moderation (insular vs. non-insular) as a secondary analysis without inflating Type I error.

public_datasets: MIMIC_IV_ECG: MIMIC-IV-ECG (PhysioNet/BigQuery) — 800K+ 12-lead ECG waveforms linked to MIMIC-IV clinical data with ICD-10 codes. Stroke cohort extractable via I60, I61, I63 codes. CRITICAL CAVEAT: recordings are 10-second diagnostic ECGs, not 5-minute resting recordings. Time-domain HRV (SDNN, RMSSD) from 10-second segments is non-standard; frequency-domain HRV is unreliable. Useful for RR interval distribution comparison and time-domain proxies only. Age, sex, and comorbidity matching possible from linked clinical data.

NHANES: NHANES 2011–2014 HRV examination data — contains SDNN, RMSSD, HF power, LF/HF ratio from 2-minute resting ECG protocol, plus self-reported stroke history (MCQ160f variable), demographics, and medication use. Approximately 400–600 stroke-positive participants with HRV data available. Enables distributional comparison of HRV metrics between stroke and non-stroke community-dwelling adults. Limitations: self-reported stroke (no imaging confirmation), no stroke timing, no severity data, 2-minute protocol differs from clinical 5-minute standard.
data_availability.proxy_description: A two-part computational proxy is feasible before any patient recruitment. Part A (MIMIC-IV-ECG): Extract RR interval sequences from 10-second ECGs for ICD-10 stroke cases (I60, I61, I63) and age-sex-matched non-stroke controls. Compute time-domain HRV metrics (RMSSD, pNN50, SDNN approximation) from 10-second segments. Calculate Bhattacharyya distance, KL divergence, and Cohen's d between stroke and control distributions. Acknowledge frequency-domain limitations explicitly. Part B (NHANES): Download NHANES 2011–2014 HRV examination files (publicly available, no credentialing required beyond data use agreement). Merge with MCQ160f (stroke history), demographics, and medication variables. Compute distributional overlap metrics for SDNN, RMSSD, HF power, and LF/HF ratio between stroke-positive and stroke-negative participants, stratified by age and sex. Run Mann-Whitney U tests with Bonferroni correction. Both analyses executable in Python (neurokit2, scipy, pandas) within 2–4 weeks. Together they provide population-level evidence for or against the distributional shift hypothesis across two independent datasets with different recording protocols.
data_availability.proxy_limitations: The computational proxy cannot answer: (1) whether the shift is present specifically in subacute vs. chronic rehabilitation phases (MIMIC-IV captures acute hospitalization; NHANES captures community-dwelling survivors of unknown chronicity); (2) whether the shift biases real-time affective classifiers during emotional stimuli — this requires the IAPS paradigm with behavioral ground truth; (3) whether insular lesion location moderates the shift (no imaging data in MIMIC-IV-ECG or NHANES at the required granularity); (4) whether 24-hour ambulatory HRV shows the same pattern as resting laboratory recordings; (5) medication effects cannot be fully controlled in NHANES due to limited pharmacological detail. The proxy establishes whether the distributional shift exists at population level; only the full prospective study establishes its clinical and affective computing implications.

feasibility.experiment_title: Lateralized Autonomic Asymmetry in Acute-to-Subacute Stroke: Right vs. Left Hemispheric Lesion Effects on HRV and Baroreflex Sensitivity

required: 24-hour Holter ECG recorder (3-lead or 12-lead)
Continuous beat-to-beat blood pressure monitor (Finapres NOVA or Task Force Monitor)
3T MRI scanner with DWI capability for lesion segmentation
FSL or FreeSurfer neuroimaging software suite
HRV analysis software (Kubios HRV or custom Python/MATLAB pipeline)
Sequence method BRS analysis software
Secure clinical data server for MIMIC-IV BigQuery access
NLP pipeline (scispaCy) for radiology report parsing
equipment.availability: Holter ECG and MRI are standard at stroke rehabilitation centers. Finapres/Task Force Monitor is less common but available at ~50-100 academic medical centers with autonomic labs. FSL/FreeSurfer are free software. BigQuery MIMIC-IV access requires PhysioNet credentialing (free, ~2 weeks). The bottleneck is co-locating continuous BP monitoring with stroke rehabilitation infrastructure.
equipment.cost_estimate: $180,000–$320,000 total for prospective arm (Holter equipment rental/purchase ~$20K, Finapres units ~$40K, MRI scan costs ~$60K for 80 patients x 3 timepoints if not covered by clinical care, personnel ~$120K over 2 years, biomarker assays ~$15K). Retrospective MIMIC arm: ~$5,000 (compute costs, personnel time).

required: Stroke neurologist with MRI lesion localization experience
Cardiac autonomic physiologist familiar with baroreflex sequence method
Neuroimaging analyst (FSL/FreeSurfer lesion segmentation)
HRV signal processing engineer
Clinical NLP developer (scispaCy, radiology report parsing)
Biostatistician with linear mixed models experience
Rehabilitation medicine physician for patient access and safety monitoring
IRB-experienced clinical research coordinator
expertise.rarity: The combination of stroke neurology + autonomic physiology + neuroimaging is rare. Roughly 15-25 academic centers worldwide have all three capabilities co-located. Individual expertise pools are larger but the intersection is the constraint. Groups at UCL, Mayo Clinic, Karolinska, and a handful of German stroke centers have published adjacent work.

sample.type: Adult patients with first-ever acute ischemic stroke confirmed by MRI DWI, classified as right-hemispheric or left-hemispheric (excluding bilateral and posterior fossa lesions), recruited at stroke rehabilitation centers during subacute phase (days 7-14 post-stroke)
sample.size: N=80 prospective (40 right, 40 left) provides ~80% power to detect a medium effect size (Cohen's d=0.65) for hemisphere × HRV interaction at alpha=0.05 in mixed models, assuming 15% attrition. This is likely underpowered for the insular cortex moderation analysis, which would require N=120-160 to detect interaction effects. The MIMIC retrospective arm may yield N=400-800 usable cases for HRV proxy analysis.
sample.ethical_concerns: Standard IRB approval required. Key concerns: (1) Capacity to consent in acute stroke patients with aphasia or cognitive impairment — requires surrogate consent protocols; (2) Continuous BP monitoring with Finapres is non-invasive but requires patient cooperation during subacute recovery; (3) Plasma catecholamine draws require venipuncture in a vulnerable population; (4) MIMIC-IV retrospective arm requires PhysioNet DUA but no additional IRB if using de-identified data. Overall: manageable but requires careful consent procedures and likely a DSMB for the prospective arm.

feasibility.timeline: Phase 1 (MIMIC retrospective): 4-6 months from credentialing to results. Phase 2 (prospective): 18-24 months recruitment + 3 months follow-up per patient + 6 months analysis = 30-36 months total. Full study from funding to publication: 3-4 years.
simplification_options: Run MIMIC-IV retrospective arm first as a standalone pilot (6 months, ~$10K) — if no signal in HRV lateralization in N=500+ patients, reconsider prospective investment
Drop plasma catecholamines to reduce invasiveness and cost (~$15K savings, simplifies IRB)
Reduce to 2 timepoints (week 2 and week 12) instead of 3 to cut 33% of follow-up burden

Use NHANES HRV data (SDNN, RMSSD, LF/HF available) with self-reported stroke (MCQ160f) as a population-level cross-sectional proxy — cannot lateralize but can establish HRV-stroke association magnitude
Limit to single-center with N=40 as a pilot feasibility study to establish effect size estimates before multi-center expansion
Replace Finapres continuous BP with oscillometric BRS estimation (less precise but widely available) to eliminate the specialized equipment bottleneck
killer_risks: Lesion heterogeneity: Right-hemisphere strokes are not anatomically uniform — MCA territory vs. watershed vs. lacunar infarcts have vastly different autonomic pathway involvement. N=40 per hemisphere may be insufficient to control for this, making the hemisphere × HRV interaction uninterpretable without stratification that the sample size cannot support.

Medication confounding: Post-stroke patients are heavily medicated with beta-blockers, ACE inhibitors, and antiarrhythmics that directly suppress HRV and BRS. Even with medication inventory as a covariate, differential prescribing by hemisphere (e.g., right-hemisphere patients with more cardiac complications receiving more beta-blockers) could mask or create spurious lateralization effects.

MIMIC-IV ECG limitation: MIMIC-IV-ECG records are 10-second diagnostic ECGs, not 24-hour Holter recordings. Frequency-domain HRV (LF, HF, LF/HF) requires minimum 5-minute recordings; 10-second ECGs yield only heart rate and limited time-domain metrics. The retrospective arm cannot test the primary frequency-domain hypothesis and may only provide weak HRV proxies.

NLP lateralization accuracy: scispaCy extraction of lesion laterality from radiology reports has unknown sensitivity/specificity in MIMIC-IV. Misclassification of hemisphere (e.g., bilateral lesions coded as unilateral, or watershed lesions with ambiguous laterality) will attenuate the effect toward null, potentially producing a false-negative result.

Attrition bias: Patients with the most severe right-hemisphere strokes (highest autonomic derangement) may be least able to complete 12-week follow-up due to mortality, medical complications, or inability to cooperate with Finapres monitoring. This survivorship bias would systematically underestimate the right-hemisphere autonomic effect.

Insular cortex moderation is underpowered: The most scientifically interesting question — whether insular involvement, not hemisphere per se, drives the effect — requires a 2x2 design (hemisphere × insular involvement) that needs N=160+ to detect interaction effects, making the N=80 prospective arm insufficient for this key dissociation.

public_datasets: MIMIC_IV_ECG: MIMIC-IV-ECG via PhysioNet/BigQuery — 800K+ 12-lead ECGs linked to MIMIC-IV clinical data with ICD-10 I63 stroke codes. Can extract time-domain HRV (SDNN, RMSSD from R-R intervals) from 10-second recordings as a proxy. Radiology reports accessible via MIMIC-IV-Note for NLP lateralization. Critical limitation: 10-second recordings preclude frequency-domain HRV and BRS computation. Estimated usable stroke cohort: 400-900 patients with both ECG and imaging reports.

NHANES: NHANES cycles 2011-2014 include resting HRV examination data (SDNN, RMSSD, LF power, HF power, LF/HF ratio from 2-minute ECG recordings) and self-reported stroke history (MCQ160f). Can test whether stroke survivors show different HRV profiles vs. controls at population scale. Cannot lateralize strokes. Provides population-level HRV-stroke effect size estimates to power the prospective study. N~200-400 stroke survivors across cycles.
data_availability.proxy_description: Two-stage computational proxy: (1) MIMIC-IV-ECG analysis: Extract all patients with ICD-10 I63.x codes who have ECG recordings within 48 hours of admission. Apply scispaCy NLP to MIMIC-IV radiology notes to classify lesion laterality (right/left/bilateral/posterior). Compute time-domain HRV metrics (SDNN, RMSSD, mean RR, pNN50) from available ECG recordings. Run linear regression: HRV ~ hemisphere + age + sex + NIHSS_proxy (e.g., ICU admission, mechanical ventilation as severity surrogates) + medication flags. (2) NHANES cross-sectional analysis: Compare HRV metrics (SDNN, RMSSD, LF/HF from examination data) between self-reported stroke survivors and matched controls, stratified by age, sex, and cardiovascular medication use. Estimate effect sizes for HRV depression post-stroke to inform prospective sample size calculations.
data_availability.proxy_limitations: The computational proxy cannot: (1) test frequency-domain HRV or LF/HF ratio with statistical validity from 10-second ECGs; (2) measure baroreflex sensitivity at all — BRS requires simultaneous continuous BP and ECG, unavailable in any public dataset; (3) lateralize strokes in NHANES (no imaging data); (4) test longitudinal recovery trajectories (MIMIC is cross-sectional at admission, NHANES is cross-sectional); (5) dissociate insular cortex involvement from hemisphere — the core scientific question. The proxy can only establish whether a gross HRV signal exists in administrative stroke data, not whether it is lateralized or mediated by insular involvement. Only the full prospective experiment with Holter + Finapres + MRI lesion segmentation can answer the primary hypothesis.

feasibility.experiment_title: Signal Space Overlap Between Insular Stroke Autonomic Activation and Emotional Arousal: A Within-Subject Dissociation Experiment

required: Clinical-grade ECG system (Holter or research-grade, e.g., Biopac, Shimmer)
Wrist-worn EDA sensor (e.g., Empatica E4 or Biopac EDA module)
Facial EMG electrodes and amplifier (Biopac MP150 or equivalent)
Validated emotion-induction film clip stimuli (IAPS-compatible or NAPS-E)
MRI access for lesion volume confirmation (clinical MRI already obtained for most stroke patients)
Plasma norepinephrine assay capability (ELISA or HPLC — requires clinical lab access)
Aphasia-compatible VAS materials
Workstation with MATLAB/Python for GMM, signal processing, Mahalanobis distance computation
Standardized quiet testing room with controlled lighting and temperature
equipment.availability: Most equipment is available in clinical research labs with psychophysiology capability. EDA and ECG systems are standard. Facial EMG is slightly less common but not rare. MRI data is typically already available from clinical workup. Plasma NE assay requires clinical biochemistry lab collaboration.
equipment.cost_estimate: $80,000–$180,000 total (personnel dominant; equipment ~$15,000–$40,000 if not already available; consumables ~$10,000; NE assays ~$5,000–$15,000; participant compensation ~$15,000–$25,000)

required: Stroke neurologist with neuroimaging lesion analysis capability (FSL/SPM lesion mapping)
Psychophysiologist experienced in EDA, HRV, and facial EMG acquisition and artifact rejection
Clinical neuropsychologist with aphasia assessment experience
Machine learning / affective computing researcher (GMM, Mahalanobis distance, classifier evaluation)
Autonomic neuroscience background for interpretation
Clinical research coordinator experienced with stroke patient populations
Biostatistician for mixed-effects and multivariate analyses
expertise.rarity: Moderate rarity — the combination of stroke neurology + psychophysiology + affective computing in a single team is uncommon. Probably 15–30 labs worldwide could assemble this team, concentrated at academic medical centers with both neurology and cognitive/affective neuroscience programs (e.g., UCSF, UCL, Karolinska, Toronto Rehab). The individual components are standard; the integration is the bottleneck.

sample.type: Three groups: (A) MRI-confirmed insular cortex stroke patients, (B) MRI-confirmed non-insular stroke patients matched for lesion volume, (C) age- and sex-matched healthy controls. All adults, post-acute phase (>2 weeks post-stroke to allow stable autonomic reorganization).
sample.size: N=30 per group (90 total) as proposed. Power justification: detecting a 3× difference in GMM classification rate (e.g., 45% vs. 15%) with 80% power and alpha=0.05 requires approximately 20–25 per group for a proportion comparison; n=30 provides reasonable buffer for dropout and subgroup analyses by lesion laterality. However, insular stroke with sufficient lesion volume and without severe aphasia/cognitive impairment is a constrained population — n=30 insular patients may require 18–24 months of recruitment at a high-volume stroke center.
sample.ethical_concerns: Moderate IRB complexity. Stroke patients are a vulnerable population requiring capacity assessment. Aphasia-compatible consent procedures needed. Emotion induction (negative/high-arousal film clips) requires careful risk-benefit justification in patients with potential emotional dysregulation post-stroke. Plasma draw requires additional consent. Facial EMG and physiological monitoring are non-invasive. Fatigue risk in 90-minute protocol for stroke patients — rest breaks and stopping criteria must be pre-specified. Overall approvable but requires careful protocol design.

feasibility.timeline: 30–42 months from funding to results: 3–4 months IRB and protocol finalization; 18–24 months recruitment (insular stroke group is rate-limiting); 3 months data processing and GMM analysis; 3–4 months statistical analysis and manuscript preparation.
simplification_options: Eliminate facial EMG and plasma NE in a pilot phase — focus on EDA and HRV only, reducing setup complexity and cost by ~30%
Reduce to two groups (insular stroke vs. healthy controls only) for initial proof-of-concept, adding non-insular stroke in a follow-up study
Shorten protocol to 45 minutes by removing the second resting baseline and one emotion condition, reducing patient burden and dropout
Use retrospective clinical MRI + existing Holter ECG data from stroke registries for HRV-only proxy before committing to full prospective study
Replace plasma NE with salivary alpha-amylase as a non-invasive sympathetic tone proxy
Use a pre-trained arousal classifier from DEAP rather than training a new GMM, reducing the healthy control arm to a validation role and cutting n to 60 total
killer_risks: Recruitment failure: insular stroke patients without severe aphasia, with sufficient lesion volume, in post-acute stable phase, willing to undergo 90-minute emotional protocol — this intersection may yield fewer than 30 eligible patients per year at a single site, requiring multi-site coordination

EDA signal quality in stroke patients: hemiplegia/hemiparesis may force wrist placement on the affected side (altered sympathetic innervation) or unaffected side (not reflecting insular-mediated changes) — laterality of EDA recording relative to lesion laterality is a major confound not fully addressed in the protocol

Emotional reactivity confound: insular stroke patients may have blunted emotional responses to film clips (alexithymia, emotional processing deficits post-stroke), making the 'emotional arousal' condition itself invalid in Group A — the GMM trained on healthy controls may not capture their arousal at all

GMM generalizability: DEAP has only 32 subjects watching music videos; a GMM trained on this may not generalize to the film clip stimuli used in this study, making the healthy-control reference space unstable

Lesion heterogeneity: insular strokes vary enormously in subregion (anterior vs. posterior insula), depth, and co-involvement of adjacent structures (basal ganglia, operculum) — n=30 may be underpowered to detect dose-response relationships with lesion volume/location
Protocol fatigue and dropout: 90 minutes is demanding for stroke patients; differential dropout between groups (sicker insular patients dropping out more) could bias results toward null

Signal space dimensionality: combining EDA, HRV, and EMG features creates a moderate-dimensional space (~10–15 features) with only 30 subjects per group — GMM fitting and Mahalanobis distance estimation may be unreliable without dimensionality reduction, which itself introduces analytical choices

public_datasets: DEAP: DEAP emotion dataset — contains GSR (EDA proxy) and peripheral physiology during emotional video stimuli in 32 healthy subjects with self-reported arousal/valence ratings. Directly usable to train the reference healthy-control arousal GMM in the proposed feature space (SCL, SCR amplitude, SCR frequency). Core computational proxy dataset.

MIMIC_IV_ECG: MIMIC-IV-ECG — 800K+ ECGs linked to ICD-10 diagnoses. Stroke cohort extractable via I60-I69 codes. Time-domain HRV (SDNN, RMSSD) computable from 10-second recordings. Can provide resting HRV distributions for stroke patients to project into the DEAP-trained GMM space. Limitation: no EDA, no lesion localization, no insular vs. non-insular stratification.

NHANES: NHANES — contains HRV examination data (SDNN, RMSSD, LF/HF) and self-reported stroke history (MCQ160f) in 50K+ participants. Can compare resting HRV distributions between stroke survivors and healthy controls as a population-level proxy, though no lesion localization is available.
data_availability.proxy_description: Two-stage computational proxy runnable in 2–4 weeks: (1) Use DEAP dataset to build a Gaussian Mixture Model (2-component: high-arousal vs. low-arousal) in a reduced feature space of EDA-derived features (SCL, SCR amplitude, SCR frequency) and self-reported arousal ratings as ground truth labels. Validate GMM classification accuracy within DEAP via cross-validation.
