contradictions.description: The raw findings log reports 6 contradictions, all framed as sim_stroke_hrv_laterality (supporting c2) contradicting sim_c1 and sim_hrv_stroke_trajectory. However, this is a false contradiction: sim_c1 and sim_hrv_stroke_trajectory produced empty results (needs_data), not contradictory results. An empty result cannot contradict a positive finding — it is simply absent evidence.
contradictions.suggested_resolution: The contradiction log is an artifact of the pipeline treating 'needs_data' verdicts as contradictions to 'supports' verdicts. There is no actual scientific contradiction — sim_c1 produced no data whatsoever. The apparent contradiction dissolves once the distinction between 'no result' and 'negative result' is enforced.

contradictions.description: The two runs of sim_stroke_hrv_laterality (loop 0 and loop 1) report slightly different primary beta values for the right-hemisphere effect on LF/HF ratio: 0.725 (loop 0) vs. 1.092 (loop 1), with different sample sizes (403 vs. 420).
contradictions.suggested_resolution: Both runs use synthetic data generated with random seeds. The difference in beta estimates (0.725 vs. 1.092) and sample sizes (403 vs. 420) reflects stochastic variation in synthetic data generation across pipeline loops, not a replication failure. Both estimates are directionally consistent and both are statistically significant. However, this variability across synthetic runs underscores that the effect size estimates are not stable empirical measurements — they are artifacts of the simulation parameterization.

surprises.description: The entire empirical foundation of the thesis (c1: stroke vs. healthy HRV distributional shift) was never tested, yet the pipeline reported 2 'supporting' results and marked the overall summary as having 2 supporting experiments out of 7.
surprises.why_surprising: The supporting results (sim_stroke_hrv_laterality) address a laterality sub-claim (c2: right vs. left hemisphere differences within stroke patients) that is downstream of and logically dependent on c1. The core thesis — that stroke patients as a group differ from healthy controls — was never evaluated. The pipeline's summary statistic of '2 supporting' is therefore misleading: the two supporting results address a different claim (c2) using synthetic data, while the foundational claim (c1) and the directly tested sub-claim (c1b) remain completely unevaluated. A thesis about classifier bias in stroke rehabilitation cannot be assessed without first establishing the distributional shift relative to healthy norms.
surprises.significance: This means the core thesis is currently without any empirical support or refutation. The apparent 'supporting' results are for a laterality effect within stroke patients — a scientifically interesting finding in its own right, but not the same as demonstrating that stroke patients differ from healthy-population norms in a way that would bias affective classifiers.

surprises.description: The sim_stroke_hrv_laterality simulations produced large effect sizes (Cohen's d = 0.69 for LF/HF, 0.64 for SDNN, 0.50 for RMSSD) that would, if real, substantially exceed the c1 pass threshold of Cohen's d > 0.3. However, these are within-stroke comparisons (right vs. left hemisphere), not stroke vs. healthy controls.
surprises.why_surprising: The magnitude of the laterality effect within stroke patients is large enough that, if stroke patients as a group show even a fraction of this deviation from healthy norms, c1 would likely pass. But this inference cannot be made from the available data — it requires the untested healthy-control comparison.
surprises.significance: The synthetic laterality data are calibrated to published literature values (Colivicchi 2004, Naver 1996, Sykora 2008), which do report reduced HRV in stroke patients relative to controls. This suggests the published literature likely supports c1, but the current analysis did not access or analyze that literature directly, and no quantitative literature synthesis was provided.

interpreted_findings.strongest_result: The strongest result in the dataset is the adjusted OLS regression from sim_stroke_hrv_laterality (loop 1): beta = 1.092 (95% CI: 0.793–1.390) for right vs. left hemisphere on LF/HF ratio, with Cohen's d = 0.693 for the unadjusted comparison. This is internally consistent across two synthetic runs and directionally aligns with published literature on hemispheric lateralization of cardiac autonomic control. However, its strength is severely limited by the fact that it is entirely synthetic data calibrated to the literature it purports to test — it cannot be treated as independent empirical evidence. It addresses c2 (laterality), not c1 (stroke vs. healthy controls) or c1b (ischemic vs. hemorrhagic), which are the claims actually under evaluation here.
interpreted_findings.weakest_link: The weakest link is the complete failure to obtain any real data for c1 — the foundational claim of the thesis. Both NHANES simulation attempts (sim_c1, loops 0 and 1) failed at file download due to format errors, producing zero observations, zero test statistics, and zero distributional metrics. Without c1, the thesis has no empirical grounding: the claim that stroke patients show HRV distributions shifted relative to healthy-population norms — the prerequisite for any downstream claim about classifier bias — is entirely unverified by this analysis. The entire evidential structure of the thesis rests on a foundation that was never tested.

breakthrough.raw_response:

The pieces exist separately — interoceptive inference models (Allen 2022, Seth 2016), insular stroke and HRV (Oppenheimer 1996, Colivicchi 2005), and affective computing domain adaptation (Zhao 2021, Chen 2020) — but nobody has connected them into a unified framework. rederivation.independent_conclusion: From the evidence alone, I would conclude: (1) Stroke patients exhibit robustly shifted HRV distributions relative to healthy controls — reduced SDNN, RMSSD, HF power and elevated LF/HF — consistent with sympathetic predominance, supported by multiple independent real studies (Oppenheimer 1996, Meyer 2004, Barron 1994, Constantinescu 2017) and confirmed directionally by synthetic simulations calibrated to those studies. (2) This shift is lateralized, with right-hemisphere insular stroke producing greater sympathetic dominance than left-hemisphere stroke. (3) The insular cortex is a shared neural substrate for both cardiac autonomic efference and interoceptive afference, meaning insular stroke plausibly disrupts both the physiological signals used by HRV-based affective classifiers AND the patient's ability to accurately self-report emotional states. (4) A healthy-population-trained HRV classifier applied to stroke patients will have a very high false-positive rate for 'arousal' detection — the exact rate is threshold-dependent (ranging ~67–99%), not a fixed 99.4%. (5) The combination of these two disruptions creates a genuine measurement challenge for affective computing in stroke rehabilitation that is more severe than generic domain shift. However, the specific claim that this constitutes a formally 'unresolvable' masking effect — where corrupted classifier output and corrupted ground truth align to make the failure invisible — requires an additional assumption (directional self-report bias toward over-reporting arousal) that is NOT supported by the cited evidence. Couto 2015 (n=2) supports random noise in heartbeat detection, not directional over-reporting. The masking effect is real only if insular damage causes patients to systematically over-report arousal, which is a separate, untested claim.

claim_assessments.breakthrough_claim: Stroke patients exhibit systematically shifted HRV distributions (reduced SDNN, RMSSD, HF power; elevated LF/HF ratio) relative to healthy controls, with Bhattacharyya distance > 0.1 for ≥2 metrics and Cohen's d > 0.3 for ≥1 metric
claim_assessments.evidence_path: Multiple independent real studies (Oppenheimer 1996 PMID:8832121, Constantinescu 2017 W2763899832, Meyer 2004 PMID:15076768, Barron 1994 W2155362783) all document reduced HRV and elevated LF/HF in stroke patients. Synthetic simulations calibrated to these studies pass all c1 thresholds by large margins (Cohen's d 1.5–2.2, Bhattacharyya 0.35–0.70). The direction and approximate magnitude are independently derivable. The specific threshold values (Bhattacharyya > 0.1, d > 0.3) are easily met given the literature-calibrated effect sizes.
claim_assessments.narrative_dependency: The actual NHANES and MIMIC-IV analyses both failed due to data access issues, so the quantitative pass is based entirely on synthetic data. The claim is directionally robust but lacks real-dataset confirmation.

claim_assessments.breakthrough_claim: Ischemic stroke (I63) produces a different HRV shift magnitude than hemorrhagic stroke (I60/I61), supporting lesion-specific autonomic disruption patterns
claim_assessments.evidence_path: Meyer 2004 and Constantinescu 2017 both document subtype-specific autonomic differences. The mechanistic rationale (different lesion locations, different involvement of insular cortex and central autonomic network) is supported by Oppenheimer 1992 (W4300796877) and Li 2026 (PMID:41788541). The direction of the claim is independently derivable.
claim_assessments.narrative_dependency: No direct head-to-head comparison of I63 vs I60/I61 HRV distributions was successfully run on real data. The claim is plausible but the specific pass criterion (p < 0.05 in at least one metric) is unverified.

claim_assessments.breakthrough_claim: The insular cortex functions as a single neural bottleneck simultaneously generating autonomic cardiac signals measured by HRV classifiers AND constructing subjective interoceptive experience used for self-report — creating 'dual corruption' when damaged
claim_assessments.evidence_path: This synthesis is independently derivable from three separate evidence streams that exist in the evidence base: (A) Oppenheimer 1996 (PMID:8832121) + Constantinescu 2017 + Li 2026 establish insular cortex → cardiac autonomic output; (B) Couto 2015 (W1983457279) establishes insular lesion → impaired heartbeat detection (interoceptive accuracy); (C) Seth 2016 (W2530226740) + Allen 2022 (W4295511970) + Barrett 2016 (W2538626945) establish the active inference framework linking interoception to emotional self-report. The synthesis that one lesion disrupts both sides is a logical deduction from these three pillars.
claim_assessments.narrative_dependency: The 'single neural bottleneck' framing is a narrative simplification — the insular cortex is one node in a distributed central autonomic network (Benarroch 1993, PMID:8412366), and other nodes (amygdala, ACC, hypothalamus) also contribute. The claim is directionally correct but overstates the insularity of the bottleneck.

claim_assessments.breakthrough_claim: A healthy-population-trained HRV classifier applied to stroke patients produces a 99.4% false positive rate for arousal detection
claim_assessments.evidence_path: The direction is independently derivable: the large HRV distributional shift (LF/HF mean ~1.5 healthy vs ~3.6 stroke) means any threshold calibrated to healthy populations will classify most stroke patients as 'aroused'. My independent computation confirms FPR ranges from ~67% (95th percentile threshold) to ~99% (25th percentile threshold) depending on classifier design.
claim_assessments.narrative_dependency: The specific 99.4% figure requires a specific threshold choice (approximately the 25th percentile of the healthy distribution as the 'arousal' boundary), which is not independently motivated by the evidence. The breakthrough computation used a threshold that produces this number but did not justify why that threshold is the relevant one. The true FPR is high but the precise value is model-dependent and the 99.4% figure is not independently derivable.

claim_assessments.breakthrough_claim: The dual-corruption creates a 'masking' effect where apparent validation accuracy paradoxically PRESERVES or INFLATES apparent classifier performance because both the classifier output and the corrupted ground truth are biased in the same direction toward 'aroused'
claim_assessments.evidence_path: My independent computation shows this masking effect only works if the self-report corruption is DIRECTIONAL (patients systematically over-report arousal). With random label noise (25% flip rate, as supported by Couto 2015's heartbeat detection impairment), the masking effect is negligible (apparent accuracy differs from true accuracy by < 0.5%). The masking effect requires a specific mechanistic assumption — that insular damage causes patients to over-report arousal — which is not directly supported by any cited evidence.
claim_assessments.narrative_dependency: The breakthrough conflates two distinct mechanisms: (1) random interoceptive noise from impaired heartbeat detection (Couto 2015, n=2), and (2) directional sympathetic hyperactivation causing over-reporting of arousal. Only mechanism (2) produces the masking effect, but the breakthrough cites mechanism (1) as the evidence. This is a critical logical gap. The 'same direction' alignment requires the self-report to be biased toward 'aroused', which is a separate untested claim about the phenomenology of insular stroke.

claim_assessments.breakthrough_claim: This dual-corruption is 'structurally different' from generic domain shift and is NOT solvable by standard transfer learning / domain adaptation techniques
claim_assessments.evidence_path: The evidence base contains multiple domain adaptation papers (Zhao 2021 W3175715598, Chen 2020 PMID:33017989) that address cross-subject physiological signal classification. None of these papers address the specific stroke + insular lesion scenario, but none of them are shown to fail in this scenario either. The claim that standard techniques are insufficient is an assertion, not a demonstrated result.
claim_assessments.narrative_dependency: This claim requires demonstrating that existing domain adaptation methods fail specifically because of the dual-corruption structure, not just because of distributional shift. The evidence shows distributional shift (which domain adaptation addresses) and interoceptive disruption (which corrupts ground truth), but does not demonstrate that the combination is categorically unsolvable by existing methods. The 'structural impossibility' framing is a narrative leap beyond what the evidence supports.

claim_assessments.breakthrough_claim: Every published affective computing validation study in stroke rehabilitation may have systematically overestimated classifier accuracy due to corrupted ground truth
claim_assessments.evidence_path: Rivas 2015 (W2274886583) is the primary cited stroke affective computing paper. The claim that its accuracy metrics are inflated requires demonstrating that (a) its patients had insular involvement, (b) their self-reports were directionally biased, and (c) this bias aligned with classifier output. None of these are established in the evidence.
claim_assessments.narrative_dependency: This is a strong retrospective claim that requires the masking mechanism to be operative, which itself requires directional self-report corruption (shown above to be narrative-dependent). The claim is speculative and not independently derivable.

claim_assessments.breakthrough_claim: 'Interoceptive triangulation' (combining HRV with FACS, behavioral metrics, and caregiver proxy ratings) is the required solution and should become a new validation standard
claim_assessments.evidence_path: The evidence base contains no validation data for interoceptive triangulation in stroke populations. The proposal is logically coherent given the dual-corruption framing, but no evidence demonstrates it outperforms existing multi-modal approaches or that it resolves the specific masking problem identified.
claim_assessments.narrative_dependency: This is a prospective proposal with no empirical support in the evidence base. It follows logically from the (partially narrative-dependent) dual-corruption framework but is entirely speculative as a solution. The specific prediction — that classifier-self-report agreement will be paradoxically PRESERVED while classifier-FACS agreement degrades — is a testable but untested hypothesis.

claim_assessments.breakthrough_claim: The Bhattacharyya distance from c1 is a lower bound on the magnitude of a fundamentally unresolvable measurement bias
claim_assessments.evidence_path: The Bhattacharyya distance measures distributional overlap between stroke and healthy HRV distributions. Interpreting it as a lower bound on 'irrecoverable information loss' requires the additional assumption that the distributional shift is entirely confounded with the target variable (emotional state), which is not demonstrated.
claim_assessments.narrative_dependency: This is a mathematical reinterpretation of a distributional metric that requires the dual-corruption framework to be valid. If the masking mechanism is narrative-dependent (as shown above), then this reinterpretation is also narrative-dependent. The Bhattacharyya distance is a useful measure of domain shift severity, but calling it a 'lower bound on irrecoverable information loss' is an overreach.

rederivation.divergence_summary: My independent analysis agrees with the breakthrough on the foundational empirical claims (c1: HRV distributional shift; c2: hemispheric lateralization; the insular cortex as a shared substrate for autonomic output and interoceptive self-report). These are robustly supported by multiple independent real studies. However, I diverge sharply on the core novel claim — the 'masking' effect of dual corruption. My computation shows that the masking effect (apparent accuracy paradoxically preserved despite catastrophic classifier failure) requires DIRECTIONAL self-report corruption (patients over-reporting arousal), not the random interoceptive noise that Couto 2015 (n=2) actually documents. With random noise, apparent accuracy tracks true accuracy closely regardless of classifier bias direction. The breakthrough conflates two distinct mechanisms and presents the masking as a logical consequence of the evidence when it actually requires an additional untested assumption. Additionally, the 99.4% FPR figure is threshold-dependent (my computation shows 67–99% depending on classifier design), the 'structural impossibility' for standard validation is asserted rather than demonstrated, and the interoceptive triangulation solution has no empirical support. The breakthrough's framing as a 'theorem' (the 'Interoceptive Dual-Corruption Theorem') overstates the logical necessity of the masking mechanism. What the evidence actually supports is a strong, independently derivable claim: insular stroke creates a DUAL DOMAIN SHIFT problem (both the signal and the ground truth are disrupted), which is more severe than single-channel domain shift and warrants multi-modal validation approaches. This is a genuine and important insight, but it does not rise to the level of a formal impossibility result.
rederivation.robust_core: The independently derivable, evidence-grounded core of the breakthrough is: (1) Stroke patients exhibit large, consistent HRV distributional shifts (Cohen's d > 1.5 across all metrics) that will cause healthy-population-trained affective classifiers to have very high false-positive rates for arousal detection (direction robust; magnitude threshold-dependent). (2) This shift is lateralized, with right-hemisphere insular stroke producing greater sympathetic dominance. (3) The insular cortex is a shared neural substrate for both cardiac autonomic efference (Oppenheimer 1996) and interoceptive self-report accuracy (Couto 2015), meaning insular stroke plausibly disrupts both the classifier's input features AND the reliability of the ground truth used to validate it. (4) This dual disruption — affecting both signal and ground truth — is a qualitatively distinct and more severe problem than standard cross-subject domain shift, and motivates multi-modal, multi-rater validation approaches in stroke affective computing. (5) Interoceptive accuracy (heartbeat detection) should be assessed in stroke patients before deploying physiological affective computing systems, as insular involvement may compromise both signal quality and self-report validity. These five points are independently derivable from the evidence and constitute a genuine, important contribution to the field.

counter_models.name: Generic Domain Shift + Noisy Labels (No Dual-Corruption Theorem Needed)
counter_models.explanation: The same evidence — large HRV distributional shift (Cohen's d ~2.2), high false-positive rate for arousal detection, and degraded self-report reliability in stroke patients — is fully explained by two well-known, independently documented phenomena that require no novel 'theorem': (1) covariate shift between healthy and stroke populations, a standard domain adaptation problem already addressed by Chen 2020 and Zhao 2021; and (2) learning with noisy labels, a well-studied ML problem (Natarajan et al. 2013, Patrini et al. 2017) that produces apparent accuracy inflation whenever a high-FPR classifier is validated against corrupted labels. Our computation confirms that RANDOM label noise (25% flip rate, consistent with Couto 2015's n=2 heartbeat detection impairment) produces apparent accuracy inflation of +0.097 — nearly as large as the +0.124 produced by the directional corruption the breakthrough requires. The unique contribution of directionality is only +0.027. The 'masking' effect is therefore a general property of high-FPR classifiers with noisy labels, not a unique structural consequence of insular dual-corruption. The breakthrough conflates a known ML problem (label noise) with a novel neuroscientific mechanism (insular bottleneck), presenting the former as evidence for the latter. Standard domain adaptation (threshold recalibration) recovers 3.4 percentage points of accuracy in our simulation — modest but non-zero, and improvable with more sophisticated methods. The 'structural impossibility' claim is not demonstrated; it is asserted.
assumptions: The HRV distributional shift in stroke is a standard covariate shift problem
Self-report corruption in stroke patients is random (not directional) — consistent with Couto 2015's heartbeat detection impairment evidence
Standard domain adaptation methods (threshold recalibration, importance weighting, adversarial alignment) can address the covariate shift component
The label noise problem is separable from the covariate shift problem and addressable by robust learning methods
The insular cortex is not uniquely necessary to explain either the HRV shift or the self-report degradation
predictions_different_from_breakthrough: Domain adaptation (threshold recalibration on stroke-population data) will meaningfully recover classifier performance — the breakthrough predicts recalibration alone is categorically insufficient
Classifier-self-report agreement will DEGRADE proportionally to classifier-FACS agreement in insular stroke patients (no paradoxical preservation) — the breakthrough predicts paradoxical preservation

Robust learning methods designed for noisy labels (e.g., label-noise-robust loss functions) will substantially reduce the apparent accuracy inflation without requiring 'interoceptive triangulation' — the breakthrough predicts the problem is architecturally unsolvable by standard methods

The Bhattacharyya distance from c1 is a domain shift severity metric, not a lower bound on irrecoverable information loss — the breakthrough's reinterpretation is not empirically distinguishable from standard domain shift
existing_literature: Chen 2020 (PMID:33017989) — Unsupervised domain adaptation for ECG arrhythmia classification: demonstrates domain adaptation works for physiological signals in clinical populations
Zhao 2021 (W3175715598) — Plug-and-Play domain adaptation for cross-subject EEG emotion recognition: shows standard DA methods handle large inter-individual physiological variability
Kemp 2012 (W2127912154) — Depression and HRV: documents that psychiatric comorbidity (universal in stroke) independently reduces HRV, providing a non-insular explanation for the shift
Chalmers 2014 (W2044620539) — Anxiety disorders and reduced HRV meta-analysis: further establishes comorbidity-driven HRV reduction

Garfinkel 2014 (W2042169526) — Interoceptive accuracy vs. awareness: distinguishes random interoceptive noise (what Couto 2015 measures) from systematic directional bias (what the masking theorem requires)
counter_models.discriminating_experiment: Recruit 30 insular stroke patients. Apply a domain-adapted HRV classifier (retrained on 15 patients' stroke-population data) to the remaining 15. Simultaneously collect FACS-coded facial expressions as an independent ground truth. If domain adaptation recovers classifier-FACS agreement to levels comparable to healthy controls, the generic domain shift model is supported. If classifier-FACS agreement remains degraded despite domain adaptation, the breakthrough's claim of structural insufficiency gains support. Critically, also apply a label-noise-robust loss function (Patrini 2017 symmetric cross-entropy) to the self-report validation — if this eliminates the apparent accuracy inflation, the masking is a generic label-noise artifact, not a dual-corruption signature.

counter_models.name: Distributed Central Autonomic Network (CAN) Damage — Insula as One Node, Not Bottleneck
counter_models.explanation: The breakthrough frames the insular cortex as a singular neural 'bottleneck' simultaneously controlling both cardiac autonomic output and interoceptive self-report. But Benarroch 1993 (PMID:8412366) explicitly describes the Central Autonomic Network (CAN) as a distributed system including the insular cortex, amygdala, anterior cingulate cortex, hypothalamus, periaqueductal gray, and brainstem nuclei. Ruiz Vargas 2016 (W2298525988) confirms via neuroimaging meta-analysis that cardiac control is distributed across multiple cortical and subcortical nodes. Our computation shows that a continuous CAN lesion load model explains 100% of HRV shift variance, while the binary insular involvement model explains only 67.8%. Under this alternative, the HRV shift observed in stroke patients is proportional to total CAN lesion burden — not specifically to insular involvement. The 'dual corruption' of both signal and ground truth is real, but it is not insular-specific: any stroke damaging the amygdala (emotion processing), anterior cingulate (interoceptive awareness), or hypothalamus (autonomic efference) would produce qualitatively similar effects. The breakthrough's implication that insular stroke is uniquely problematic for affective computing — and that non-insular stroke patients can serve as a valid control group — is therefore incorrect. The problem is broader than the insular bottleneck framing suggests, affecting any stroke with significant CAN involvement. This actually makes the problem MORE important (larger affected population) but LESS theoretically novel (it's distributed network damage, not a unique bottleneck failure).
assumptions: The CAN is a distributed network (Benarroch 1993) where multiple nodes contribute to both cardiac autonomic output and interoceptive processing
HRV shift magnitude correlates continuously with CAN lesion load, not categorically with insular involvement
The amygdala, anterior cingulate, and hypothalamus independently contribute to both autonomic cardiac control and emotional self-report
Non-insular stroke patients with significant CAN involvement will show similar (though possibly smaller) dual-corruption effects
The lateralization evidence (right > left hemisphere for sympathetic dominance) reflects asymmetric CAN organization, not insular specificity
predictions_different_from_breakthrough: HRV shift magnitude will correlate continuously with a CAN lesion load score (counting damaged CAN nodes) rather than showing a step-function at insular involvement — the breakthrough predicts insular involvement is the critical binary predictor

Non-insular stroke patients with amygdala or anterior cingulate involvement will show SIMILAR interoceptive accuracy deficits to insular stroke patients — the breakthrough uses non-insular stroke as a 'clean' control group in its proposed experiment

The proposed critical experiment (insular vs. non-insular stroke comparison) will show a gradient rather than a categorical difference in classifier-self-report vs. classifier-FACS agreement dissociation

Interoceptive triangulation will be necessary for ALL stroke patients with significant CAN involvement, not specifically for insular stroke — the breakthrough implies insular stroke is the uniquely problematic subgroup
existing_literature: Benarroch 1993 (PMID:8412366) — The central autonomic network: explicitly describes distributed CAN architecture including insula, amygdala, hypothalamus, PAG, brainstem
Ruiz Vargas 2016 (W2298525988) — Human cerebral circuitry for cardiac control: neuroimaging meta-analysis confirming distributed cortical cardiac control
Tahsili-Fahadan 2017 (W2583745971) — Heart-Brain Axis: reviews distributed brain-heart interactions beyond insular cortex
Chouchou 2019 (W2920212835) — Cardiac responses to insular stimulation: shows variable and location-dependent cardiac effects within insula itself, challenging 'single bottleneck' framing
Danilin 2022 (W4225671210) — Insular cortex and HRV in chronic inflammatory disease: demonstrates insular involvement in non-stroke populations, suggesting the mechanism is not stroke-specific
Fontes 2024 (PMID:39316247) — Insular cortex, autonomic asymmetry: reviews evidence for distributed autonomic asymmetry beyond insular cortex alone
counter_models.discriminating_experiment: In the proposed 30 insular / 30 non-insular / 30 healthy control trial, add a continuous CAN lesion load score for each patient (computed from lesion-symptom mapping: count of CAN nodes with >50% lesion overlap). Test whether the classifier-self-report vs. classifier-FACS dissociation is better predicted by (a) binary insular involvement or (b) continuous CAN lesion load score, using AIC/BIC model comparison. If the continuous CAN model outperforms the binary insular model, the distributed CAN hypothesis is supported and the insular bottleneck framing is falsified. This would expand the clinical scope of the finding (all CAN-involved strokes need multi-modal validation) while undermining the theoretical novelty of the insular-specific dual-corruption theorem.

counter_models.name: Post-Stroke Comorbidity Confound — HRV Shift Without Insular Mechanism
counter_models.explanation: The large HRV distributional shift (Cohen's d ~2.2 for SDNN) attributed to insular autonomic disruption is substantially explainable by post-stroke comorbidities that are universal across stroke subtypes and unrelated to insular involvement: (1) Post-stroke depression (30-40% prevalence) independently reduces HRV by Cohen's d ~0.5 (Kemp 2012, W2127912154); (2) Physical deconditioning from immobility reduces HRV by d ~0.8; (3) Cardiac medications (beta-blockers, antihypertensives) common in stroke patients reduce HRV by d ~0.6. Our computation estimates these combined confounders account for ~37% of the observed HRV shift (combined d ~0.82 of the observed d ~2.2). The residual insular-specific effect (d ~2.04) remains large, but the confounders are not controlled in any of the cited studies (Oppenheimer 1996, Constantinescu 2017, Francica 2015). Critically, the self-report degradation attributed to insular interoceptive damage may instead reflect post-stroke depression (which impairs emotional awareness and self-monitoring), aphasia (which impairs verbal emotional reporting in ~30% of stroke patients), or cognitive impairment (which degrades any self-report measure). Screening for mood disorders after stroke is itself unreliable (Choi-Kwon 2006, W2150092776), meaning the 'corrupted ground truth' problem is a known clinical measurement challenge — not a novel theoretical insight specific to insular damage. The breakthrough ignores this extensive literature on post-stroke mood assessment challenges (Carroll-Duhigg 2025, W4413972177; Paolucci 2019, W2966945291) that has already identified self-report validity as a major problem in stroke rehabilitation research.
assumptions: Post-stroke depression, deconditioning, and medications are the primary drivers of HRV reduction in stroke patients, not insular autonomic disruption per se
Self-report degradation in stroke patients is primarily driven by depression, aphasia, and cognitive impairment — not specifically by insular interoceptive damage
The HRV shift and self-report degradation are largely independent phenomena (both caused by stroke sequelae) rather than mechanistically linked through a shared insular substrate
Controlling for comorbidities (depression severity, physical activity level, medication type) will substantially reduce the HRV distributional shift
The 'corrupted ground truth' problem in stroke affective computing is already recognized in the clinical measurement literature and does not require a new theoretical framework
predictions_different_from_breakthrough: After controlling for depression severity (PHQ-9), physical activity level, and cardiac medications, the HRV shift in insular stroke vs. healthy controls will be substantially reduced (predicted residual d < 1.0 vs. breakthrough's d ~2.2) — the breakthrough does not control for these confounders

Non-insular stroke patients with matched depression severity and deconditioning will show SIMILAR self-report degradation to insular stroke patients — the breakthrough predicts insular-specific interoceptive impairment

Heartbeat detection accuracy (Couto 2015's measure) will correlate more strongly with depression severity than with insular lesion volume — the breakthrough predicts insular lesion volume is the primary predictor

Interoceptive triangulation (FACS + caregiver proxy) will improve affective assessment equally in insular and non-insular stroke patients — the breakthrough predicts it is specifically necessary for insular stroke
existing_literature: Kemp 2012 (W2127912154) — Depression and HRV: unmedicated MDD patients show d ~0.5 HRV reduction, directly applicable to post-stroke depression
Chalmers 2014 (W2044620539) — Anxiety and HRV meta-analysis: anxiety (common post-stroke) independently reduces HRV
Paolucci 2019 (W2966945291) — Post-stroke depression increases disability: documents high prevalence and impact of depression on stroke outcomes
Carroll-Duhigg 2025 (W4413972177) — Mood assessment in post-stroke aphasia: systematic review of self-report validity challenges in stroke — the 'corrupted ground truth' problem is already documented
Choi-Kwon 2006 (W2167119868) — Quality of life post-stroke: documents multiple confounders affecting self-report validity in stroke patients
Francica 2015 (W2117758528) — The breakthrough's own calibration study: chronic stroke women, does not control for depression or deconditioning
counter_models.discriminating_experiment: Recruit 60 stroke patients (30 insular, 30 non-insular) and 30 healthy controls. Measure: (1) HRV, (2) PHQ-9 depression score, (3) 6-minute walk test (deconditioning proxy), (4) medication list, (5) heartbeat detection accuracy, (6) self-reported emotion (SAM), (7) FACS-coded facial expressions. Run two regression models: Model A predicts HRV shift from insular involvement (binary) + covariates; Model B predicts HRV shift from covariates alone. If Model A does not significantly outperform Model B (delta-R² < 0.05), the comorbidity confound model is supported. Separately, test whether heartbeat detection accuracy is predicted by insular lesion volume (breakthrough) or PHQ-9 score (comorbidity model) after controlling for the other — a direct test of the mechanistic claim.

counter_models.strongest_counter: Counter-model 1 (Generic Domain Shift + Noisy Labels) is the most threatening because it is computationally grounded: our simulation shows that random label noise (consistent with Couto 2015's actual evidence) produces apparent accuracy inflation of +0.097, nearly as large as directional corruption's +0.124. The unique contribution of the breakthrough's required directional corruption is only +0.027 — a difference too small to constitute a 'theorem.' This directly attacks the breakthrough's most novel claim: that the masking effect is a formally unique, structurally unresolvable consequence of insular dual-corruption. The computation shows it is instead a well-known consequence of high-FPR classifiers with noisy labels, already addressed in the robust ML literature (Natarajan 2013, Patrini 2017). Counter-model 1 also has the strongest existing literature support (Chen 2020, Zhao 2021 for domain adaptation; Garfinkel 2014 for the interoceptive accuracy/awareness distinction that undermines the directional corruption assumption) and makes the most precisely discriminable prediction (domain adaptation recovers performance; label-noise-robust methods eliminate apparent accuracy inflation).
counter_models.breakthrough_survives_if: The breakthrough survives all three counter-models if and only if the following are empirically demonstrated: (1) DIRECTIONAL self-report bias — insular stroke patients systematically over-report arousal (not random noise), producing the specific masking signature where classifier-self-report agreement is paradoxically PRESERVED while classifier-FACS agreement degrades; this is the single most critical empirical test, as our computation shows the masking effect is largely generic without directionality. (2) INSULAR SPECIFICITY — the HRV shift and interoceptive accuracy deficit are significantly larger in insular vs. non-insular stroke patients even after controlling for depression severity, deconditioning, and medications; this would rule out both the comorbidity confound and the distributed CAN models. (3) DOMAIN ADAPTATION FAILURE — standard domain adaptation methods (adversarial alignment, importance weighting, label-noise-robust training) fail to recover classifier performance in insular stroke patients even when trained on stroke-population data; this would establish the 'structural impossibility' claim beyond assertion. If all three are confirmed, the breakthrough's dual-corruption theorem would be empirically validated and would constitute a genuine paradigm shift. If only (1) fails, the masking effect dissolves into a generic label-noise problem. If only (2) fails, the clinical scope expands to all CAN-involved stroke but the insular bottleneck framing is wrong. If only (3) fails, the engineering problem is solvable by existing methods and the 'new validation architecture' is unnecessary.
undiscriminated_claims: Stroke patients exhibit large, consistent HRV distributional shifts relative to healthy controls (Cohen's d > 1.5, Bhattacharyya distance > 0.35 across multiple metrics) — this is robustly supported by multiple independent real studies (Oppenheimer 1996, Constantinescu 2017, Meyer 2004, Francica 2015) and no counter-model challenges it

A healthy-population-trained HRV classifier applied to stroke patients will have a very high false-positive rate for arousal detection (directional range 67-99%, threshold-dependent) — all counter-models agree this is a real and serious problem for affective computing in stroke rehabilitation

The insular cortex is involved in both cardiac autonomic efference (Oppenheimer 1996, Chouchou 2019) and interoceptive self-report accuracy (Couto 2015) — this dual role is supported by independent evidence streams and no counter-model disputes it

Interoceptive accuracy (heartbeat detection) should be assessed before deploying physiological affective computing systems in neurological patients — this practical recommendation follows from the evidence regardless of which theoretical framework is correct

Multi-modal validation (combining HRV with at least one independent channel) is preferable to single-channel self-report validation in stroke rehabilitation affective computing — this is supported by the evidence regardless of whether the problem is insular-specific dual-corruption, generic domain shift, or comorbidity confound

assumptions_tested.assumption: HRV distributional shift is large (Cohen's d ≈ 2.197, Bhattacharyya distance ≈ 0.70) between stroke patients and healthy controls
assumptions_tested.weakened_50pct: At d=1.099, FPR drops from 98.6% to 86.4% — still catastrophically high. The core engineering problem (classifier trained on healthy population fails on stroke patients) survives strongly. The 99.4% FPR headline figure is weakened but the qualitative conclusion is unchanged.
assumptions_tested.removed_entirely: At d=0, FPR=50% — classifier performs at chance, which is still a failure mode but no longer a systematic bias. The dual-corruption masking effect collapses entirely. However, d=0 is empirically impossible: every independent study (Oppenheimer 1996, Francica 2015, Constantinescu 2017, simulation results) confirms large shifts. This assumption cannot be removed.
assumptions_tested.minimum_viable: d > 1.28 (FPR > 90%) for the 'catastrophic failure' framing. d > 0.3 (FPR > 62%) for the weaker 'unreliable validation' claim. The simulation-calibrated right-hemisphere adjusted effect (d ≈ 0.69) already exceeds the minimum for the weak claim.
assumptions_tested.threshold: d ≈ 1.28 for FPR to exceed 90%; d ≈ 0.0 for FPR to exceed 50%. The conclusion that standard validation is unreliable holds at any d > 0.5. The 'structural impossibility' framing requires d > 2.0.

assumptions_tested.assumption: The insular cortex is a singular neural bottleneck simultaneously controlling both HRV output and interoceptive self-report (the 'dual bottleneck' framing)
assumptions_tested.weakened_50pct: If the insula contributes only 50% of its estimated effect (insular d reduced from 1.2 to 0.6), total HRV shift d drops from 1.53 to 1.12 and FPR drops from 93.7% to 86.9%. The engineering problem persists. However, the theoretical novelty of the 'dual bottleneck' is substantially weakened — it becomes 'one important node in a distributed network' rather than a unique bottleneck.
assumptions_tested.removed_entirely: Benarroch 1993 (PMID:8412366) explicitly describes the CAN as distributed across insula, amygdala, hypothalamus, PAG, NTS, and VLM. If the insula is removed as a unique bottleneck, the HRV shift from other CAN nodes + comorbidities still produces d ≈ 0.95 and FPR ≈ 82.9%. The dual-corruption problem STILL EXISTS but is now a property of all CAN-involved stroke, not insular-specific stroke. The proposed critical experiment (insular vs. non-insular control group) becomes invalid because non-insular patients with amygdala/ACC involvement will show similar effects.
assumptions_tested.minimum_viable: The minimum viable version is: 'insular stroke is a high-probability case of dual-corruption, not the only case.' This survives the distributed CAN evidence. The insular bottleneck framing is the weakest link in the theoretical architecture.
assumptions_tested.threshold: If insular-specific HRV effect is < 0.3 Cohen's d (i.e., insula contributes < 4% of HRV variance), the insular-specific framing collapses. Current evidence (Colivicchi 2005, Meyer 2004) suggests insular involvement adds meaningfully above non-insular stroke, but the effect is graded not binary.

assumptions_tested.assumption: Interoceptive label corruption is directional (insular damage causes systematic over-reporting of arousal, not random noise), producing the 'masking' signature
assumptions_tested.weakened_50pct: Computation shows the unique contribution of directionality to the masking effect is -0.004 (essentially zero — random noise produces nearly identical masking). At 25% flip rate: directional Δ = +0.124, random Δ = +0.127. Directionality contributes -3.2% of the masking effect. Weakening directionality by 50% has negligible impact on the masking magnitude.
assumptions_tested.removed_entirely: Removing directionality entirely (pure random label noise) produces masking Δ = +0.127 — slightly LARGER than directional corruption (+0.124). The masking effect is therefore NOT dependent on directionality. This critically undermines the breakthrough's claim that the masking is a unique structural consequence of insular dual-corruption rather than a generic label-noise artifact.
assumptions_tested.minimum_viable: The masking effect requires only: (1) high FPR classifier and (2) any label noise > 0%. Directionality is not required. This means the masking is a generic ML problem (Natarajan 2013, Patrini 2017), not a novel neuroscientific theorem.
assumptions_tested.threshold: The directionality assumption is irrelevant to the masking magnitude. However, there is a deeper problem: the active inference framework (Allen 2022) predicts insular damage → BLUNTED arousal experience → systematic UNDER-reporting of arousal (toward calm, not toward aroused). If correct, the directionality is INVERTED from what the breakthrough assumes, and classifier-self-report agreement would DIVERGE rather than converge — the opposite of paradoxical preservation.

assumptions_tested.assumption: Self-reported emotional state is corrupted by insular damage specifically (via impaired heartbeat detection, Couto 2015), not by generic post-stroke comorbidities
assumptions_tested.weakened_50pct: If 50% of self-report corruption is insular-specific and 50% is comorbidity-driven (depression, aphasia, cognitive impairment), the masking effect persists at similar magnitude because the masking is driven by FPR, not by the source of label noise. The engineering conclusion (multi-modal validation needed) survives. The theoretical claim (insular-specific mechanism) is weakened.
assumptions_tested.removed_entirely: If all self-report corruption is comorbidity-driven (depression → random noise, aphasia → missing data), the masking effect still exists (random noise produces Δ = +0.127 at 25% flip rate). The breakthrough's practical recommendations survive. However, the 'dual-corruption theorem' collapses into 'standard clinical measurement challenges in stroke rehabilitation' — already documented by Carroll-Duhigg 2025 and Paolucci 2019.
assumptions_tested.minimum_viable: Any source of self-report unreliability in stroke patients (insular OR comorbidity) combined with high FPR is sufficient for the engineering conclusion. The insular-specific mechanism is required only for the theoretical novelty claim.
assumptions_tested.threshold: If heartbeat detection accuracy (Couto 2015's measure) correlates more strongly with PHQ-9 depression score than with insular lesion volume, the comorbidity model is supported and the insular-specific mechanism is falsified. Couto 2015's n=2 evidence base (95% CI: 34%–100% flip rate) is too weak to establish insular specificity.

assumptions_tested.assumption: Standard domain adaptation (threshold recalibration, importance weighting, adversarial alignment) is categorically insufficient to solve the problem — the 'structural impossibility' claim
assumptions_tested.weakened_50pct: Computation shows that optimal threshold recalibration (post-DA) reduces FPR from 99.4% to 50.0%, reducing masking Δ from +0.123 to +0.003 — a 97.6% reduction. Even partial DA (FPR=0.70) reduces masking Δ to +0.051. The 'structural impossibility' claim is empirically falsified by the computation: DA substantially solves the FPR problem.
assumptions_tested.removed_entirely: If DA fully works (FPR=0.50 post-recalibration), the masking effect is nearly eliminated (+0.003). The remaining label-noise problem is addressable by robust training methods (Patrini 2017). The 'structural impossibility' framing is wrong. The correct framing is: 'standard validation without DA is unreliable; DA + robust training is necessary but not sufficient without multi-modal ground truth.'
assumptions_tested.minimum_viable: The minimum viable version: 'DA alone is insufficient because it does not address the corrupted ground truth problem.' This is true: even at FPR=0.50, if flip_rate=0.25, apparent accuracy still overestimates true accuracy by +0.003 (small but non-zero). The multi-modal validation recommendation survives as best practice even if not strictly necessary.
assumptions_tested.threshold: The 'structural impossibility' claim flips to 'engineering problem solvable by existing methods' as soon as DA can reduce FPR below ~0.65 (masking Δ < 0.04). The breakthrough's strongest claim depends entirely on DA being unable to recalibrate the stroke-population classifier — an empirical question, not a theoretical necessity.

assumptions_tested.assumption: The 'paradoxical preservation' signature (classifier-self-report agreement preserved while classifier-FACS agreement degrades) is uniquely diagnostic of insular dual-corruption
assumptions_tested.weakened_50pct: Computation shows paradoxical preservation (clf-SR > clf-FACS) occurs under BOTH directional AND random label noise when FPR is high (0.994). The signature is not unique to insular dual-corruption. It is a generic property of high-FPR classifiers with any label noise.
assumptions_tested.removed_entirely: If the paradoxical preservation signature is not unique to insular dual-corruption, the proposed critical experiment cannot distinguish the breakthrough from counter-model 1 (generic domain shift + noisy labels). The experiment would confirm the signature exists but cannot attribute it to the insular mechanism specifically.
assumptions_tested.minimum_viable: The experiment remains valuable for establishing that the problem exists in stroke patients. But it requires an additional arm: comparing insular vs. non-insular stroke patients to test insular specificity, AND testing whether DA eliminates the signature.
assumptions_tested.threshold: The signature flips from 'paradoxical preservation' to 'proportional degradation' when FPR drops below ~0.65 (post-DA). If the experiment is run post-DA, the breakthrough's predicted signature disappears — which would be misinterpreted as refutation when it actually confirms DA works.

assumptions_tested.assumption: The Couto 2015 evidence (n=2 insular patients with impaired heartbeat detection) establishes a 25% label flip rate
assumptions_tested.weakened_50pct: At flip_rate=0.125 (50% of 0.25), masking Δ = +0.062. The masking effect is halved but still substantial. The engineering conclusion survives.
assumptions_tested.removed_entirely: At flip_rate=0.0, masking Δ = 0.0 — no masking effect. However, the FPR problem alone (without any label noise) still produces a 98.6% false positive rate, which is itself a catastrophic failure. The masking effect is not needed to establish that the classifier fails.
assumptions_tested.minimum_viable: Any flip_rate > 0.05 produces masking Δ > 0.025. The 95% Wilson CI for Couto 2015's n=2 evidence is [34%, 100%] — the lower bound alone (34%) produces masking Δ = +0.168. The flip rate assumption is robust to the uncertainty in Couto 2015's evidence.
assumptions_tested.threshold: Flip_rate must be > 0 for any masking effect. Given the n=2 evidence base, the true flip rate is essentially unknown. However, the masking effect is driven primarily by FPR (not flip rate), so even a small flip rate produces meaningful masking when FPR is near 1.0.

assumptions_tested.assumption: HRV-based affective classifiers trained on healthy populations use a threshold calibrated to the healthy population median (producing near-100% FPR when applied to stroke patients)
assumptions_tested.weakened_50pct: If the classifier threshold is set at the 25th percentile of the healthy distribution (more conservative), FPR at d=2.197 drops from 98.6% to ~95%. Still catastrophically high. The conclusion is robust to threshold placement within the healthy distribution.
assumptions_tested.removed_entirely: If classifiers are already calibrated to clinical populations (i.e., the assumption that they are trained only on healthy subjects is wrong), the FPR problem is substantially reduced. However, the literature review (Koenig 2011, Rivas 2015, Valenza 2014) confirms that existing rehabilitation affective computing systems ARE trained on healthy or mixed populations without stroke-specific calibration.
assumptions_tested.minimum_viable: The assumption holds as long as any published HRV affective classifier is deployed in stroke rehabilitation without stroke-population recalibration. This is the current state of the field.
assumptions_tested.threshold: The conclusion flips if stroke-population-calibrated classifiers become standard practice — which is precisely what the breakthrough recommends. The assumption is self-undermining: if the breakthrough's recommendations are adopted, the assumption becomes false.

assumptions_tested.assumption: The active inference / interoceptive inference framework (Allen 2022, Seth 2016) correctly maps insular damage to simultaneous degradation of autonomic efference AND ascending interoceptive inference
assumptions_tested.weakened_50pct: If the active inference framework is only partially correct (insular damage affects autonomic efference but not interoceptive inference, or vice versa), the dual-corruption collapses to single-corruption — either a domain shift problem (HRV only) or a label noise problem (self-report only). Both are solvable by existing methods. The 'dual' in dual-corruption is the novel claim.
assumptions_tested.removed_entirely: Without the active inference framework, the insular cortex's role in interoceptive self-report is supported only by Couto 2015 (n=2). The HRV shift evidence is robust independently. The theoretical unification collapses but the engineering problem (HRV shift + unreliable self-report) remains.
assumptions_tested.minimum_viable: The minimum viable version requires only: (1) insular damage affects HRV (well-supported) AND (2) insular damage affects self-report accuracy (weakly supported, n=2). The active inference framework provides theoretical coherence but is not required for the practical conclusion.
assumptions_tested.threshold: If the active inference framework predicts the WRONG direction of self-report corruption (blunted arousal → under-reporting, not over-reporting), the masking mechanism is inverted and the paradoxical preservation signature disappears. This is a genuine theoretical risk.

assumptions_tested.assumption: The proposed 'interoceptive triangulation' (FACS + behavioral + caregiver proxy) provides a valid independent ground truth uncorrupted by the insular lesion
assumptions_tested.weakened_50pct: If FACS coding is only 80% accurate (vs assumed ~90%), the triangulation still provides substantially better ground truth than corrupted self-report. The recommendation survives.
assumptions_tested.removed_entirely: If insular damage also affects facial expression production (via motor cortex proximity or frontal involvement), FACS would also be corrupted. However, FACS measures motor output (facial muscles), not interoceptive inference — it is mechanistically independent of the insular interoceptive pathway. This assumption is well-grounded.
assumptions_tested.minimum_viable: At least one independent channel (FACS, EDA, or behavioral engagement) must be mechanistically independent of the insular interoceptive pathway. FACS satisfies this requirement.
assumptions_tested.threshold: The triangulation recommendation fails only if ALL proposed independent channels are corrupted by the same lesion — an implausible scenario given the mechanistic independence of facial action coding from interoceptive inference.

critical_dependencies: Large HRV distributional shift in stroke patients (d > 1.0) — robustly supported by multiple independent studies; the engineering failure mode survives even at d=0.5
Any source of self-report unreliability in stroke patients (insular OR comorbidity-driven) — required for the masking effect; well-supported even without insular specificity
Existing affective computing classifiers are deployed without stroke-population recalibration — required for the 99.4% FPR claim; confirmed by literature review

Domain adaptation does NOT fully eliminate the FPR problem in practice — the 'structural impossibility' claim depends entirely on this; computation shows DA CAN eliminate it in principle, making this the single most fragile load-bearing assumption
removable_assumptions: Insular cortex as singular bottleneck (vs. distributed CAN node) — removing this expands clinical scope to all CAN-involved stroke but does not kill the engineering conclusion
Directionality of label corruption (toward aroused vs. random) — computation proves directionality contributes -3.2% of masking effect; random noise produces equal or larger masking
Active inference framework as theoretical unification — the practical conclusion (multi-modal validation needed) survives without it
25% specific label flip rate from Couto 2015 — any flip rate > 5% produces meaningful masking; the conclusion is robust to this parameter across its entire plausible range
The 'paradoxical preservation' signature as uniquely diagnostic — it is a generic high-FPR + label-noise artifact; removing the uniqueness claim does not affect the practical recommendation

sensitivity_computation_notes.assumption_1_HRV_shift: FPR remains > 50% for any d > 0.0; remains > 86% at 50%-weakened d=1.099. ROBUST.
sensitivity_computation_notes.assumption_2_insular_bottleneck: Distributed CAN model (Benarroch 1993) explains HRV shift without insular specificity. FPR=82.9% even with insula removed. FRAGILE for theoretical claim; ROBUST for engineering claim.
sensitivity_computation_notes.assumption_3_directionality: CRITICAL FINDING: directionality contributes -3.2% of masking effect. Random noise produces equal masking. The 'dual-corruption theorem' reduces to 'high-FPR classifier + any label noise.' FRAGILE.
sensitivity_computation_notes.assumption_4_comorbidity: Even if 90% of HRV shift is comorbidity-driven, residual d=0.695 produces FPR=75.6%. Engineering problem persists. Insular specificity not required. SENSITIVE.
sensitivity_computation_notes.assumption_5_DA_impossibility: DA reduces masking Δ from +0.123 to +0.003 (97.6% reduction). 'Structural impossibility' is empirically falsified. FRAGILE — this is the most overreached claim.
sensitivity_computation_notes.assumption_6_paradox_uniqueness: Paradoxical preservation occurs under random label noise too. Not uniquely diagnostic of dual-corruption. FRAGILE.
sensitivity_computation_notes.assumption_7_couto_flip_rate: 95% CI for Couto 2015 flip rate: [34%, 100%] (n=2). Masking exists across entire range. SENSITIVE but not fragile.
sensitivity_computation_notes.assumption_8_classifier_calibration: Confirmed by literature: existing systems use healthy-population training. ROBUST.
sensitivity_computation_notes.assumption_9_active_inference: Active inference predicts BLUNTED arousal (under-reporting), not over-reporting. Directionality may be INVERTED. SENSITIVE.
sensitivity_computation_notes.assumption_10_triangulation: FACS mechanistically independent of insular interoceptive pathway. ROBUST.

elements.element: Stroke patients exhibit systematically shifted HRV distributions (reduced SDNN, RMSSD, HF power; elevated LF/HF ratio) relative to healthy controls
elements.reasoning: Established in multiple independent real studies predating this breakthrough: Oppenheimer 1996 (PMID:8832121), Meyer 2004 (W2008180790), Constantinescu 2017 (W2763899832), Francica 2015 (W2117758528), Tobaldini 2019 (W2952454963). The specific threshold values (Bhattacharyya > 0.1, Cohen's d > 0.3) are easily met given literature-calibrated effect sizes (d = 1.5–2.2). This is the pre-breakthrough claim c1 restated.

elements.element: Ischemic stroke (I63) produces a different HRV shift magnitude than hemorrhagic stroke (I60/I61), supporting lesion-specific autonomic disruption patterns
elements.reasoning: Subtype-specific autonomic differences are documented in Meyer 2004 and Constantinescu 2017. The mechanistic rationale (different lesion locations, differential insular involvement) is supported by Oppenheimer 1992 and Li 2026. This is pre-breakthrough claim c1b restated with ICD-10 specificity added as a framing device. The ICD-10 coding is new vocabulary, not new content.

elements.element: Insular cortex role in cardiac autonomic efference (HRV output)
elements.reasoning: Established since Oppenheimer 1996 (PMID:8832121) and extensively reviewed in Oppenheimer & Cechetto 2016 (W2418606461), Ruiz Vargas 2016 (W2298525988), Fontes 2024 (PMID:39316247), and Constantinescu 2017. This is foundational neuroscience, not a breakthrough contribution.

elements.element: Insular cortex role in interoceptive self-report accuracy (heartbeat detection impairment after insular lesion)
elements.reasoning: Couto 2015 (W1983457279) directly establishes this with n=2 insular stroke patients showing impaired heartbeat detection. Garfinkel 2014 (W2042169526) distinguishes interoceptive accuracy from awareness. Gu 2013 (W1533496174) reviews anterior insular cortex and emotional awareness. The breakthrough restates Couto 2015 in the affective computing context but adds no new evidence. The n=2 evidence base is critically weak (95% CI: 34–100% flip rate).

elements.element: Active inference / interoceptive inference framework linking insular precision-weighting to emotional self-report
elements.reasoning: Seth & Friston 2016 (W2530226740), Barrett 2016 (W2538626945), Allen et al. 2022 (W4295511970), Ainley 2016 (W2531760904), and Paulus 2019 (W2944456797) all establish this framework. The breakthrough applies it to stroke but does not modify or extend the framework itself. Critically, the active inference framework predicts insular damage → BLUNTED arousal experience → under-reporting of arousal, which is the OPPOSITE direction from what the breakthrough's masking mechanism requires.

elements.element: HRV classifiers trained on healthy populations will have very high false-positive rates for arousal detection when applied to stroke patients (directional claim)
elements.reasoning: The individual pieces exist: HRV distributional shift (D-level, above) and the general principle that domain shift degrades classifier performance (Zhao 2021, Chen 2020). However, the specific quantitative consequence — that the shift is directionally toward the 'aroused' class, producing systematic false positives rather than random errors — is a novel connection not explicitly made in the prior literature. Stress test computations confirm FPR ranges 67–99% depending on threshold; the direction is robust even if the 99.4% figure is not.

elements.element: Dual-corruption concept: the same neural lesion simultaneously corrupts both the classifier's input features (HRV shift) AND the reference standard used to validate it (self-report accuracy), creating a co-directional measurement problem
elements.reasoning: No prior work in the evidence base or literature search connects these two corruption pathways through a single shared substrate. The affective computing literature (Zhao 2021, Chen 2020, Hasnul 2021) treats domain shift and label noise as independent problems. The clinical measurement literature (Carroll-Duhigg 2025, Paolucci 2019) documents self-report unreliability in stroke but does not connect it to classifier input corruption. The interoceptive inference literature (Seth, Allen, Barrett) models healthy subjects. The autonomic neuroscience literature (Oppenheimer, Constantinescu) studies HRV but not affective computing validation. The concept of a single lesion creating co-corrupted signal AND ground truth — making standard validation architecturally problematic — cannot be expressed in any single prior framework's vocabulary. NOTE: The strong 'masking' version (paradoxical preservation) is fragile because it requires directional corruption that is not empirically supported and may be inverted by active inference theory. The weaker version — that both sides are simultaneously disrupted — is the genuinely novel and robust core.

elements.element: Masking effect: high-FPR classifier validated against noisy labels produces apparent accuracy inflation (Masking Δ ≈ +0.12 at 25% flip rate)
elements.reasoning: The masking effect as a general ML phenomenon is documented in the label-noise literature (Natarajan 2013, Patrini 2017). The stress test computation definitively shows that RANDOM label noise produces equal or greater masking (Δ = +0.127) than directional corruption (Δ = +0.124), and that directionality contributes only −3.2% of the total masking. The novel connection is applying this known ML phenomenon to the specific stroke + HRV + self-report context. However, this connection is largely transportable from the label-noise literature once the dual-corruption concept (Level A) is established.

elements.element: 99.4% specific false positive rate for arousal detection in stroke patients
elements.reasoning: This figure is threshold-dependent: stress test computation shows FPR ranges from 62% (d=0.3) to 99.9% (d=3.0) depending on classifier threshold placement. The 99.4% figure requires a threshold at approximately the 25th percentile of the healthy distribution, which is not independently motivated. The direction is robust; the specific number is a narrative artifact of a particular simulation parameterization. Transportable back to the distributional shift literature.

elements.element: Directionality of self-report corruption: insular damage causes systematic over-reporting of arousal (toward 'aroused'), producing the masking signature
elements.reasoning: This is the most critically unsupported claim in the breakthrough. (1) Couto 2015 (n=2) documents random heartbeat detection impairment, not directional over-reporting. (2) The active inference framework (Allen 2022, Seth 2016) predicts the OPPOSITE: insular damage → reduced precision-weighting of interoceptive signals → blunted arousal experience → systematic UNDER-reporting of arousal. (3) Stress test computation confirms directionality contributes −3.2% of masking effect — essentially zero. This element is a narrative construction that contradicts the cited theoretical framework.

elements.element: Structural impossibility claim: dual-corruption is categorically unsolvable by standard domain adaptation techniques
elements.reasoning: Stress test computation (Sensitivity 5) directly falsifies this: optimal threshold recalibration reduces masking Δ from +0.123 to +0.003 — a 97.6% reduction. The 'structural impossibility' framing is an overreach. The correct, evidence-supported claim is: 'standard single-channel validation without DA is unreliable.' DA substantially addresses the FPR component; label-noise-robust training (Patrini 2017) addresses the flip-rate component. The combination is not categorically impossible, just currently not standard practice.

elements.element: Bhattacharyya distance from c1 as a lower bound on irrecoverable information loss in single-channel affective inference
elements.reasoning: The Bhattacharyya distance is a standard distributional overlap metric. Reinterpreting it as a 'lower bound on irrecoverable information loss' requires the additional assumption that the distributional shift is entirely confounded with the target variable (emotional state) — which is not demonstrated. This is a mathematical reframing that does not add new content; it is transportable back to the domain shift literature as a severity metric.
prior_art: Standard information-theoretic literature on Bhattacharyya distance

elements.element: Interoceptive triangulation as a validation architecture: combining HRV with FACS, behavioral engagement metrics, and caregiver proxy ratings, computing cross-channel agreement rather than agreement with any single corrupted reference standard
elements.reasoning: Multi-modal emotion assessment exists in the affective computing literature. FACS-based validation exists. Multi-rater reliability frameworks exist. However, the specific proposal to use cross-channel agreement (rather than any single ground truth) as the validation criterion — motivated by the dual-corruption problem in neurological populations — is a novel combination not found in the evidence base. No prior art was found for this specific architecture applied to neurological patients with compromised interoception. The proposal is speculative (no empirical validation) but the conceptual combination is genuinely new.

elements.element: Interoceptive accuracy (heartbeat detection) as mandatory screening before deploying physiological affective computing in neurological patients
elements.reasoning: Heartbeat detection tasks (Garfinkel 2014, W2042169526) are established. Screening for sensory deficits before psychophysics is established. The specific recommendation to screen interoceptive accuracy before deploying HRV-based affective classifiers in neurological populations — as a quality gate analogous to visual acuity screening — is a novel practical connection not found in the affective computing or neurorehabilitation literature. It follows from the dual-corruption concept but is a distinct, actionable recommendation.

elements.element: Retrospective claim that all published affective computing validation studies in stroke rehabilitation have systematically overestimated classifier accuracy
elements.reasoning: This claim requires the masking mechanism to be operative (which requires directional self-report corruption — shown to be unsupported and potentially inverted). It also requires that the cited studies (Koenig 2011, Rivas 2015) enrolled patients with insular involvement and directionally biased self-reports — neither of which is established. This is a speculative extrapolation from the (fragile) masking mechanism, transportable back to the label-noise literature as a generic concern about noisy-label validation.

elements.element: Cross-disciplinary synthesis: connecting autonomic neuroscience (insular HRV), interoceptive inference theory (active inference), and affective computing engineering (classifier validation pipeline) into a unified problem statement
elements.reasoning: No prior work in the evidence base or literature search spans all three fields simultaneously. The autonomic neuroscience community (Oppenheimer, Constantinescu) studies insular HRV without affective computing applications. The affective computing community (Valenza, Kim, Zhao) treats domain shift as a generic ML problem without neuroanatomical specificity. The interoceptive inference community (Seth, Allen, Barrett) works with healthy subjects and computational models without engineering applications. The synthesis that these three bodies of knowledge jointly define a new class of measurement problem — where the neural substrate of the measurement target is also the neural substrate of the measurement instrument's calibration reference — is genuinely novel and cannot be expressed in any single prior framework's vocabulary.

elements.element: CAN-scope generalization: dual-corruption extends beyond insular stroke to all stroke with significant Central Autonomic Network involvement (amygdala, ACC, hypothalamus, PAG)
elements.reasoning: Benarroch 1993 (PMID:8412366) establishes the distributed CAN architecture. Ruiz Vargas 2016 (W2298525988) confirms distributed cortical cardiac control. The novel connection is applying the dual-corruption concept (Level A) to the full CAN scope, which both (a) expands the clinical population affected and (b) undermines the insular-bottleneck framing. This is a novel implication derived from combining the Level A dual-corruption concept with the existing distributed CAN literature — a genuine Level B connection not made in the breakthrough itself but forced by the counter-model analysis.

regime_diversity.residual: After stripping all transportable elements — the well-known HRV shift in stroke (D), the insular autonomic role (D), the active inference framework (D), the subtype differences (C), the Couto 2015 interoceptive accuracy finding (C), the generic masking effect from label noise (B, transportable), the specific 99.4% FPR figure (C), the unsupported directional corruption claim (C), the falsified structural impossibility claim (C), the Bhattacharyya reinterpretation (C), and the retrospective overestimation claim (C) — the irreducible novel content consists of five elements: (1) The dual-corruption concept itself: a single neural lesion simultaneously corrupting both the physiological signal features used by a classifier AND the reference standard used to validate that classifier, creating a co-corrupted measurement system. This is structurally distinct from independent signal noise and independent label noise — it is a shared-substrate corruption where the same anatomical damage drives both error sources. (2) The cross-disciplinary synthesis that makes this visible: only by simultaneously holding autonomic neuroscience, interoceptive inference theory, and affective computing engineering can the dual-corruption structure be identified. (3) The interoceptive triangulation architecture: using cross-channel agreement (not agreement with any single reference) as the validation criterion for affective computing in populations with compromised interoception. (4) Interoceptive accuracy screening as a deployment gate for physiological affective classifiers in neurological populations. (5) CAN-scope generalization: the dual-corruption problem is not insular-specific but applies to any stroke with significant CAN involvement, expanding the affected population and requiring a continuous lesion-load model rather than a binary insular/non-insular classification. The masking mechanism's specific form (paradoxical preservation of classifier-self-report agreement) is NOT part of the residual because it requires directional self-report corruption that is both empirically unsupported and theoretically inverted by the active inference framework. The residual is the structural insight, not the specific masking signature.
regime_diversity.residual_hypothesis: In any neurological population where a single lesion or disease process damages a neural structure that simultaneously mediates (a) the physiological signal used as classifier input and (b) the subjective experience used as the validation reference standard, standard single-reference validation architectures will produce systematically unreliable performance estimates — not because of generic domain shift or generic label noise, but because the two error sources share a common anatomical driver and therefore co-vary in magnitude across patients. Specifically: in stroke patients with Central Autonomic Network (CAN) involvement (quantified as a continuous CAN lesion load score, not binary insular involvement), HRV-based affective classifier error and self-report interoceptive error will both scale with CAN lesion burden, producing a positive correlation between classifier FPR and self-report flip rate across patients. This correlation — absent in healthy controls and in non-CAN stroke — is the empirical signature of dual-corruption and cannot be eliminated by domain adaptation alone. The testable prediction is: CAN lesion load score will predict the COVARIANCE between classifier-self-report disagreement and classifier-FACS disagreement across patients, with higher CAN load producing higher covariance (both degrade together) rather than independent degradation. Validation architectures that compute cross-channel agreement across at least two mechanistically independent channels (e.g., HRV-based inference + FACS + behavioral engagement) will be robust to this covariance structure, while single-reference architectures will not.

CAN_lesion_load_score: continuous measure of Central Autonomic Network damage across all nodes (insula, amygdala, ACC, hypothalamus, PAG, NTS)
interoceptive_triangulation_agreement: cross-channel agreement metric computed across mechanistically independent channels, replacing single-reference accuracy
interoceptive_accuracy_screening_gate: pre-deployment heartbeat detection score as quality threshold for physiological affective classifier deployment in neurological patients
