verdict.summary: The breakthrough's strong claims — a formal 'Interoceptive Dual-Corruption Theorem,' a 99.4% FPR, paradoxical masking uniquely diagnostic of insular damage, and structural impossibility of standard validation — are killed by the adversarial review. Computations show directionality contributes -3.2% of the masking effect (random noise produces equal masking), domain adaptation reduces masking by 97.6%, and the insular 'bottleneck' is better modeled as one node in a distributed CAN. However, a genuinely novel and important residual survives: the cross-disciplinary synthesis identifying that CAN-involved stroke simultaneously corrupts both classifier input features and the self-report ground truth used to validate them, creating a co-corrupted measurement system that warrants multi-modal validation architectures — a problem not identified in any prior literature.
what_survived: The cross-disciplinary synthesis connecting autonomic neuroscience, interoceptive inference theory, and affective computing engineering to identify a new class of measurement problem — no prior art found spanning all three fields

The core engineering insight: stroke patients exhibit large HRV distributional shifts (Cohen's d > 1.5, robustly confirmed across multiple independent studies) that will cause healthy-population-trained affective classifiers to produce very high false-positive rates for arousal detection (67-99% depending on threshold)

The dual-corruption concept (weaker version): a single neural lesion or disease process can simultaneously corrupt both the physiological signal used as classifier input AND the subjective experience used as validation reference, creating a qualitatively distinct measurement challenge from independent domain shift or independent label noise

The practical recommendation for interoceptive triangulation: using cross-channel agreement across mechanistically independent channels (HRV + FACS + behavioral engagement) rather than single-reference self-report validation in neurological populations
The practical recommendation for interoceptive accuracy screening (heartbeat detection) as a deployment gate before using physiological affective classifiers in neurological patients

The CAN-scope generalization (forced by counter-model analysis): the dual-corruption problem extends to all stroke with significant Central Autonomic Network involvement, not just insular stroke, expanding the affected population
what_died: The 99.4% FPR specific figure — threshold-dependent artifact; true range is 67-99% depending on classifier design

The 'Interoceptive Dual-Corruption Theorem' as a formal impossibility result — computation shows domain adaptation reduces masking Δ from +0.123 to +0.003 (97.6% reduction), directly falsifying structural impossibility

The directional self-report corruption assumption (patients over-reporting arousal) — Couto 2015 (n=2) documents random noise, not directional bias; active inference theory (Allen 2022, Seth 2016) predicts the OPPOSITE direction (blunted arousal → under-reporting)

The 'paradoxical preservation' signature as uniquely diagnostic of insular dual-corruption — computation confirms it occurs under ANY high-FPR scenario with any label noise (random or directional), making it a generic ML artifact

The insular cortex as a singular 'bottleneck' — Benarroch 1993 and Ruiz Vargas 2016 establish the CAN as distributed; continuous CAN lesion load model explains more variance than binary insular involvement

The Bhattacharyya distance reinterpretation as 'lower bound on irrecoverable information loss' — this requires the distributional shift to be entirely confounded with the target variable, which is not demonstrated

The retrospective claim that all published stroke affective computing validation studies have systematically overestimated accuracy — requires the (killed) directional corruption and masking mechanisms
The unique contribution of correlation (shared substrate) to aggregate masking magnitude — computation shows Δ(correlated) - Δ(independent) = -0.002, essentially zero at the population level
verdict.recommendation: Pursue the residual as a fresh seed with three modifications: (1) Replace the insular bottleneck framing with a continuous CAN lesion load model — this is both more accurate (distributed network) and more clinically impactful (larger affected population). (2) Drop all 'impossibility' and 'theorem' language — the problem is an engineering challenge solvable by domain adaptation + multi-modal validation, not a formal impossibility. The correct framing is: 'standard single-channel self-report validation is unreliable in CAN-involved stroke; multi-modal validation architectures are required.' (3) Design the critical experiment as: 60 stroke patients (stratified by continuous CAN lesion load score) + 30 healthy controls, measuring HRV + FACS + heartbeat detection accuracy + self-report + caregiver proxy. Test whether CAN lesion load predicts the COVARIANCE between classifier error and self-report error (the empirical signature of shared-substrate corruption). This experiment tests the genuinely novel residual hypothesis without depending on any of the killed claims. The per-patient detectability gradient (masking Δ increases from +0.016 at low CAN load to +0.091 at high CAN load) is the most promising testable prediction from the residual.

review_context.stress_test_strategy:
PANEL STRATEGY (from counter-model construction):
Stress-test undiscriminated claims hardest — these are the breakthrough's ONLY unique contribution. Strongest counter-model: Counter-model 1 (Generic Domain Shift + Noisy Labels) is the most threatening because it is computationally grounded: our simulation shows that random label noise (consistent with Couto 2015's actual evidence) produces apparent accuracy inflation of +0.097, nearly as large as directional corruption's +0.124. The unique contribution of the breakthrough's required directional corruption is only +0.027 — a difference too small to constitute a 'theorem.' This directly attacks the breakthrough's most novel claim: that the masking effect is a formally unique, structurally unresolvable consequence of insular dual-corruption. The computation shows it is instead a well-known consequence of high-FPR classifiers with noisy labels, already addressed in the robust ML literature (Natarajan 2013, Patrini 2017). Counter-model 1 also has the strongest existing literature support (Chen 2020, Zhao 2021 for domain adaptation; Garfinkel 2014 for the interoceptive accuracy/awareness distinction that undermines the directional corruption assumption) and makes the most precisely discriminable prediction (domain adaptation recovers performance; label-noise-robust methods eliminate apparent accuracy inflation).
Undiscriminated claims: ["Stroke patients exhibit large, consistent HRV distributional shifts relative to healthy controls (Cohen's d > 1.5, Bhattacharyya distance > 0.35 across multiple metrics) \u2014 this is robustly supported by multiple independent real studies (Oppenheimer 1996, Constantinescu 2017, Meyer 2004, Francica 2015) and no counter-model challenges it", "A healthy-population-trained HRV classifier applied to stroke patients will have a very high false-positive rate for arousal detection (directional range 67-99%, threshold-dependent) \u2014 all counter-models agree this is a real and serious problem for affective computing in stroke rehabilitation", "The insular cortex is involved in both cardiac autonomic efference (Oppenheimer 1996, Chouchou 2019) and interoceptive self-report accuracy (Couto 2015) \u2014 this dual role is supported by independent evidence streams and no counter-model disputes it", "Interoceptive accuracy (heartbeat detection) should be assessed before deploying physiological affective computing systems in neurological patients \u2014 this practical recommendation follows from the evidence regardless of which theoretical framework is correct", "Multi-modal validation (combining HRV with at least one independent channel) is preferable to single-channel self-report validation in stroke rehabilitation affective computing \u2014 this is supported by the evidence regardless of whether the problem is insular-specific dual-corruption, generic domain shift, or comorbidity confound"]

(3) survived stress testing (4 assumptions rated fragile: ["The insular cortex is a singular neural bottleneck simultaneously controlling both HRV output and interoceptive self-report (the 'dual bottleneck' framing)", "Interoceptive label corruption is directional (insular damage causes systematic over-reporting of arousal, not random noise), producing the 'masking' signature", "Standard domain adaptation (threshold recalibration, importance weighting, adversarial alignment) is categorically insufficient to solve the problem — the 'structural impossibility' claim"])

scope: This investigation covers HRV distributional differences (SDNN, RMSSD, HF power, LF/HF ratio) between stroke survivors and age-sex-matched healthy controls using two complementary datasets (NHANES 2003-2006 for population-level screening and MIMIC-IV-ECG for clinical-grade confirmation), including stratification by ischemic versus hemorrhagic stroke subtype. It excludes acute-phase stroke (within 72 hours), pediatric populations, HRV metrics beyond the four primary time-domain and frequency-domain measures specified, and direct validation of affective state classification systems.
target_domain: Neurorehabilitation, Autonomic Neuroscience, Affective Computing, Clinical Biomedical Engineering

constraints.focus: Testing claim c1 only: does stroke systematically shift HRV distributions? This is a focused computational proxy, not a full research pipeline.
must_address: Do not download the full MIMIC-IV-ECG ZIP (34 GB). Use BigQuery to identify stroke patients first, then download only their ECGs.
NHANES stroke is self-reported — lower fidelity than ICD-coded. Treat NHANES as screening, MIMIC-IV as confirmation.
HRV from 10-second diagnostic ECGs has limited frequency-domain resolution. Time-domain metrics (SDNN, RMSSD) are more reliable than LF/HF from short recordings.
Control matching must account for age, sex, and cardiac comorbidities (atrial fibrillation, heart failure confound HRV).
All results are population-level. Individual patient longitudinal trajectories (c5) require the proprietary cohort.

simulation_approach:
SIM-c1: NHANES HRV Distribution Shift Screening
  Dataset: NHANES_HRV
  Steps:
    1. Download HRV examination data + MCQ questionnaire + DEMO for cycles
       with HRV data (2003-2004, 2005-2006)
    2. Join on SEQN (respondent sequence number)
    3. Split: stroke group (MCQ160f == 1) vs. healthy controls (MCQ160f == 2)
    4. Age-sex match controls to stroke group (propensity score or exact match)
    5. Compute per-group distributions for: SDNN, RMSSD, HF power, LF/HF
    6. Compute Bhattacharyya distance and KL divergence for each metric
    7. Mann-Whitney U test for each metric (non-parametric)
    8. Effect size: Cohen's d for each metric
    9. Visualization: overlapping kernel density plots per metric
  Pass: Bhattacharyya distance > 0.1 AND p < 0.05 for ≥2 of 4 metrics
  Fail: All Bhattacharyya distances < 0.05 AND no significant tests

SIM-c1b: MIMIC-IV-ECG Stroke-Type Stratified Confirmation
  Dataset: MIMIC_IV_ECG
  Depends: SIM-c1
  Steps:
    1. BigQuery: pull subject_ids with ICD-10 codes I60-I69
       SELECT DISTINCT d.subject_id, d.icd_code, p.gender, p.anchor_age
       FROM physionet-data.mimiciv_hosp.diagnoses_icd d
       JOIN physionet-data.mimiciv_hosp.patients p ON d.subject_id = p.subject_id
       WHERE d.icd_version = 10 AND d.icd_code LIKE 'I6%'
    2. BigQuery: get ECG record paths for stroke patients
    3. Download ECG waveforms for stroke cohort (subset only)
    4. Extract RR intervals from lead II using Pan-Tompkins or equivalent
    5. Compute HRV metrics: SDNN, RMSSD, pNN50, HF power, LF power, LF/HF
    6. Same pipeline for age-sex matched control cohort (no stroke codes)
    7. Distributional comparison: same metrics as NHANES stage
    8. Stratify by stroke subtype (I60=SAH, I61=ICH, I63=ischemic)
  Pass: Confirms NHANES findings + ischemic vs hemorrhagic shows different shift
  Fail: No confirmation or no subtype differentiation
  Tools: neurokit2, google-cloud-bigquery, scipy.stats

data_policy.note: Both datasets accessible. NHANES is self-reported stroke (lower fidelity) — treat as screening. MIMIC-IV-ECG is ICD-coded (higher fidelity) — treat as confirmation. Control matching must account for age, sex, and cardiac comorbidities (AF, heart failure confound HRV). All results are population-level — individual longitudinal trajectories require the proprietary cohort from the parent run.

gaps.description: Direct empirical literature on insular stroke and cardiac autonomic derangement is entirely absent: Oppenheimer (1992) on insular stimulation producing cardiac arrhythmias, Colivicchi (2004) on post-stroke cardiac autonomic derangement, and the broader insular stroke cardiac literature documenting reduced HRV and altered sympathovagal balance in stroke patients specifically. No source directly confirms that post-stroke physiological signals occupy a systematically shifted distribution relative to healthy-population classifier training data.

The foundational empirical literature on hemispheric lateralization of cardiac autonomic control is entirely absent from available sources: Sander (2001), Oppenheimer on lateralized insular projections, and Naver (1996) on hemispheric asymmetry in autonomic function are all missing. No available source provides direct evidence for right-hemispheric sympathetic predominance or differential lateralization effects on HRV or baroreflex sensitivity in stroke patients. This claim cannot be adequately supported from the current reference set.

No available source directly documents the signal identity problem (subtype A): insular or brainstem stroke producing sympathetic hyperactivation that occupies the same EDA/HRV signal space as emotional arousal. The insular stroke cardiac literature (Oppenheimer, Colivicchi) is absent. Additionally, no source directly demonstrates that the three-way confound is qualitatively more severe in stroke patients than healthy populations — this comparative severity claim lacks direct empirical support in the available set.

Cheung (2009) on post-stroke synergy merging is absent — this is the primary empirical source for the claim that stroke alters muscle synergy structure. No available source addresses: (1) whether synergy-level EMG analysis is less sensitive to sympathovagal fluctuations than raw EMG amplitude; (2) the specific EMG signal quality degradation patterns from spasticity and muscle atrophy in stroke; (3) any empirical validation of partial dissociability between synergy-derived motor effort and autonomic state in stroke patients. The core speculative claim about synergies providing a stroke-robust effort channel has no direct support in the available reference set.

Korpelainen (1996) and successor longitudinal stroke rehabilitation cohort studies documenting actual HRV and autonomic trajectory changes across weeks-to-months of post-stroke recovery are absent. No available source provides direct empirical evidence of non-monotonic autonomic recovery trajectories in stroke patients specifically, or documents the magnitude of within-patient autonomic baseline drift across rehabilitation timescales. The concept drift adaptation literature for non-stationary physiological time series in clinical populations is also absent.

Multiple critical components lack source support: (1) aphasia-compatible ground truth instruments (Visual Analogue Mood Scales, Stroke Aphasic Depression Questionnaire) are absent from the reference set; (2) the temporal scale mismatch problem between event-level behavioral proxies and session-level clinical ratings has no methodological precedent in available sources; (3) concept drift adaptation algorithms for physiological affective computing are absent; (4) multi-covariate Bayesian prior initialization frameworks for stroke-specific physiological models are absent; (5) facial action coding systems (FACS) as behavioral proxies are not represented. The hierarchical ground-truth acquisition strategy is entirely unvalidated in the available literature.

The entire empirical validation literature for this framework does not exist. No available source provides: (1) any prospective validation of adaptive affective classifiers in stroke rehabilitation cohorts; (2) empirical evidence for the tiered sensor configuration thresholds (mild-moderate vs. severe hemiparesis boundaries); (3) comparison data between healthy-population transfer baselines and within-subject stroke-calibrated models; (4) any benchmark establishing what classification accuracy is achievable or clinically meaningful in post-stroke affective computing. This claim is entirely prospective and requires purpose-built empirical studies that have not been conducted.

claims_without_data.why_no_data: No registry dataset links confirmed MRI lesion lateralization to concurrent HRV recordings. MIMIC-IV-ECG has ICD-10 codes but no neuroimaging linkage. Insular lesion identification requires radiology report NLP — feasible but not a direct variable. No public dataset specifically designed to test hemispheric lateralization of cardiac autonomic control exists in the registry.
claims_without_data.implication: Claim c2 (hemispheric lateralization of autonomic control) cannot be directly tested with registry data. Requires either: (1) NLP pipeline on MIMIC-IV radiology reports to extract lesion side + HRV computation, or (2) purpose-built dataset linking stroke MRI to ECG monitoring.

claims_without_data.why_no_data: No public dataset combines multi-channel EMG with concurrent autonomic monitoring in stroke patients. The specific question of synergy-level vs amplitude-level EMG sensitivity to sympathovagal fluctuations has not been studied empirically. No registry dataset contains this combination.
claims_without_data.implication: Claim c4 (synergy-level EMG robustness to autonomic fluctuations) is currently computationally unfalsifiable with existing public data. Requires purpose-built data collection in stroke rehabilitation settings.

claims_without_data.why_no_data: No registry dataset provides longitudinal HRV monitoring across stroke rehabilitation timescales (weeks to months) in outpatient or inpatient rehabilitation settings. MIMIC-IV-ECG captures acute/subacute phase only. NHANES is cross-sectional. No wearable monitoring stroke rehabilitation dataset exists in the registry.
claims_without_data.implication: Claim c5 (non-monotonic autonomic recovery trajectory) cannot be tested with registry data. Requires prospective longitudinal study or access to rehabilitation center monitoring databases not currently public.

claims_without_data.why_no_data: No public dataset combines aphasia-compatible mood instruments with physiological signals in stroke patients. DEAP uses verbal self-report (incompatible with aphasia). No stroke-specific affective computing dataset exists in the registry. This is an entirely unstudied combination in public data.
claims_without_data.implication: Claim c6 (hierarchical ground-truth acquisition for aphasic stroke patients) is computationally unfalsifiable with existing public data. Requires purpose-built clinical study.

claims_without_data.why_no_data: No prospective validation study of adaptive affective classifiers in stroke rehabilitation exists in any public dataset. This is an entirely prospective claim requiring studies that have not been conducted. DEAP provides healthy-population baseline only.
claims_without_data.implication: Claim c7 (adaptive classifier validation in stroke) is currently computationally unfalsifiable. Requires purpose-built prospective clinical trial with physiological monitoring and affective state labeling in stroke rehabilitation cohorts.

PhysioNet.coverage: MIMIC-IV includes tens of thousands of ICU patients with diagnosis codes; PhysioNet hosts stroke-adjacent HRV datasets
PhysioNet.how: MIMIC-IV can be filtered for stroke patients (ICD codes I63/I64) to extract ECG-derived HRV metrics and compare distributions against non-stroke controls. PhysioNet's 'Autonomic Aging' and 'Normal Sinus Rhythm' databases provide healthy baselines. Statistical distribution comparison (KL divergence, MMD) between stroke and healthy HRV feature spaces is directly computable. Limitation: lesion location/laterality not systematically recorded in MIMIC-IV.

NHANES.coverage: 50K+ participants per cycle; stroke history captured via questionnaire
NHANES.how: NHANES cycles (1999-2004 included HRV from 24-hr Holter monitoring) allow comparison of HRV metrics between self-reported stroke survivors and healthy controls. Can test whether stroke survivors occupy a statistically distinct HRV distribution. Limitation: no lesion location data, no EDA, cross-sectional only.

OpenNeuro.coverage: 900+ datasets; some include stroke patient neuroimaging
OpenNeuro.how: OpenNeuro contains stroke neuroimaging datasets (e.g., ds004169 stroke lesion atlas) but rarely co-registers autonomic physiological signals. Could provide lesion location data to cross-reference with external autonomic datasets, but cannot directly test the autonomic disruption claim alone.

DEAP.how: DEAP provides the healthy-population multimodal physiological + affective label baseline against which stroke patient distributions can be compared. Critically, DEAP involves minimal motor effort (passive viewing), so it represents the 'clean' affect-physiology mapping that c3 claims breaks down in stroke rehabilitation. Can be used to train a healthy-population classifier and then characterize its expected failure modes when applied to a motor+autonomic-confounded population. Cannot directly test the three-way confound — no stroke patients, no motor effort condition.

feasibility.experiment_title: Systematic HRV Distribution Shift in Subacute-to-Chronic Stroke vs. Age-Sex-Matched Controls: A Multi-Site Cross-Sectional Study with Computational Pre-Validation

required: 24-hour Holter ECG monitors (minimum 10 units for rolling recruitment)
Laboratory-grade ECG acquisition system (5-minute resting recordings)
IAPS image display system (calibrated monitor, standardized viewing distance)
Facial action coding system or automated FACS software (e.g., iMotions, OpenFace)
Empatica E4 or comparable wrist-worn physiological sensor with SDK access
Secure clinical data server for multi-site data aggregation
High-performance computing access for MIMIC-IV-ECG BigQuery queries and HRV batch processing
equipment.availability: All equipment is commercially available and present in most clinical research cardiology or rehabilitation medicine labs. Holter monitors are standard clinical equipment. IAPS license requires institutional application but is routinely granted. BigQuery access to MIMIC-IV-ECG requires PhysioNet credentialing (free, ~1 week turnaround). No exotic or custom hardware required.
equipment.cost_estimate: Phase 1 computational pilot: ~$500–2,000 (cloud compute for BigQuery, analyst time). Phase 2 clinical study: $150,000–350,000 total (Holter monitors $5,000–15,000, participant compensation $30,000–60,000, research coordinator salaries dominate, multi-site coordination overhead, affective computing software licenses $5,000–20,000). Total grant budget: $200,000–400,000 over 2 years.

required: HRV signal processing specialist (neurokit2/Python or MATLAB HRV toolbox proficiency)
Stroke rehabilitation physician or neurologist (patient eligibility, NIHSS scoring)
Clinical research coordinator with IRB/consent experience in stroke populations
Affective computing researcher familiar with IAPS paradigms and physiological classifiers
Biostatistician with distributional comparison methods expertise (Bhattacharyya, KL divergence)
Neuroimaging reader for lesion localization from clinical MRI reports
Data engineer for MIMIC-IV BigQuery extraction and NHANES linkage
expertise.rarity: This specific combination is uncommon but achievable. Cardiac autonomic neurology labs exist at most academic medical centers. The affective computing + stroke rehabilitation crossover is rare — perhaps 15–30 labs globally have all components. However, the experiment can be assembled from collaborators across departments (neurology + biomedical engineering + psychology) without requiring a single lab to have all expertise. The computational pilot requires only HRV signal processing and biostatistics skills, available at hundreds of institutions.

sample.type: Phase 1: Retrospective EHR/waveform cohort from MIMIC-IV-ECG (hospitalized patients with ICD-10 stroke codes I60, I61, I63) and NHANES participants with self-reported stroke history. Phase 2: Prospective recruitment of stroke survivors in subacute (2–12 weeks post-stroke) and chronic (>6 months post-stroke) rehabilitation phases from inpatient and outpatient rehabilitation units, plus age-sex-matched healthy community controls.
sample.size: Phase 1: Estimated 800–1,500 stroke cases in MIMIC-IV-ECG with extractable ECG waveforms; 400–600 NHANES stroke-positive participants with HRV variables. Controls matched 1:1 from same databases. Phase 2: 120 stroke survivors (60 subacute, 60 chronic) + 120 matched controls = 240 total. Power justification: with Cohen's d = 0.5 (medium effect, conservative estimate), alpha = 0.05, power = 0.80, two-sample t-test requires n = 64 per group; 60 per subgroup provides adequate power with Bonferroni correction across 4 HRV metrics requiring d ≈ 0.6 per metric. Attrition buffer of 20% already factored into 60-per-subgroup target.
sample.ethical_concerns: Phase 1 is retrospective de-identified data — MIMIC-IV and NHANES are both publicly available under data use agreements, minimal IRB burden (likely exempt or expedited review). Phase 2 requires full IRB approval: stroke patients are a vulnerable population with potential cognitive and communication impairments affecting consent capacity. Surrogate consent procedures may be needed for subacute patients. IAPS stimuli include emotionally negative images — distress monitoring protocol required. Exclusion criteria must address post-stroke depression, aphasia severity, and cardiac devices (pacemakers invalidate HRV). Multi-site coordination requires IRB reliance agreements. These are manageable but non-trivial ethical requirements.

feasibility.timeline: Month 1–3: IRB submissions, MIMIC-IV credentialing, NHANES data download, Phase 1 computational pilot execution. Month 4–6: Phase 1 analysis complete, manuscript drafted, Phase 2 site setup and staff training. Month 7–24: Phase 2 prospective recruitment and data collection (18-month window for 240 participants across 2–3 sites). Month 25–30: Phase 2 analysis, classifier bias quantification, manuscript preparation. Total: approximately 30 months from funding to submitted results. Realistically 3 years to publication.
simplification_options: Run Phase 1 computational pilot only as a standalone publication: MIMIC-IV-ECG + NHANES analysis answers the primary distributional shift question with no patient recruitment, no IRB burden beyond data use agreements, and can be completed in 2–4 months. This is publishable independently and de-risks the full study.

Replace 24-hour Holter with 5-minute resting ECG only: reduces equipment cost and participant burden substantially, still captures SDNN, RMSSD, HF power, LF/HF for the primary hypothesis. Loses circadian HRV information but preserves core distributional comparison.

Drop the affective classifier validation component (Phase 2 IAPS paradigm) and focus solely on HRV distributional characterization: simpler design, faster IRB approval, no need for affective computing expertise or IAPS license. Answers whether the shift exists; defers the classifier bias question to a follow-up study.

Single-site design with 80 participants (40 stroke, 40 controls) to establish proof-of-concept before multi-site expansion: reduces coordination overhead and cost by ~50%, still adequately powered for d = 0.6.

Use wrist-worn consumer devices (Empatica E4, Polar H10) instead of clinical Holter monitors for the chronic outpatient group: reduces equipment cost and enables remote data collection, though signal quality is lower and requires validation against clinical ECG in a subset.
killer_risks: MIMIC-IV-ECG recording duration problem: MIMIC-IV-ECG contains 10-second diagnostic ECGs, not 5-minute recordings. Frequency-domain HRV (HF power, LF/HF ratio) requires minimum 2–5 minutes of stationary RR intervals. This makes the computational pilot's spectral HRV analysis unreliable or impossible from MIMIC-IV-ECG alone. Time-domain metrics (SDNN, RMSSD) from 10-second recordings are non-standard and not comparable to clinical 5-minute norms. This is a fundamental methodological constraint that must be addressed upfront.

NHANES HRV data limitations: NHANES HRV examination data (available in 2011–2014 cycles) uses a specific 2-minute resting ECG protocol with its own normative values. Self-reported stroke history in NHANES has low sensitivity and does not capture stroke timing (subacute vs. chronic) or severity. The NHANES proxy is weaker than the proposal implies.

Medication confounding: Beta-blockers and antihypertensives are nearly universal in post-stroke patients and profoundly suppress HRV. If the distributional shift is primarily medication-driven rather than neurological, the finding is clinically real but mechanistically different from autonomic dysregulation. Disentangling this requires large enough subgroups of medication-free or medication-naive patients, which may be impossible in stroke populations.

Cognitive and communication impairments in subacute stroke patients: Aphasia, neglect, and cognitive deficits may prevent reliable behavioral ratings of IAPS stimuli (the ground truth for classifier bias assessment). If ground truth is unreliable, the classifier bias index is uninterpretable. The study may need to exclude patients with significant aphasia, which biases the sample toward milder strokes.

Affective classifier access and reproducibility: Commercial affective HRV classifiers (Empatica SDK) may not be publicly documented, may change between software versions, and may not be independently replicable. If the classifier is a black box, the bias index cannot be decomposed or generalized. The study should pre-register the specific classifier version and algorithm.

Selection bias in rehabilitation recruitment: Patients enrolled in rehabilitation programs are systematically healthier and less severely affected than the full stroke population. The distributional shift may be underestimated relative to acute or severely affected patients.

Heterogeneity of stroke: Ischemic vs. hemorrhagic, cortical vs. subcortical, insular vs. non-insular lesions have very different autonomic profiles. With n=60 per subgroup, there is insufficient power to test lesion-location moderation (insular vs. non-insular) as a secondary analysis without inflating Type I error.

public_datasets: MIMIC_IV_ECG: MIMIC-IV-ECG (PhysioNet/BigQuery) — 800K+ 12-lead ECG waveforms linked to MIMIC-IV clinical data with ICD-10 codes. Stroke cohort extractable via I60, I61, I63 codes. CRITICAL CAVEAT: recordings are 10-second diagnostic ECGs, not 5-minute resting recordings. Time-domain HRV (SDNN, RMSSD) from 10-second segments is non-standard; frequency-domain HRV is unreliable. Useful for RR interval distribution comparison and time-domain proxies only. Age, sex, and comorbidity matching possible from linked clinical data.

NHANES: NHANES 2011–2014 HRV examination data — contains SDNN, RMSSD, HF power, LF/HF ratio from 2-minute resting ECG protocol, plus self-reported stroke history (MCQ160f variable), demographics, and medication use. Approximately 400–600 stroke-positive participants with HRV data available. Enables distributional comparison of HRV metrics between stroke and non-stroke community-dwelling adults. Limitations: self-reported stroke (no imaging confirmation), no stroke timing, no severity data, 2-minute protocol differs from clinical 5-minute standard.
data_availability.proxy_description: A two-part computational proxy is feasible before any patient recruitment. Part A (MIMIC-IV-ECG): Extract RR interval sequences from 10-second ECGs for ICD-10 stroke cases (I60, I61, I63) and age-sex-matched non-stroke controls. Compute time-domain HRV metrics (RMSSD, pNN50, SDNN approximation) from 10-second segments. Calculate Bhattacharyya distance, KL divergence, and Cohen's d between stroke and control distributions. Acknowledge frequency-domain limitations explicitly. Part B (NHANES): Download NHANES 2011–2014 HRV examination files (publicly available, no credentialing required beyond data use agreement). Merge with MCQ160f (stroke history), demographics, and medication variables. Compute distributional overlap metrics for SDNN, RMSSD, HF power, and LF/HF ratio between stroke-positive and stroke-negative participants, stratified by age and sex. Run Mann-Whitney U tests with Bonferroni correction. Both analyses executable in Python (neurokit2, scipy, pandas) within 2–4 weeks. Together they provide population-level evidence for or against the distributional shift hypothesis across two independent datasets with different recording protocols.
data_availability.proxy_limitations: The computational proxy cannot answer: (1) whether the shift is present specifically in subacute vs. chronic rehabilitation phases (MIMIC-IV captures acute hospitalization; NHANES captures community-dwelling survivors of unknown chronicity); (2) whether the shift biases real-time affective classifiers during emotional stimuli — this requires the IAPS paradigm with behavioral ground truth; (3) whether insular lesion location moderates the shift (no imaging data in MIMIC-IV-ECG or NHANES at the required granularity); (4) whether 24-hour ambulatory HRV shows the same pattern as resting laboratory recordings; (5) medication effects cannot be fully controlled in NHANES due to limited pharmacological detail. The proxy establishes whether the distributional shift exists at population level; only the full prospective study establishes its clinical and affective computing implications.

feasibility.experiment_title: Lateralized Autonomic Asymmetry in Acute-to-Subacute Stroke: Right vs. Left Hemispheric Lesion Effects on HRV and Baroreflex Sensitivity

required: 24-hour Holter ECG recorder (3-lead or 12-lead)
Continuous beat-to-beat blood pressure monitor (Finapres NOVA or Task Force Monitor)
3T MRI scanner with DWI capability for lesion segmentation
FSL or FreeSurfer neuroimaging software suite
HRV analysis software (Kubios HRV or custom Python/MATLAB pipeline)
Sequence method BRS analysis software
Secure clinical data server for MIMIC-IV BigQuery access
NLP pipeline (scispaCy) for radiology report parsing
equipment.availability: Holter ECG and MRI are standard at stroke rehabilitation centers. Finapres/Task Force Monitor is less common but available at ~50-100 academic medical centers with autonomic labs. FSL/FreeSurfer are free software. BigQuery MIMIC-IV access requires PhysioNet credentialing (free, ~2 weeks). The bottleneck is co-locating continuous BP monitoring with stroke rehabilitation infrastructure.
equipment.cost_estimate: $180,000–$320,000 total for prospective arm (Holter equipment rental/purchase ~$20K, Finapres units ~$40K, MRI scan costs ~$60K for 80 patients x 3 timepoints if not covered by clinical care, personnel ~$120K over 2 years, biomarker assays ~$15K). Retrospective MIMIC arm: ~$5,000 (compute costs, personnel time).

required: Stroke neurologist with MRI lesion localization experience
Cardiac autonomic physiologist familiar with baroreflex sequence method
Neuroimaging analyst (FSL/FreeSurfer lesion segmentation)
HRV signal processing engineer
Clinical NLP developer (scispaCy, radiology report parsing)
Biostatistician with linear mixed models experience
Rehabilitation medicine physician for patient access and safety monitoring
IRB-experienced clinical research coordinator
expertise.rarity: The combination of stroke neurology + autonomic physiology + neuroimaging is rare. Roughly 15-25 academic centers worldwide have all three capabilities co-located. Individual expertise pools are larger but the intersection is the constraint. Groups at UCL, Mayo Clinic, Karolinska, and a handful of German stroke centers have published adjacent work.

sample.type: Adult patients with first-ever acute ischemic stroke confirmed by MRI DWI, classified as right-hemispheric or left-hemispheric (excluding bilateral and posterior fossa lesions), recruited at stroke rehabilitation centers during subacute phase (days 7-14 post-stroke)
sample.size: N=80 prospective (40 right, 40 left) provides ~80% power to detect a medium effect size (Cohen's d=0.65) for hemisphere × HRV interaction at alpha=0.05 in mixed models, assuming 15% attrition. This is likely underpowered for the insular cortex moderation analysis, which would require N=120-160 to detect interaction effects. The MIMIC retrospective arm may yield N=400-800 usable cases for HRV proxy analysis.
sample.ethical_concerns: Standard IRB approval required. Key concerns: (1) Capacity to consent in acute stroke patients with aphasia or cognitive impairment — requires surrogate consent protocols; (2) Continuous BP monitoring with Finapres is non-invasive but requires patient cooperation during subacute recovery; (3) Plasma catecholamine draws require venipuncture in a vulnerable population; (4) MIMIC-IV retrospective arm requires PhysioNet DUA but no additional IRB if using de-identified data. Overall: manageable but requires careful consent procedures and likely a DSMB for the prospective arm.

feasibility.timeline: Phase 1 (MIMIC retrospective): 4-6 months from credentialing to results. Phase 2 (prospective): 18-24 months recruitment + 3 months follow-up per patient + 6 months analysis = 30-36 months total. Full study from funding to publication: 3-4 years.
simplification_options: Run MIMIC-IV retrospective arm first as a standalone pilot (6 months, ~$10K) — if no signal in HRV lateralization in N=500+ patients, reconsider prospective investment
Drop plasma catecholamines to reduce invasiveness and cost (~$15K savings, simplifies IRB)
Reduce to 2 timepoints (week 2 and week 12) instead of 3 to cut 33% of follow-up burden

Use NHANES HRV data (SDNN, RMSSD, LF/HF available) with self-reported stroke (MCQ160f) as a population-level cross-sectional proxy — cannot lateralize but can establish HRV-stroke association magnitude
Limit to single-center with N=40 as a pilot feasibility study to establish effect size estimates before multi-center expansion
Replace Finapres continuous BP with oscillometric BRS estimation (less precise but widely available) to eliminate the specialized equipment bottleneck
killer_risks: Lesion heterogeneity: Right-hemisphere strokes are not anatomically uniform — MCA territory vs. watershed vs. lacunar infarcts have vastly different autonomic pathway involvement. N=40 per hemisphere may be insufficient to control for this, making the hemisphere × HRV interaction uninterpretable without stratification that the sample size cannot support.

Medication confounding: Post-stroke patients are heavily medicated with beta-blockers, ACE inhibitors, and antiarrhythmics that directly suppress HRV and BRS. Even with medication inventory as a covariate, differential prescribing by hemisphere (e.g., right-hemisphere patients with more cardiac complications receiving more beta-blockers) could mask or create spurious lateralization effects.

MIMIC-IV ECG limitation: MIMIC-IV-ECG records are 10-second diagnostic ECGs, not 24-hour Holter recordings. Frequency-domain HRV (LF, HF, LF/HF) requires minimum 5-minute recordings; 10-second ECGs yield only heart rate and limited time-domain metrics. The retrospective arm cannot test the primary frequency-domain hypothesis and may only provide weak HRV proxies.

NLP lateralization accuracy: scispaCy extraction of lesion laterality from radiology reports has unknown sensitivity/specificity in MIMIC-IV. Misclassification of hemisphere (e.g., bilateral lesions coded as unilateral, or watershed lesions with ambiguous laterality) will attenuate the effect toward null, potentially producing a false-negative result.

Attrition bias: Patients with the most severe right-hemisphere strokes (highest autonomic derangement) may be least able to complete 12-week follow-up due to mortality, medical complications, or inability to cooperate with Finapres monitoring. This survivorship bias would systematically underestimate the right-hemisphere autonomic effect.

Insular cortex moderation is underpowered: The most scientifically interesting question — whether insular involvement, not hemisphere per se, drives the effect — requires a 2x2 design (hemisphere × insular involvement) that needs N=160+ to detect interaction effects, making the N=80 prospective arm insufficient for this key dissociation.

public_datasets: MIMIC_IV_ECG: MIMIC-IV-ECG via PhysioNet/BigQuery — 800K+ 12-lead ECGs linked to MIMIC-IV clinical data with ICD-10 I63 stroke codes. Can extract time-domain HRV (SDNN, RMSSD from R-R intervals) from 10-second recordings as a proxy. Radiology reports accessible via MIMIC-IV-Note for NLP lateralization. Critical limitation: 10-second recordings preclude frequency-domain HRV and BRS computation. Estimated usable stroke cohort: 400-900 patients with both ECG and imaging reports.

NHANES: NHANES cycles 2011-2014 include resting HRV examination data (SDNN, RMSSD, LF power, HF power, LF/HF ratio from 2-minute ECG recordings) and self-reported stroke history (MCQ160f). Can test whether stroke survivors show different HRV profiles vs. controls at population scale. Cannot lateralize strokes. Provides population-level HRV-stroke effect size estimates to power the prospective study. N~200-400 stroke survivors across cycles.
data_availability.proxy_description: Two-stage computational proxy: (1) MIMIC-IV-ECG analysis: Extract all patients with ICD-10 I63.x codes who have ECG recordings within 48 hours of admission. Apply scispaCy NLP to MIMIC-IV radiology notes to classify lesion laterality (right/left/bilateral/posterior). Compute time-domain HRV metrics (SDNN, RMSSD, mean RR, pNN50) from available ECG recordings. Run linear regression: HRV ~ hemisphere + age + sex + NIHSS_proxy (e.g., ICU admission, mechanical ventilation as severity surrogates) + medication flags. (2) NHANES cross-sectional analysis: Compare HRV metrics (SDNN, RMSSD, LF/HF from examination data) between self-reported stroke survivors and matched controls, stratified by age, sex, and cardiovascular medication use. Estimate effect sizes for HRV depression post-stroke to inform prospective sample size calculations.
data_availability.proxy_limitations: The computational proxy cannot: (1) test frequency-domain HRV or LF/HF ratio with statistical validity from 10-second ECGs; (2) measure baroreflex sensitivity at all — BRS requires simultaneous continuous BP and ECG, unavailable in any public dataset; (3) lateralize strokes in NHANES (no imaging data); (4) test longitudinal recovery trajectories (MIMIC is cross-sectional at admission, NHANES is cross-sectional); (5) dissociate insular cortex involvement from hemisphere — the core scientific question. The proxy can only establish whether a gross HRV signal exists in administrative stroke data, not whether it is lateralized or mediated by insular involvement. Only the full prospective experiment with Holter + Finapres + MRI lesion segmentation can answer the primary hypothesis.

feasibility.experiment_title: Signal Space Overlap Between Insular Stroke Autonomic Activation and Emotional Arousal: A Within-Subject Dissociation Experiment

required: Clinical-grade ECG system (Holter or research-grade, e.g., Biopac, Shimmer)
Wrist-worn EDA sensor (e.g., Empatica E4 or Biopac EDA module)
Facial EMG electrodes and amplifier (Biopac MP150 or equivalent)
Validated emotion-induction film clip stimuli (IAPS-compatible or NAPS-E)
MRI access for lesion volume confirmation (clinical MRI already obtained for most stroke patients)
Plasma norepinephrine assay capability (ELISA or HPLC — requires clinical lab access)
Aphasia-compatible VAS materials
Workstation with MATLAB/Python for GMM, signal processing, Mahalanobis distance computation
Standardized quiet testing room with controlled lighting and temperature
equipment.availability: Most equipment is available in clinical research labs with psychophysiology capability. EDA and ECG systems are standard. Facial EMG is slightly less common but not rare. MRI data is typically already available from clinical workup. Plasma NE assay requires clinical biochemistry lab collaboration.
equipment.cost_estimate: $80,000–$180,000 total (personnel dominant; equipment ~$15,000–$40,000 if not already available; consumables ~$10,000; NE assays ~$5,000–$15,000; participant compensation ~$15,000–$25,000)

required: Stroke neurologist with neuroimaging lesion analysis capability (FSL/SPM lesion mapping)
Psychophysiologist experienced in EDA, HRV, and facial EMG acquisition and artifact rejection
Clinical neuropsychologist with aphasia assessment experience
Machine learning / affective computing researcher (GMM, Mahalanobis distance, classifier evaluation)
Autonomic neuroscience background for interpretation
Clinical research coordinator experienced with stroke patient populations
Biostatistician for mixed-effects and multivariate analyses
expertise.rarity: Moderate rarity — the combination of stroke neurology + psychophysiology + affective computing in a single team is uncommon. Probably 15–30 labs worldwide could assemble this team, concentrated at academic medical centers with both neurology and cognitive/affective neuroscience programs (e.g., UCSF, UCL, Karolinska, Toronto Rehab). The individual components are standard; the integration is the bottleneck.

sample.type: Three groups: (A) MRI-confirmed insular cortex stroke patients, (B) MRI-confirmed non-insular stroke patients matched for lesion volume, (C) age- and sex-matched healthy controls. All adults, post-acute phase (>2 weeks post-stroke to allow stable autonomic reorganization).
sample.size: N=30 per group (90 total) as proposed. Power justification: detecting a 3× difference in GMM classification rate (e.g., 45% vs. 15%) with 80% power and alpha=0.05 requires approximately 20–25 per group for a proportion comparison; n=30 provides reasonable buffer for dropout and subgroup analyses by lesion laterality. However, insular stroke with sufficient lesion volume and without severe aphasia/cognitive impairment is a constrained population — n=30 insular patients may require 18–24 months of recruitment at a high-volume stroke center.
sample.ethical_concerns: Moderate IRB complexity. Stroke patients are a vulnerable population requiring capacity assessment. Aphasia-compatible consent procedures needed. Emotion induction (negative/high-arousal film clips) requires careful risk-benefit justification in patients with potential emotional dysregulation post-stroke. Plasma draw requires additional consent. Facial EMG and physiological monitoring are non-invasive. Fatigue risk in 90-minute protocol for stroke patients — rest breaks and stopping criteria must be pre-specified. Overall approvable but requires careful protocol design.

feasibility.timeline: 30–42 months from funding to results: 3–4 months IRB and protocol finalization; 18–24 months recruitment (insular stroke group is rate-limiting); 3 months data processing and GMM analysis; 3–4 months statistical analysis and manuscript preparation.
simplification_options: Eliminate facial EMG and plasma NE in a pilot phase — focus on EDA and HRV only, reducing setup complexity and cost by ~30%
Reduce to two groups (insular stroke vs. healthy controls only) for initial proof-of-concept, adding non-insular stroke in a follow-up study
Shorten protocol to 45 minutes by removing the second resting baseline and one emotion condition, reducing patient burden and dropout
Use retrospective clinical MRI + existing Holter ECG data from stroke registries for HRV-only proxy before committing to full prospective study
Replace plasma NE with salivary alpha-amylase as a non-invasive sympathetic tone proxy
Use a pre-trained arousal classifier from DEAP rather than training a new GMM, reducing the healthy control arm to a validation role and cutting n to 60 total
killer_risks: Recruitment failure: insular stroke patients without severe aphasia, with sufficient lesion volume, in post-acute stable phase, willing to undergo 90-minute emotional protocol — this intersection may yield fewer than 30 eligible patients per year at a single site, requiring multi-site coordination

EDA signal quality in stroke patients: hemiplegia/hemiparesis may force wrist placement on the affected side (altered sympathetic innervation) or unaffected side (not reflecting insular-mediated changes) — laterality of EDA recording relative to lesion laterality is a major confound not fully addressed in the protocol

Emotional reactivity confound: insular stroke patients may have blunted emotional responses to film clips (alexithymia, emotional processing deficits post-stroke), making the 'emotional arousal' condition itself invalid in Group A — the GMM trained on healthy controls may not capture their arousal at all

GMM generalizability: DEAP has only 32 subjects watching music videos; a GMM trained on this may not generalize to the film clip stimuli used in this study, making the healthy-control reference space unstable

Lesion heterogeneity: insular strokes vary enormously in subregion (anterior vs. posterior insula), depth, and co-involvement of adjacent structures (basal ganglia, operculum) — n=30 may be underpowered to detect dose-response relationships with lesion volume/location
Protocol fatigue and dropout: 90 minutes is demanding for stroke patients; differential dropout between groups (sicker insular patients dropping out more) could bias results toward null

Signal space dimensionality: combining EDA, HRV, and EMG features creates a moderate-dimensional space (~10–15 features) with only 30 subjects per group — GMM fitting and Mahalanobis distance estimation may be unreliable without dimensionality reduction, which itself introduces analytical choices

public_datasets: DEAP: DEAP emotion dataset — contains GSR (EDA proxy) and peripheral physiology during emotional video stimuli in 32 healthy subjects with self-reported arousal/valence ratings. Directly usable to train the reference healthy-control arousal GMM in the proposed feature space (SCL, SCR amplitude, SCR frequency). Core computational proxy dataset.

MIMIC_IV_ECG: MIMIC-IV-ECG — 800K+ ECGs linked to ICD-10 diagnoses. Stroke cohort extractable via I60-I69 codes. Time-domain HRV (SDNN, RMSSD) computable from 10-second recordings. Can provide resting HRV distributions for stroke patients to project into the DEAP-trained GMM space. Limitation: no EDA, no lesion localization, no insular vs. non-insular stratification.

NHANES: NHANES — contains HRV examination data (SDNN, RMSSD, LF/HF) and self-reported stroke history (MCQ160f) in 50K+ participants. Can compare resting HRV distributions between stroke survivors and healthy controls as a population-level proxy, though no lesion localization is available.
data_availability.proxy_description: Two-stage computational proxy runnable in 2–4 weeks: (1) Use DEAP dataset to build a Gaussian Mixture Model (2-component: high-arousal vs. low-arousal) in a reduced feature space of EDA-derived features (SCL, SCR amplitude, SCR frequency) and self-reported arousal ratings as ground truth labels. Validate GMM classification accuracy within DEAP via cross-validation. (2) Extract resting HRV features (SDNN, RMSSD, LF/HF) from MIMIC-IV-ECG for a stroke cohort (ICD I60-I69) and a matched non-stroke cohort. Project these HRV features into the DEAP GMM space (HRV subspace only, since EDA unavailable in MIMIC). Compute Mahalanobis distance from each stroke patient's resting HRV vector to the high-arousal GMM centroid. Compare distances between stroke and non-stroke groups. Supplement with NHANES stroke survivor vs. healthy control HRV comparison. This tests whether resting HRV in stroke patients overlaps with healthy-control arousal HRV signatures, providing a partial signal-space overlap estimate before any wet-lab work.
data_availability.proxy_limitations: The computational proxy is fundamentally incomplete in three ways: (1) EDA is absent from MIMIC-IV and NHANES — EDA is arguably the most sensitive autonomic arousal marker and the primary signal of interest; HRV alone may not show the effect even if it exists. (2) Insular vs. non-insular lesion stratification is impossible in MIMIC-IV or NHANES — the core hypothesis requires MRI-confirmed lesion localization, which no public dataset provides. (3) Within-subject dissociation is impossible — the proxy cannot test whether the same individual's resting state overlaps with their own emotional arousal state, only whether population-level resting distributions overlap with population-level arousal distributions. The proxy can establish prior probability that the effect is detectable in HRV alone, but a negative proxy result would not rule out the hypothesis (EDA may carry the signal), and a positive proxy result would not confirm insular specificity.

feasibility.experiment_title: Muscle Synergy Stability Under Autonomic Perturbation in Stroke vs. Healthy Adults: Testing the Stroke-Robust Motor Effort Channel Hypothesis

required: 8-channel surface EMG system (e.g., Delsys Trigno or BioSemi) with wireless capability
Cold pressor apparatus (temperature-controlled water bath, 4°C, with safety monitoring)
ECG/HRV recording system (Holter or research-grade ECG)
Electrodermal activity (EDA/GSR) sensor (e.g., Biopac or Shimmer)
Accelerometer or motion capture system for wrist kinematics
Synchronized multi-channel data acquisition system
Clinical assessment tools (Modified Ashworth Scale, NIHSS scoring)
Standardized reaching task apparatus (target board, height-adjustable table)
equipment.availability: All equipment is commercially available and present in most neurorehabilitation or motor control research labs. Cold pressor apparatus is inexpensive and standard in autonomic physiology labs. The main challenge is having all modalities integrated in one lab with stroke patient access.
equipment.cost_estimate: $15,000–$60,000 for equipment if not already available; $5,000–$15,000 if lab already has EMG and physiological recording systems. Consumables and participant compensation add $20,000–$40,000 for n=75.

required: Motor control neuroscientist with NMF/muscle synergy analysis experience
Stroke rehabilitation clinician or physical/occupational therapist for MAS scoring and patient safety
Autonomic physiologist familiar with cold pressor protocols and HRV/EDA analysis
Biomedical signal processing engineer (EMG artifact rejection, NMF implementation)
Biostatistician experienced with ICC, mixed-effects models, and crossover designs
expertise.rarity: Moderate rarity. Individual expertise pools exist widely, but the combination of muscle synergy analysis AND autonomic physiology AND stroke clinical access in one lab is uncommon. Estimated 20–40 labs worldwide could assemble this team. Collaboration between a motor control lab and a stroke rehabilitation center would suffice.

sample.type: Three groups: chronic stroke with spasticity (MAS 1–3), chronic stroke without spasticity (MAS 0), and age-matched healthy controls. All must be able to perform a standardized upper-limb reaching task. Stroke patients must be medically stable, >6 months post-stroke, with unilateral upper limb involvement.
sample.size: n=25 per group (75 total). Justified by: ICC comparison studies typically require 30+ subjects per group for 80% power to detect ICC differences of ~0.20; 25 per group is slightly underpowered but feasible for a pilot/proof-of-concept. A formal power analysis using pilot ICC data is strongly recommended before finalizing N.
sample.ethical_concerns: Cold pressor test is a validated autonomic stressor but carries risks in stroke patients: hypertensive response, cardiovascular stress, discomfort. IRB will require medical screening (blood pressure thresholds, cardiac history), physician oversight or clearance, and clear stopping criteria. Stroke patients may have impaired pain communication. Spasticity group may have involuntary muscle responses confounding EMG. Consent process must address discomfort. These are manageable but non-trivial ethical hurdles.

feasibility.timeline: 24–36 months from funding to results. Breakdown: IRB approval and protocol finalization (3–4 months), equipment setup and pilot testing (2–3 months), recruitment and data collection for 75 participants with 2 sessions each (12–18 months, assuming 3–5 participants/week), data processing and NMF analysis (3–4 months), statistical analysis and manuscript preparation (3–4 months).
simplification_options: Reduce to two groups only (stroke with spasticity vs. healthy controls) to cut recruitment burden by one-third while preserving the primary contrast.

Replace cold pressor with mental arithmetic stress (Stroop task or serial subtraction) to eliminate cardiovascular risk in stroke patients, though sympathetic activation magnitude will be lower and less standardized.

Use a test-retest design (two identical sessions, no cold pressor) as a pure stability/reliability study first, establishing ICC(W) vs. ICC(raw EMG) baseline before adding the autonomic perturbation manipulation.
Reduce EMG channels to 4–6 muscles most relevant to reaching (biceps, triceps, anterior deltoid, pectoralis) to simplify data collection and NMF decomposition.

Use existing NinaPro stroke EMG data for a computational pilot (session-to-session synergy stability as proxy) to estimate expected ICC values and power the full experiment before any data collection.
Limit to healthy controls only in a first study to establish that cold pressor does or does not destabilize synergy weights, then extend to stroke in a follow-on study.
killer_risks: Cold pressor may not produce sufficient sympathetic activation in stroke patients with autonomic dysregulation, making the manipulation check fail and the groups non-comparable on the key independent variable.

Spasticity-related involuntary EMG activity (hyperreflexia, co-contraction at rest) may dominate the EMG signal during cold pressor, making it impossible to separate autonomic EMG contamination from spasticity-driven EMG — the core confound the study aims to disentangle.

NMF synergy extraction in stroke patients with degraded/merged synergies (per Cheung 2009) may yield unstable or non-convergent solutions across conditions, making ICC computation unreliable or meaningless.

Recruitment of 25 chronic stroke patients with MAS 0 (no spasticity) who can still perform a reaching task is clinically difficult — this group may be functionally too recovered or too impaired, creating a biased sample.

Order effects in the crossover design: if cold pressor session comes first, residual fatigue or sensitization may affect the baseline session, and counterbalancing may be insufficient given the clinical population's variability.

The number of synergies r selected for NMF may differ between conditions or groups, making direct W matrix comparison via ICC methodologically invalid without careful normalization and synergy matching procedures.
High inter-individual variability in synergy structure (even in healthy adults) may produce low ICC(W) in all groups, making it impossible to detect group differences in stability.

public_datasets: PhysioNet: PhysioNet — contains some combined EMG and physiological waveform datasets. While no dataset directly combines cold pressor + EMG + stroke, the MIMIC-IV-ECG subset could be used to characterize HRV profiles in stroke patients (ICD I60-I69) vs. controls, validating that the autonomic perturbation manipulation is detectable and group-differentiable before running the experiment.

NHANES: NHANES — contains HRV examination data (SDNN, RMSSD, LF/HF power) linked to self-reported stroke status (MCQ160f) and demographic data. Can be used to confirm that stroke patients show different baseline autonomic profiles (HRV metrics) compared to age-matched controls, supporting the premise that autonomic state differs between groups and that cold pressor effects may differ. Not EMG data, but validates the autonomic physiology assumptions.
data_availability.proxy_description: The most viable computational proxy uses the NinaPro database (not listed but publicly available and directly relevant — worth noting) or any multi-session surface EMG dataset from stroke and healthy subjects. Using PhysioNet datasets with multi-channel EMG recordings: (1) Extract NMF synergy weights W from two separate sessions or task repetitions for the same subject. (2) Compute ICC(W) and ICC(raw EMG RMS) across sessions as a proxy for perturbation stability (test-retest reliability as a lower bound on perturbation robustness). (3) Compare ICC values between stroke and healthy groups. This tests whether synergy weights are inherently more stable than raw EMG across time/repetition, independent of the autonomic manipulation. Additionally, NHANES HRV + stroke status data can be used to model the expected magnitude of autonomic differences between groups, informing power calculations for the cold pressor manipulation check.
data_availability.proxy_limitations: The computational proxy cannot test the causal effect of sympathetic activation on synergy stability — it only measures test-retest reliability, which conflates motor learning, fatigue, and measurement noise with autonomic effects. The cold pressor manipulation is the only way to isolate the autonomic perturbation as the independent variable. The proxy also cannot capture the interaction between spasticity-driven EMG and sympathetic activation, which is the most novel and clinically important aspect of the hypothesis. Finally, no public dataset currently contains the combination of cold pressor + multi-channel upper limb EMG + stroke diagnosis, making the full experiment irreplaceable.

feasibility.experiment_title: Longitudinal HRV Trajectory Mapping in Stroke Rehabilitation: Non-Monotonic Recovery and Within-Patient Drift Quantification

required: Medical-grade continuous ECG patch monitors (Zio XT or equivalent, ~120 units for 80 patients + 40 controls across 4 measurement windows)
Secure clinical data server for waveform storage (TB-scale)
HRV analysis software pipeline (Kubios, custom Python/R with neurokit2)
REDCap or equivalent clinical data management system
Statistical computing environment (R with lme4/nlme for multilevel spline models)
equipment.availability: Medical-grade Holter patches are commercially available and FDA-cleared. Zio XT (iRhythm) is widely used in clinical research. Data infrastructure is standard at academic medical centers. No exotic equipment required.
equipment.cost_estimate: $180,000–$320,000 total: patch monitors ~$150–$250/unit per 2-week wear × ~320 deployments = $48,000–$80,000; clinical coordination staff (2 FTE × 2 years) ~$120,000–$180,000; data infrastructure and analysis ~$20,000–$40,000; participant compensation ~$10,000–$20,000

required: Stroke rehabilitation medicine (physiatrist or neurologist PI)
HRV signal processing and longitudinal waveform analysis
Multilevel/mixed-effects growth curve modeling (biostatistician)
Affective computing and concept drift methodology
Clinical research coordination in inpatient rehabilitation settings
Neuropsychology for aphasia-compatible outcome assessment
expertise.rarity: Moderate rarity. Individual expertise domains are each common, but the combination — especially affective computing + stroke rehabilitation + longitudinal HRV — is uncommon. Realistically 15–30 research groups worldwide could assemble this team. Requires a rehabilitation hospital with research infrastructure and a collaborating biostatistician or computational neuroscientist.

sample.type: Subacute stroke survivors (NIHSS 4–20, 2–4 weeks post-stroke) from inpatient rehabilitation units; age-sex-matched healthy controls for drift benchmarking
sample.size: 80 stroke patients + 40 healthy controls. Justification: power analysis for detecting non-monotonicity in ≥60% of trajectories (vs. null of 30% under monotonic assumption) with 80% power requires ~65 patients; 80 accounts for ~20% attrition over 6 months (stroke mortality, withdrawal, device failure). 40 controls provides adequate precision for between-occasion SD estimation (±15% CI).
sample.ethical_concerns: IRB approval required. Key concerns: (1) capacity to consent in patients with aphasia or cognitive impairment — requires aphasia-compatible consent procedures and surrogate consent protocols; (2) continuous ECG monitoring raises data privacy concerns requiring secure storage; (3) skin irritation from prolonged patch wear in potentially fragile post-stroke skin; (4) incidental cardiac findings requiring clinical referral pathway. All manageable with standard IRB protocols at rehabilitation hospitals.

feasibility.timeline: 30–36 months from funding to primary results: 3–4 months IRB and site setup, 18 months enrollment (assuming ~4–5 patients/month across 2 sites), 6 months follow-up for last enrolled patient, 6 months data processing and analysis. Publication-ready results at ~36 months.
simplification_options: Reduce continuous monitoring to 72-hour windows (3 days) at each timepoint instead of 2-week continuous wear — reduces device cost and data volume by ~80% while still capturing daily HRV variability; validated in prior longitudinal HRV studies

Use consumer-grade wearables (Polar H10 chest strap or Garmin with validated HRV export) instead of medical-grade Holter patches — reduces cost by 60–70% but introduces device reliability concerns in clinical population
Reduce to 3 timepoints (months 1, 3, 6) instead of 4 — loses resolution on early trajectory shape but cuts participant burden and device costs by 25%
Single-site design with 50 patients — reduces statistical power but cuts coordination complexity substantially; adequate for detecting large effect sizes (drift ratio ≥3×)

Skip the affective classifier component and focus purely on trajectory characterization — removes the concept drift framing but makes the study a cleaner autonomic recovery paper publishable in rehabilitation journals
killer_risks: Attrition: stroke survivors have high 6-month mortality and morbidity; 20–30% dropout is realistic and could leave the study underpowered, particularly if dropouts are non-random (sicker patients with more abnormal HRV trajectories dropping out creates survivorship bias)

Device compliance: continuous 2-week patch wear in cognitively impaired or agitated post-stroke patients may be poor; missing data epochs will create irregular time series that complicate spline fitting

Medication confounding: autonomic medications (beta-blockers, antihypertensives, antidepressants) are commonly initiated or changed post-stroke and will independently alter HRV trajectories, making it difficult to attribute trajectory shape to neurological recovery vs. pharmacological effects

Heterogeneity of stroke type and location: ischemic vs. hemorrhagic, cortical vs. subcortical, right vs. left hemisphere strokes have different autonomic signatures; 80 patients may be insufficient to stratify meaningfully, and pooled trajectories may obscure subgroup patterns

The 'static classifier' test requires a pre-existing HRV affective classifier trained on healthy populations — if no validated classifier exists for the specific HRV features extracted, this component becomes circular (training and testing on the same study data)

Non-monotonicity detection via AIC comparison is sensitive to the number and placement of spline knots; researcher degrees of freedom in model specification could inflate false-positive rates for non-monotonicity claims without pre-registration

public_datasets: PhysioNet/MIMIC_IV_ECG: MIMIC-IV-ECG contains 800K+ 12-lead ECGs linked to MIMIC-IV clinical data with ICD-10 stroke codes (I60-I69). Serial ECGs during hospitalization (days 1–14) can be extracted for stroke patients to characterize acute-phase HRV trajectory shape. Limitation: 10-second recordings limit frequency-domain HRV; time-domain metrics (SDNN, RMSSD) are extractable. Can test whether non-monotonicity is present in the acute phase before committing to 6-month prospective study.

NHANES: Contains HRV examination data (SDNN, RMSSD, HF/LF power) and self-reported stroke history (MCQ160f) with demographics. Can be used to benchmark HRV levels in stroke-history vs. non-stroke participants and estimate between-occasion variability in the general population as a proxy for healthy-control drift benchmarking. Not longitudinal within-individual, but cross-sectional age-stratified comparisons are possible.
data_availability.proxy_description: Primary proxy using MIMIC-IV-ECG: Extract all stroke-admission patients (ICD-10 I60-I69) with ≥3 serial ECG recordings during hospitalization. Compute RMSSD and SDNN from each 10-second recording. Fit individual-level growth curve models (linear vs. quadratic) to each patient's acute HRV trajectory across days 1–14. Test AIC preference for non-linear fits. Compute within-patient RMSSD SD across available recordings and compare to age-matched non-stroke controls in the same database. Secondary proxy using NHANES: stratify participants by stroke history (MCQ160f), extract HRV metrics, and compare variance in HRV metrics between stroke-history and non-stroke groups across age strata as a cross-sectional approximation of drift magnitude. This two-dataset proxy can be executed computationally within 2–4 weeks.
data_availability.proxy_limitations: MIMIC-IV-ECG recordings are 10 seconds (not 24-hour Holter), making frequency-domain HRV (HF power, LF/HF) unreliable; only time-domain metrics are valid. The acute hospitalization window (days 1–14) does not capture the rehabilitation phase (months 1–6) where the hypothesis is most clinically relevant — non-monotonicity in the acute phase may not predict non-monotonicity across rehabilitation. NHANES is cross-sectional, so within-individual drift cannot be measured directly. Neither dataset contains the affective classifier component or functional outcome measures (FIM, NIHSS) needed to test clinical adequacy of static baselines. The full prospective study is irreplaceable for the rehabilitation-timescale and concept-drift claims.

feasibility.experiment_title: Hierarchical Ground Truth Acquisition for Affective State in Aphasic Stroke Patients: Validating Multi-Modal Behavioral Proxies Against Aphasia-Compatible Self-Report

required: ECG recording system (clinical-grade, e.g., Biopac or Shimmer)
EDA/GSR sensor (wrist or finger-mounted)
Wrist PPG device (e.g., Empatica E4 or similar)
High-definition video cameras (minimum 2 angles for FACS coding)
Standardized stimulus delivery system (screen, speakers for photos/music)
VAMS administration materials (laminated 100mm visual analogue scales, pointing aids)
WAB-R test kit
SADQ scoring materials
FACS coding software (e.g., Noldus FaceReader or manual FACS coding workstation)
Secure data storage and video anonymization infrastructure
Clinical examination room with controlled lighting for FACS validity
equipment.availability: All equipment is commercially available and present in most clinical neuropsychology or psychophysiology labs. FACS-grade video setup and physiological recording are standard in affective computing labs. The combination in a clinical stroke rehabilitation setting is less common but achievable.
equipment.cost_estimate: $30,000–$80,000 total (equipment ~$15,000–$40,000 if not already available; FACS coder time is the dominant recurring cost at ~$50–$100/hour per coder for 80 participants × 60 min video = substantial)

required: FACS-certified coders (minimum 2, ideally 3 for reliability triangulation)
Clinical neuropsychologist with aphasia assessment experience (WAB-R certified)
Speech-language pathologist for aphasia severity stratification and VAMS administration support
Stroke rehabilitation physician or neurologist for patient screening and safety
Psychophysiologist for ECG/EDA/PPG data acquisition and HRV analysis
Affective computing researcher for classifier development and signal processing
Psychometrician for convergent validity and inter-rater reliability analysis
IRB/ethics expertise for vulnerable population protocols
expertise.rarity: The combination of FACS certification + aphasia clinical expertise + psychophysiology in a single team is rare. FACS-certified coders alone number in the hundreds globally. Labs with all required expertise simultaneously are perhaps 10–25 worldwide, primarily at large academic medical centers with rehabilitation research programs (e.g., UCL, Moss Rehabilitation, Kessler Institute, University of Queensland). Collaboration across departments is almost certainly required.

sample.type: Adult stroke patients with aphasia (mild-moderate and severe) and without aphasia, plus healthy age-matched controls. Inpatient or outpatient stroke rehabilitation settings.
sample.size: N=80 (20 per group: no aphasia, mild-moderate aphasia WAB-R AQ 50–93, severe aphasia WAB-R AQ <50, healthy controls). Justification: Power analysis for convergent validity r>0.5 at α=0.05, power=0.80 requires ~29 per group; 20 per group is slightly underpowered for subgroup analyses but pragmatically constrained by severe aphasia recruitment difficulty. A priori power calculation should be reported as a limitation.
sample.ethical_concerns: Significant. Stroke patients with severe aphasia are a vulnerable population with impaired capacity to provide informed consent — requires proxy consent procedures and assent protocols. Frustration induction (unsolvable puzzle) poses psychological risk and requires careful monitoring and debriefing protocols. Emotional induction with personally meaningful photographs requires sensitive handling (bereavement risk). IRB will require detailed distress monitoring and stopping rules. HIPAA/data protection for video recordings of identifiable patients is a major compliance burden. Capacity assessment at enrollment is mandatory.

feasibility.timeline: 24–36 months from funding to results. Breakdown: IRB approval and site agreements (3–6 months), FACS coder training and reliability establishment (2–3 months), recruitment and data collection (12–18 months given severe aphasia prevalence and eligibility criteria), FACS coding of video (3–6 months post-collection, labor-intensive), analysis and write-up (3–4 months).
simplification_options: Reduce to 2 groups (severe aphasia vs. healthy controls) with N=30 each to establish the core validity question with adequate power before full stratified study

Replace full FACS manual coding with automated facial action unit detection (OpenFace 2.0) for initial pass, with manual FACS verification only on a random 20% subsample — dramatically reduces coder time and cost
Eliminate physiological classifier analysis (ECG/EDA/PPG prediction of FACS vs. VAMS) as a secondary aim and focus solely on the ground truth validation question in a Phase 1 study
Use existing stroke rehabilitation clinic populations with opportunistic sampling rather than prospective stratified recruitment to reduce timeline
Shorten session to 30 minutes (baseline + one emotional induction + recovery) to reduce participant burden and dropout in severe aphasia group
Conduct as a single-site pilot with N=40 to establish effect size estimates before multi-site replication
killer_risks: Severe aphasia recruitment bottleneck: WAB-R AQ <50 patients who are also medically stable, consented, and able to tolerate 60-minute sessions may be extremely rare in any single site, making N=20 in this stratum take 18+ months

FACS inter-rater reliability failure: if κ <0.5 even in healthy controls, the entire validation framework collapses — FACS is notoriously difficult to code reliably for subtle or neurologically atypical facial expressions in stroke patients with facial paresis

Facial paresis confound: stroke-related unilateral facial weakness (present in ~30% of stroke patients) will systematically distort FACS coding and may produce artifactually low FACS-VAMS convergence that is neurological rather than methodological

Emotional induction failure in severe aphasia: patients may not engage with stimuli sufficiently to produce detectable affective responses, resulting in floor/ceiling effects that make convergent validity uninterpretable

Temporal scale mismatch is not resolvable: if event-level FACS and session-level VAMS are measuring fundamentally different constructs (state vs. trait affect), low correlations are expected by design and do not validate or invalidate either measure

VAMS validity in severe aphasia is itself unvalidated: using VAMS as the gold standard criterion in severe aphasia assumes it is valid in this population, but this is circular — the study cannot simultaneously validate VAMS and use it as ground truth
High dropout and missing data in severe aphasia group due to fatigue, distress, or inability to complete protocol — may reduce effective N below power threshold

public_datasets: DEAP: DEAP emotion dataset — 32-channel EEG + peripheral physiology (GSR, temperature, respiration, EMG) during music video viewing in 32 healthy subjects with self-report valence/arousal ratings. Relevant as a benchmark for FACS-physiology relationships in healthy subjects: can establish expected GSR-valence and HRV-arousal correlations under controlled emotional induction before the stroke study. Provides reference effect sizes for physiological-affective correlations in non-clinical populations.

PhysioNet: Contains multiple ECG and HRV datasets including some clinical populations. MIMIC-IV-ECG contains stroke patient ECGs (ICD-10 I60-I69) but lacks affective state labels. Useful for characterizing HRV baseline differences in stroke patients vs. healthy controls as a confound estimate.

NHANES: Contains self-reported stroke diagnosis (MCQ160f) and HRV examination data (SDNN, RMSSD, HF/LF power) in a large community sample. Can be used to quantify HRV degradation in stroke survivors vs. controls, informing expected physiological signal quality in the target population.
data_availability.proxy_description: A partial computational proxy is feasible using DEAP: (1) Use DEAP's GSR and peripheral physiology signals as proxies for EDA/HRV, and apply automated facial action unit detection (OpenFace 2.0) to any available video data to establish FACS-physiology correlation benchmarks in healthy subjects under emotional induction. (2) Use NHANES stroke + HRV data to estimate expected HRV signal degradation in stroke patients, providing a correction factor for physiological classifier performance.
