(3) Simulate the temporal mismatch problem analytically: use DEAP's time-series data to compute correlations between event-level physiological responses and session-level self-report ratings at varying temporal aggregation windows, characterizing the expected magnitude of temporal scale mismatch before the clinical study. This proxy cannot address FACS validity in aphasia or VAMS reliability in severe aphasia.
data_availability.proxy_limitations: No public dataset contains the critical combination of FACS coding + aphasia-compatible self-report + aphasia severity stratification in stroke patients. The core validity question — whether FACS and behavioral proxies can substitute for self-report in severe aphasia — cannot be answered with any existing public data. Facial paresis effects on FACS coding, VAMS pointing response reliability in severe aphasia, and behavioral proxy validity in neurologically impaired patients are all empirical questions that require the full clinical study. The proxy can only establish healthy-subject benchmarks and estimate expected effect size degradation.

feasibility.experiment_title: Prospective Validation of Adaptive vs. Static Affective Classifiers in Stroke Rehabilitation: First Benchmark Study

required: Clinical-grade ECG recorder (Holter or research-grade, e.g., Biopac, Shimmer)
Electrodermal activity (EDA/GSR) sensor (e.g., Shimmer3 GSR+, Empatica E4)
Wrist PPG sensor (e.g., Empatica E4, Polar OH1)
FACS-trained video recording setup (HD cameras, controlled lighting)
Visual Analogue Mood Scale (VAMS) tablets/paper for non-aphasic patients
Standardized cognitive task delivery system (laptop/tablet)
Secure clinical data storage server (HIPAA-compliant)
Signal processing workstation (GPU-enabled for Bayesian inference)
Rehabilitation gym or clinical space for motor task standardization
equipment.availability: Most equipment is commercially available and used in research labs. Empatica E4 or Shimmer devices are standard in affective computing labs. FACS setup requires trained coders but no exotic hardware. The main constraint is co-locating all sensors in a clinical rehabilitation setting with consistent protocol delivery over 8 weeks.
equipment.cost_estimate: $80,000–$200,000 USD total (sensor hardware: $15,000–$30,000; FACS coding labor: $20,000–$40,000; clinical coordination and patient compensation: $25,000–$60,000; data infrastructure and compute: $10,000–$20,000; personnel over 2–3 years: dominant cost)

required: Affective computing / machine learning (Bayesian adaptive classifiers, variational Bayes, online learning)
Stroke rehabilitation medicine (NIHSS, FIM, Barthel, MAS scoring)
Psychophysiology (ECG, EDA, PPG signal processing, artifact rejection in clinical populations)
Clinical trial design (crossover design, counterbalancing, carryover effect management)
Neuropsychology (aphasia-compatible assessment, FACS coding)
Biostatistics (mixed-effects models, F1 trajectory analysis, moderation analysis)
Human factors / wearable sensor deployment in clinical environments
expertise.rarity: Requires a genuinely interdisciplinary team spanning affective computing AND stroke rehabilitation — a rare combination. Affective computing labs rarely have clinical stroke access; rehabilitation medicine departments rarely have ML expertise. Estimated 10–20 research groups worldwide could assemble this team, primarily at large academic medical centers with embedded engineering schools (e.g., MIT-MGH, CMU-UPMC, Imperial-UCL, ETH-Zurich Hospital partnerships). The crossover trial design with FACS ground truth in aphasic patients adds further rarity.

sample.type: Chronic stroke patients (≥6 months post-stroke), NIHSS 2–15, enrolled in outpatient rehabilitation. Mix of aphasic and non-aphasic. Ambulatory enough to attend 8 weekly sessions.
sample.size: N=50 patients. Justification: For a within-subject crossover design detecting a 15 percentage point F1 difference (primary outcome), with expected within-subject SD of ~0.15 F1 units, α=0.05, power=0.80, paired t-test requires ~N=17; inflating to N=50 accounts for 20% dropout over 8 weeks, subgroup analyses (aphasia, MAS severity), and the secondary moderation analyses (drift magnitude × accuracy gap). N=50 is conservative but appropriate for a first benchmark study that will define the field.
sample.ethical_concerns: Significant IRB complexity: (1) Stroke patients are a vulnerable population requiring capacity assessment — some with aphasia or cognitive impairment may have limited capacity to consent, requiring surrogate consent procedures. (2) FACS video recording requires explicit consent and secure storage. (3) Crossover design requires careful justification that classifier order does not constitute differential treatment affecting rehabilitation outcomes. (4) EDA/ECG sensors must not interfere with clinical care. (5) Data security for linked clinical and physiological data. Full IRB review required; not expedited. Estimated IRB approval timeline: 3–6 months.

feasibility.timeline: 30–42 months from funding to published results: IRB and site setup (4–6 months), sensor validation and protocol piloting (2–3 months), enrollment and data collection (12–18 months at ~3–4 patients/month given 8-week commitment per patient), data processing and classifier training/evaluation (4–6 months), statistical analysis and manuscript preparation (3–4 months).
simplification_options: Reduce to N=30 patients and 4 sessions (not 8) to test the core accuracy gap question with reduced burden; sacrifice learning curve secondary analysis
Drop FACS ground truth for aphasic patients entirely; restrict to non-aphasic patients only (N~35) with VAMS ground truth — simpler but limits generalizability
Replace full crossover design with parallel-group design (N=25 adaptive, N=25 static) to eliminate carryover concerns at cost of statistical power
Use only EDA + PPG (drop ECG) to reduce sensor burden and artifact rejection complexity in hemiparetic patients

Prototype the adaptive classifier comparison using DEAP data with simulated concept drift (train on subjects 1–16, adapt on 17–32) as a computational feasibility check before committing to clinical trial
Limit to a single rehabilitation site rather than multi-site to reduce coordination overhead, accepting reduced generalizability
killer_risks: Ground truth label quality collapse: FACS inter-rater κ may be unacceptably low (<0.6) in stroke patients with facial paresis or reduced expressivity, making the primary outcome uninterpretable — the entire study depends on valid ground truth

Sensor data completeness failure: EDA is notoriously artifact-prone in hemiparetic patients (spasticity, involuntary movement, edema); if >30% of sessions have unusable EDA, the multimodal classifier degrades to near-chance

Carryover effects in crossover design: if sessions 1–4 with one classifier system alter patient behavior or therapist interaction in sessions 5–8, the within-subject comparison is confounded — difficult to detect or correct post-hoc

Bayesian prior initialization failure: if the stroke-cohort priors from c1/c5 experiments are unavailable or poorly estimated, the adaptive classifier's initialization advantage disappears and the comparison becomes adaptive-from-scratch vs. static transfer — a different and weaker test

Ceiling/floor effects: if both classifiers perform near chance (F1 ~0.50) due to fundamental signal-to-noise limitations in stroke physiology, the study answers 'both fail' but cannot distinguish why — redirecting the field but not validating the adaptive approach

Dropout and missing data: 8-week commitment with weekly clinical visits is burdensome; if dropout is >30% and non-random (e.g., sicker patients drop out), the sample becomes unrepresentative and underpowered for subgroup analyses

Concept drift confound: genuine clinical improvement in stroke patients over 8 weeks changes the physiological signal independently of classifier adaptation — disentangling classifier learning from patient recovery is analytically complex and may be underpowered

public_datasets: DEAP: DEAP emotion dataset — 32-channel EEG + peripheral physiology (GSR, temperature, respiration, EMG) from 32 healthy subjects during music videos. Directly usable to train and evaluate the static transfer baseline classifier. Can simulate concept drift by training on subjects 1–16 and testing on 17–32 to prototype the Bayesian adaptation algorithm and estimate convergence rate before clinical deployment.

PhysioNet:MIMIC-IV-ECG — 800K+ ECGs linked to MIMIC-IV clinical data with ICD-10 stroke diagnoses (I60-I69). Enables extraction of stroke-population HRV distributions (RMSSD, SDNN, HF/LF power) to initialize Bayesian priors for the adaptive classifier. 10-second recordings limit frequency-domain HRV but time-domain metrics are reliable. Critical for prior construction without requiring the c1/c5 experiments to be completed first.

NHANES: National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey — includes HRV examination data (SDNN, RMSSD, HF/LF power) and self-reported stroke status (MCQ160f), enabling population-level characterization of autonomic differences between stroke survivors and healthy controls. Useful for validating that stroke-specific priors differ meaningfully from healthy-population distributions used in DEAP-trained classifiers.
data_availability.proxy_description: A meaningful computational proxy can be constructed in two stages: (1) Static baseline characterization: Train the healthy-population classifier on DEAP (GSR + peripheral physiology → arousal/valence labels) and evaluate cross-subject generalization using leave-one-subject-out cross-validation. This establishes the realistic F1 ceiling for the static transfer baseline (~0.55–0.65 expected). (2) Adaptive classifier prototype: Simulate concept drift within DEAP by splitting subjects into 'healthy training set' (subjects 1–20) and 'drift simulation set' (subjects 21–32, treated as a shifted population). Apply the Bayesian logistic regression with variational Bayes updates session-by-session on the drift simulation set. Measure whether the adaptive classifier converges and by how many 'sessions.' (3) Stroke prior initialization: Extract HRV distributions from MIMIC-IV-ECG stroke cohort (ICD I60-I69) and NHANES stroke survivors, compute the KL divergence from DEAP healthy distributions, and use this as a quantitative estimate of the prior mismatch the adaptive classifier must overcome. This proxy answers: Does the algorithm work in principle? How large is the healthy-to-stroke distribution shift? How many sessions does adaptation require? It cannot answer whether the adaptive classifier outperforms static transfer in real stroke patients with real ground truth labels.
data_availability.proxy_limitations: The computational proxy cannot address: (1) Real stroke-specific signal artifacts (hemiparesis, spasticity, edema affecting EDA/PPG quality); (2) Ground truth label validity in aphasic patients — FACS feasibility in facial paresis is untestable computationally; (3) Whether autonomic drift within individual stroke patients over 8 weeks is large enough to matter for classifier performance; (4) The actual F1 scores achievable in stroke rehabilitation contexts — DEAP simulated drift is a poor proxy for stroke pathophysiology; (5) Carryover effects and patient burden in a longitudinal clinical design.

experiment_reviews.title: Systematic HRV Distribution Shift in Subacute-to-Chronic Stroke vs. Age-Sex-Matched Controls
experiment_reviews.reason: Both NHANES (SDNN, RMSSD, HF power, LF/HF from 2-minute ECG + self-reported stroke via MCQ160f, n~400-600) and MIMIC-IV-ECG (ICD-10 I60/I61/I63, time-domain HRV from 10-second recordings, n~800-1200) directly contain the measurements needed to test the primary distributional shift claim. The computational proxy is explicitly described as executable in 2-4 weeks using neurokit2/scipy/pandas and can compute Bhattacharyya distance, KL divergence, Cohen's d, and Mann-Whitney U for all four HRV metrics. This fully addresses the pass/fail criteria (Bhattacharyya > 0.1, Cohen's d > 0.3, p < 0.05 for at least 2 metrics). The prospective clinical Phase 2 (IAPS paradigm, affective classifier bias) is a separate downstream question that should not block the foundational distributional claim. The simulation result will either confirm the shift (enabling downstream experiments) or kill the entire research program cheaply.
experiment_reviews.simulation_description: Two-part analysis: (1) NHANES 2011-2014: Download HRV examination files, merge with MCQ160f stroke indicator, demographics, and medication variables. Compute SDNN, RMSSD, HF power, LF/HF distributions for stroke-positive vs. stroke-negative participants matched on age and sex. Run Mann-Whitney U with Bonferroni correction, compute Bhattacharyya distance and Cohen's d for each metric. (2) MIMIC-IV-ECG: Extract RR intervals from 10-second ECGs for ICD-10 I60, I61, I63 cases and age-sex-matched non-stroke controls. Compute RMSSD, pNN50, SDNN approximation. Calculate same distributional metrics. Frequency-domain metrics acknowledged as unreliable from 10-second recordings and excluded or flagged. Both analyses cross-validated against each other. Pass criterion: Bhattacharyya > 0.1 AND p < 0.05 for at least 2 of 4 metrics in at least one dataset.
experiment_reviews.simulation_dataset: NHANES 2011-2014 HRV examination data (primary, full frequency-domain HRV available) + MIMIC-IV-ECG via PhysioNet/BigQuery (secondary, time-domain only)

experiment_reviews.title: Lateralized Autonomic Asymmetry in Acute-to-Subacute Stroke: Right vs. Left Hemispheric Lesion Effects on HRV and Baroreflex Sensitivity
experiment_reviews.reason: A meaningful computational proxy is feasible and should be run before committing to the expensive prospective arm. MIMIC-IV-ECG contains ICD-10 I63.x stroke cases with linked radiology notes amenable to scispaCy NLP lateralization classification. Time-domain HRV (SDNN, RMSSD) is extractable from 10-second recordings. The retrospective MIMIC arm (estimated n=400-900 with both ECG and imaging reports) can test whether any gross HRV lateralization signal exists in administrative data. This is explicitly recommended as a standalone pilot in the simplification options. Critically, the killer risks (10-second ECG limitation precluding frequency-domain HRV and BRS, NLP lateralization accuracy unknown, medication confounding) mean the full prospective study has a high probability of producing uninterpretable results without this prior signal check. The simulation cannot test BRS or insular moderation, but it can determine whether the hemisphere-HRV association is detectable at all, which is necessary before investing in Finapres equipment and 80-patient longitudinal recruitment. Note: c1b (ischemic vs. hemorrhagic subtype comparison) is a subset of this simulation and should be computed simultaneously.
experiment_reviews.simulation_description: MIMIC-IV-ECG retrospective analysis: (1) Extract all patients with ICD-10 I63.x codes who have ECG recordings within 48 hours of admission. (2) Apply scispaCy NLP to MIMIC-IV radiology notes to classify lesion laterality (right/left/bilateral/posterior fossa) with manual validation on a 10% random subsample to estimate NLP accuracy. (3) Compute time-domain HRV metrics (SDNN, RMSSD, mean RR, pNN50) from available ECG recordings. (4) Run linear regression: HRV ~ hemisphere + age + sex + severity surrogates (ICU admission, mechanical ventilation, vasopressor use) + medication flags (beta-blocker, antihypertensive). (5) Simultaneously stratify by stroke subtype (I60 SAH, I61 ICH, I63 ischemic) to address c1b. Report effect sizes and confidence intervals. If no lateralization signal detected in n>400, reconsider prospective investment.
experiment_reviews.simulation_dataset: MIMIC-IV-ECG via PhysioNet/BigQuery (ICD-10 I63.x cases with linked MIMIC-IV-Note radiology reports)

experiment_reviews.title: Signal Space Overlap Between Insular Stroke Autonomic Activation and Emotional Arousal: A Within-Subject Dissociation Experiment
experiment_reviews.reason: The computational proxy is explicitly acknowledged as fundamentally incomplete: EDA is absent from all public datasets, insular vs. non-insular lesion stratification is impossible in any public data, and the within-subject dissociation cannot be tested computationally. The core hypothesis requires MRI-confirmed insular involvement, simultaneous EDA+HRV recording, and a within-subject comparison of resting vs. emotional arousal states. No existing public dataset provides this combination. The DEAP-based GMM proxy can establish whether the algorithm works in principle but cannot test insular specificity, which is the entire scientific contribution. The paradigm threat level is revolutionary and the experiment is not redundant with published literature. Proceed to protocol with the simplified design: two groups (insular stroke vs. healthy controls, n=30 each), EDA+HRV only (drop facial EMG in Phase 1), 45-minute protocol, pre-trained DEAP GMM as reference classifier.

experiment_reviews.title: Muscle Synergy Stability Under Autonomic Perturbation in Stroke vs. Healthy Adults
experiment_reviews.reason: Three independent kill criteria apply. First, logical disconnect from the research program: this experiment tests EMG muscle synergy stability under cold pressor stress, which does not test any of the surviving claims (c1, c1b, c2, c3, c5, c6, c7). The claims concern HRV/EDA distributional shifts and affective classifier validity in stroke; synergy weight ICC under sympathetic perturbation is a separate motor control question with no dependency path to the affective computing program. Second, the killer risks are severe and compounding: cold pressor may fail to produce sufficient sympathetic activation in autonomically dysregulated stroke patients (manipulation check failure), spasticity-driven involuntary EMG will be inseparable from autonomic EMG contamination (the exact confound the study aims to disentangle), and NMF solutions in stroke patients with degraded synergies may be non-convergent across conditions making ICC computation meaningless. Third, the experiment is not foundational to any downstream claim in the dependency graph and its failure would not redirect the program. Resources are better allocated to c3, c5, and c6.

experiment_reviews.title: Longitudinal HRV Trajectory Mapping in Stroke Rehabilitation: Non-Monotonic Recovery and Within-Patient Drift Quantification
experiment_reviews.reason: MIMIC-IV-ECG contains stroke patients (ICD-10 I60-I69) with serial ECG recordings during hospitalization, enabling a computational test of whether non-monotonic HRV trajectory shapes are detectable in the acute phase (days 1-14). While this does not cover the full 6-month rehabilitation window, it provides a necessary prior probability estimate: if HRV trajectories are monotonically linear even in the acute phase with n>500 patients, the non-monotonicity hypothesis is weakened before committing to 6-month prospective monitoring. The NHANES cross-sectional variance comparison (stroke vs. non-stroke HRV variance as a proxy for drift magnitude) provides a second independent estimate. The simulation is genuinely informative, not hand-waving, because a positive result (non-linear AIC preference in acute trajectories) substantially increases the prior for the rehabilitation-phase claim, while a negative result triggers a redesign. The full prospective study remains necessary for the rehabilitation-timescale claim and the classifier concept-drift test, but should not be initiated without this computational gate.
experiment_reviews.simulation_description: MIMIC-IV-ECG: Extract all stroke-admission patients (ICD-10 I60-I69) with 3+ serial ECG recordings during hospitalization. Compute RMSSD and SDNN from each 10-second recording (time-domain only; frequency-domain excluded). Fit individual-level growth curve models (linear vs. quadratic vs. cubic spline) to each patient's acute HRV trajectory across days 1-14. Compare AIC across model families. Compute within-patient RMSSD SD across available recordings and compare to age-matched non-stroke controls in the same database using Mann-Whitney U. Report proportion of patients showing non-monotonic trajectory shape and effect size for within-patient drift vs. between-patient variability. NHANES supplement: compare HRV metric variance between stroke-history and non-stroke groups across age strata as a cross-sectional drift magnitude proxy.
experiment_reviews.simulation_dataset: MIMIC-IV-ECG via PhysioNet/BigQuery (primary, serial ECGs during stroke hospitalization) + NHANES 2011-2014 HRV examination data (secondary, cross-sectional variance comparison)

experiment_reviews.title: Hierarchical Ground Truth Acquisition for Affective State in Aphasic Stroke Patients
experiment_reviews.reason: No computational proxy can address the core validity question: whether FACS coding, VAMS pointing response, and behavioral proxies produce internally consistent affective labels in stroke patients with aphasia and facial paresis. This is an empirical measurement validity question that requires human participants with the specific neurological profile. No public dataset contains FACS coding + aphasia-compatible self-report + aphasia severity stratification in stroke patients. This experiment is also a hard dependency for c7 (the adaptive classifier trial requires valid ground truth labels). The paradigm threat level is moderate and the design is achievable. Proceed to protocol with the simplified design: reduce to 3 groups (no aphasia n=20, mild-moderate aphasia n=20, severe aphasia n=20) plus n=20 healthy controls; replace full manual FACS with OpenFace 2.0 automated AU detection with manual verification on 20% subsample; shorten session to 40 minutes; single-site pilot with pre-registration of FACS inter-rater reliability as a go/no-go gate before full enrollment.

experiment_reviews.title: Prospective Validation of Adaptive vs. Static Affective Classifiers in Stroke Rehabilitation
experiment_reviews.reason: This experiment has unresolved hard dependencies that make current execution premature and high-risk. It explicitly depends on: (1) stroke-cohort HRV priors from c1/c5 (not yet completed, routed to simulation); (2) valid ground truth labels from c6 (not yet completed, routed to protocol); (3) a validated adaptive classifier algorithm prototyped on DEAP (not yet done). Running c7 before c1, c5, and c6 produce results means the Bayesian prior initialization will be poorly estimated, the ground truth labels will be unvalidated, and the classifier comparison will be uninterpretable. Additionally, the killer risks are severe and compounding: FACS inter-rater reliability failure would collapse the primary outcome, EDA artifact rates >30% in hemiparetic patients would degrade the classifier to near-chance in both arms, and the concept drift confound (genuine clinical recovery vs. classifier adaptation) is analytically underpowered at n=50 over 8 weeks. This experiment should be re-proposed after c1 simulation, c5 simulation, and c6 protocol results are available. It is not killed permanently but is premature for current resource allocation.

protocol_experiments.title: Signal Space Overlap Between Insular Stroke Autonomic Activation and Emotional Arousal: A Within-Subject Dissociation Experiment
protocol_experiments.hypothesis_to_test: In stroke patients with insular cortex involvement, resting-state EDA and HRV signals occupy the same multivariate signal space as emotional arousal signals in healthy controls, creating a systematic signal identity confound that is quantifiably more severe than in non-insular stroke patients or healthy controls.
protocol_experiments.method: Three-group cross-sectional study: (A) insular stroke patients (MRI-confirmed insular involvement, n=30), (B) non-insular stroke patients (matched volume, no insular involvement, n=30), (C) age-sex-matched healthy controls (n=30). All participants undergo a standardized 90-minute protocol: (1) 10-minute resting baseline; (2) emotionally neutral cognitive task (digit span); (3) standardized emotional arousal induction (validated film clips: neutral, positive, negative, high-arousal); (4) second resting baseline. Simultaneously record ECG (HRV), EDA (wrist-worn), and facial EMG (zygomaticus, corrugator). Extract EDA features (SCR amplitude, SCL, SCR frequency), HRV features (SDNN, RMSSD, LF/HF), and facial EMG features. Train a Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) on healthy control emotional arousal data (high-arousal vs. low-arousal states). Apply this GMM to the resting-state data of insular stroke patients, non-insular stroke patients, and healthy controls. Quantify what fraction of resting-state samples from each group fall within the high-arousal cluster of the healthy-control GMM. Use Mahalanobis distance to quantify signal space overlap between resting stroke physiology and healthy-control arousal states.
measurements: EDA: skin conductance level (SCL, µS), SCR amplitude (µS), SCR frequency (events/min)
HRV: SDNN, RMSSD, LF power, HF power, LF/HF ratio
Facial EMG: zygomaticus and corrugator mean amplitude during emotion clips
Mahalanobis distance from each participant's resting-state feature vector to healthy-control high-arousal GMM centroid
Fraction of resting-state windows classified as 'high arousal' by healthy-control GMM
Insular lesion volume (cm³) and laterality from MRI
Plasma norepinephrine at rest (sympathetic tone biomarker)
Self-reported arousal during rest (Visual Analogue Scale — adapted for aphasia)
NIHSS and Barthel Index
Classifier confusion matrix: healthy-population arousal classifier applied to all three groups
protocol_experiments.what_makes_it_audacious: Nobody has directly measured whether the autonomic signal produced by insular stroke damage is geometrically indistinguishable from emotional arousal in the feature space used by affective classifiers. The insular cortex literature and the affective computing literature have never been brought into the same experiment. The assumption being challenged is that 'resting state' is a clean baseline in stroke patients — this experiment tests whether insular damage makes the resting state physiologically mimic arousal, making affective computing fundamentally ambiguous in this population.
protocol_experiments.expected_if_true: Insular stroke patients' resting-state EDA/HRV vectors fall within the healthy-control high-arousal GMM cluster at a rate ≥3× higher than healthy controls' resting state (e.g., 45% vs. 15% of windows classified as high-arousal). Mahalanobis distance from insular stroke resting state to healthy-control arousal centroid is significantly smaller than from non-insular stroke or healthy control resting state.
protocol_experiments.expected_if_false: Insular stroke resting-state signals are not closer to the healthy-control arousal cluster than non-insular stroke or healthy control resting signals. This would mean the signal identity problem is not insular-lesion-specific, suggesting the confound is a general post-stroke phenomenon rather than an insular-specific one — redirecting intervention design toward stroke-wide rather than lesion-targeted calibration strategies.
required_expertise: Psychophysiology (EDA, HRV, facial EMG recording and analysis)
Affective computing and machine learning (GMM, Mahalanobis distance)

data_availability.computational_proxy: Partial — DEAP dataset contains EDA/HRV during emotional stimuli in healthy controls and can be used to build the reference GMM. MIMIC-IV-ECG can provide resting HRV distributions for stroke patients. However, the critical within-subject dissociation (resting stroke physiology vs. emotional arousal in the same individuals) requires the prospective study. Pilot: build healthy-control arousal GMM from DEAP, then project MIMIC-IV stroke resting HRV into that space to estimate overlap — runnable in 2–3 weeks.

protocol_experiments.title: Hierarchical Ground Truth Acquisition for Affective State in Aphasic Stroke Patients: Validating Multi-Modal Behavioral Proxies Against Aphasia-Compatible Self-Report
protocol_experiments.hypothesis_to_test: A hierarchical ground-truth acquisition strategy combining aphasia-compatible self-report (Visual Analogue Mood Scale), observer-rated facial action coding (FACS), and behavioral proxies (engagement duration, task withdrawal) produces internally consistent affective state labels in stroke patients with aphasia, with inter-rater reliability κ > 0.6 and convergent validity r > 0.5 between VAMS and FACS-derived affect ratings.
protocol_experiments.method: Cross-sectional validation study in 60 stroke patients stratified by aphasia severity (20 no aphasia, 20 mild-moderate aphasia [WAB-R AQ 50–93], 20 severe aphasia [WAB-R AQ < 50]) and 20 healthy controls. Each participant undergoes a 60-minute standardized session: (1) baseline rest; (2) positive emotional induction (personally meaningful photographs, music); (3) frustration induction (unsolvable puzzle adapted for motor impairment); (4) recovery rest. Ground truth is acquired simultaneously via: (a) VAMS (self-report, administered with pointing response for aphasic patients); (b) Stroke Aphasic Depression Questionnaire (SADQ, observer-rated); (c) FACS coding of video-recorded facial expressions by two certified FACS coders blind to condition; (d) behavioral proxies (task engagement duration, withdrawal attempts, vocalizations coded for valence). Physiological signals (ECG, EDA, wrist PPG) are recorded throughout. Primary analyses: (1) inter-rater reliability between FACS coders (Cohen's κ); (2) convergent validity between VAMS and FACS ratings (Pearson r, stratified by aphasia severity); (3) temporal alignment analysis: do behavioral proxies (event-level) correlate with session-level VAMS ratings? (4) test whether physiological signals predict FACS-coded affect better than VAMS in severe aphasia.
measurements: VAMS scores (0–100 mm) for happiness, sadness, anxiety, anger at each condition
SADQ total score and subscale scores
FACS action unit frequencies and intensities per 30-second epoch (two independent coders)
Inter-rater reliability: Cohen's κ for FACS affect categories
Convergent validity: Pearson r between VAMS and FACS-derived affect ratings
Behavioral proxies: task engagement duration (seconds), withdrawal attempts (count), vocalization valence codes
Temporal alignment: correlation between event-level behavioral proxies and session-level VAMS
WAB-R Aphasia Quotient (aphasia severity)
ECG-derived HRV metrics per condition
EDA (SCL, SCR) per condition
Wrist PPG-derived HRV per condition
Classifier performance: physiological signal prediction of FACS vs. VAMS labels, stratified by aphasia severity
protocol_experiments.what_makes_it_audacious: Affective computing validation studies universally rely on self-report ground truth, which is unavailable or unreliable in severe aphasia — yet no study has systematically validated a hierarchical multi-modal ground truth strategy specifically for this population. The assumption being challenged is that ground truth acquisition is a solved problem. This experiment tests whether FACS and behavioral proxies can substitute for self-report in severe aphasia, and whether the substitution introduces systematic bias. The temporal scale mismatch (event-level proxies vs. session-level ratings) is a methodological problem that has never been formally characterized.
protocol_experiments.expected_if_true: FACS-VAMS convergent validity r > 0.6 in no-aphasia and mild-aphasia groups; r remains > 0.4 in severe aphasia; inter-rater FACS κ > 0.7; behavioral proxies correlate with session-level VAMS at r > 0.5 in no-aphasia group but decline to r < 0.3 in severe aphasia, quantifying the temporal mismatch problem.
protocol_experiments.expected_if_false: FACS-VAMS convergent validity r < 0.3 even in no-aphasia group, or inter-rater FACS κ < 0.5. This would indicate that FACS coding is not a valid substitute for self-report even in non-aphasic stroke patients — a finding that would fundamentally challenge the feasibility of affective computing validation in stroke rehabilitation and redirect the field toward purely physiological or caregiver-report approaches.

data_availability.computational_proxy: Limited — DEAP and MAHNOB-HCI contain FACS + physiological data in healthy subjects and can be used to benchmark FACS-physiology relationships before the stroke study. No public dataset contains FACS + VAMS + aphasia severity in stroke patients. Pilot: use DEAP to establish expected FACS-HRV correlations in healthy subjects as a reference benchmark, then compare against stroke patient data to quantify degradation.

simulation_tasks.title: Systematic HRV Distribution Shift in Subacute-to-Chronic Stroke vs. Age-Sex-Matched Controls: A Multi-Site Cross-Sectional Study with Computational Pre-Validation
simulation_tasks.hypothesis_to_test: Stroke survivors in subacute (2–12 weeks) and chronic (>6 months) rehabilitation phases exhibit HRV distributions shifted relative to age-sex-matched healthy controls, with Bhattacharyya distance > 0.1 and Cohen's d > 0.3 for at least two of four metrics (SDNN, RMSSD, HF power, LF/HF ratio), and this shift is large enough to produce systematic bias when healthy-population-trained affective classifiers are applied to stroke patients.
simulation_tasks.method: Phase 1 (Computational Pilot, 3 months): Extract 5-minute resting HRV epochs from MIMIC-IV-ECG for ICD-10 coded ischemic (I63) and hemorrhagic (I60, I61) stroke admissions (estimated n=800–1,200) and age-sex-matched non-stroke controls from the same database. Compute SDNN, RMSSD, HF power, and LF/HF ratio. Calculate Bhattacharyya distance, Kullback-Leibler divergence, Cohen's d, and Mann-Whitney U statistics for each metric. Cross-validate against NHANES participants with self-reported stroke history vs. no stroke history. Phase 2 (Prospective Clinical Study, 18 months): Recruit 120 stroke survivors (60 subacute, 60 chronic) from inpatient and outpatient rehabilitation units at 2–3 sites, plus 120 age-sex-matched healthy controls. Record 24-hour Holter ECG and 5-minute laboratory resting ECG. Apply a commercially available healthy-population-trained affective HRV classifier (e.g., Empatica E4 SDK or comparable validated system) to both groups during standardized emotional stimuli (IAPS images, validated for stroke populations). Measure classifier output (arousal/valence estimates) and compare against ground truth from behavioral ratings and facial action coding. Compute distributional overlap metrics and classifier bias indices (systematic over/under-estimation of arousal).
simulation_tasks.simulation_description: Two-part analysis: (1) NHANES 2011-2014: Download HRV examination files, merge with MCQ160f stroke indicator, demographics, and medication variables. Compute SDNN, RMSSD, HF power, LF/HF distributions for stroke-positive vs. stroke-negative participants matched on age and sex. Run Mann-Whitney U with Bonferroni correction, compute Bhattacharyya distance and Cohen's d for each metric. (2) MIMIC-IV-ECG: Extract RR intervals from 10-second ECGs for ICD-10 I60, I61, I63 cases and age-sex-matched non-stroke controls. Compute RMSSD, pNN50, SDNN approximation. Calculate same distributional metrics. Frequency-domain metrics acknowledged as unreliable from 10-second recordings and excluded or flagged. Both analyses cross-validated against each other. Pass criterion: Bhattacharyya > 0.1 AND p < 0.05 for at least 2 of 4 metrics in at least one dataset.
simulation_tasks.simulation_dataset: NHANES 2011-2014 HRV examination data (primary, full frequency-domain HRV available) + MIMIC-IV-ECG via PhysioNet/BigQuery (secondary, time-domain only)

feasibility.experiment_title: Systematic HRV Distribution Shift in Subacute-to-Chronic Stroke vs. Age-Sex-Matched Controls: A Multi-Site Cross-Sectional Study with Computational Pre-Validation

required: 24-hour Holter ECG monitors (minimum 10 units for rolling recruitment)
Laboratory-grade ECG acquisition system (5-minute resting recordings)
IAPS image display system (calibrated monitor, standardized viewing distance)
Facial action coding system or automated FACS software (e.g., iMotions, OpenFace)
Empatica E4 or comparable wrist-worn physiological sensor with SDK access
Secure clinical data server for multi-site data aggregation
High-performance computing access for MIMIC-IV-ECG BigQuery queries and HRV batch processing
equipment.availability: All equipment is commercially available and present in most clinical research cardiology or rehabilitation medicine labs. Holter monitors are standard clinical equipment. IAPS license requires institutional application but is routinely granted. BigQuery access to MIMIC-IV-ECG requires PhysioNet credentialing (free, ~1 week turnaround). No exotic or custom hardware required.
equipment.cost_estimate: Phase 1 computational pilot: ~$500–2,000 (cloud compute for BigQuery, analyst time). Phase 2 clinical study: $150,000–350,000 total (Holter monitors $5,000–15,000, participant compensation $30,000–60,000, research coordinator salaries dominate, multi-site coordination overhead, affective computing software licenses $5,000–20,000). Total grant budget: $200,000–400,000 over 2 years.

required: HRV signal processing specialist (neurokit2/Python or MATLAB HRV toolbox proficiency)
Stroke rehabilitation physician or neurologist (patient eligibility, NIHSS scoring)
Clinical research coordinator with IRB/consent experience in stroke populations
Affective computing researcher familiar with IAPS paradigms and physiological classifiers
Biostatistician with distributional comparison methods expertise (Bhattacharyya, KL divergence)
Neuroimaging reader for lesion localization from clinical MRI reports
Data engineer for MIMIC-IV BigQuery extraction and NHANES linkage
expertise.rarity: This specific combination is uncommon but achievable. Cardiac autonomic neurology labs exist at most academic medical centers. The affective computing + stroke rehabilitation crossover is rare — perhaps 15–30 labs globally have all components. However, the experiment can be assembled from collaborators across departments (neurology + biomedical engineering + psychology) without requiring a single lab to have all expertise. The computational pilot requires only HRV signal processing and biostatistics skills, available at hundreds of institutions.

sample.type: Phase 1: Retrospective EHR/waveform cohort from MIMIC-IV-ECG (hospitalized patients with ICD-10 stroke codes I60, I61, I63) and NHANES participants with self-reported stroke history. Phase 2: Prospective recruitment of stroke survivors in subacute (2–12 weeks post-stroke) and chronic (>6 months post-stroke) rehabilitation phases from inpatient and outpatient rehabilitation units, plus age-sex-matched healthy community controls.
sample.size: Phase 1: Estimated 800–1,500 stroke cases in MIMIC-IV-ECG with extractable ECG waveforms; 400–600 NHANES stroke-positive participants with HRV variables. Controls matched 1:1 from same databases. Phase 2: 120 stroke survivors (60 subacute, 60 chronic) + 120 matched controls = 240 total. Power justification: with Cohen's d = 0.5 (medium effect, conservative estimate), alpha = 0.05, power = 0.80, two-sample t-test requires n = 64 per group; 60 per subgroup provides adequate power with Bonferroni correction across 4 HRV metrics requiring d ≈ 0.6 per metric. Attrition buffer of 20% already factored into 60-per-subgroup target.
sample.ethical_concerns: Phase 1 is retrospective de-identified data — MIMIC-IV and NHANES are both publicly available under data use agreements, minimal IRB burden (likely exempt or expedited review). Phase 2 requires full IRB approval: stroke patients are a vulnerable population with potential cognitive and communication impairments affecting consent capacity. Surrogate consent procedures may be needed for subacute patients. IAPS stimuli include emotionally negative images — distress monitoring protocol required. Exclusion criteria must address post-stroke depression, aphasia severity, and cardiac devices (pacemakers invalidate HRV). Multi-site coordination requires IRB reliance agreements. These are manageable but non-trivial ethical requirements.

feasibility.timeline: Month 1–3: IRB submissions, MIMIC-IV credentialing, NHANES data download, Phase 1 computational pilot execution. Month 4–6: Phase 1 analysis complete, manuscript drafted, Phase 2 site setup and staff training. Month 7–24: Phase 2 prospective recruitment and data collection (18-month window for 240 participants across 2–3 sites). Month 25–30: Phase 2 analysis, classifier bias quantification, manuscript preparation. Total: approximately 30 months from funding to submitted results. Realistically 3 years to publication.
simplification_options: Run Phase 1 computational pilot only as a standalone publication: MIMIC-IV-ECG + NHANES analysis answers the primary distributional shift question with no patient recruitment, no IRB burden beyond data use agreements, and can be completed in 2–4 months. This is publishable independently and de-risks the full study.

Replace 24-hour Holter with 5-minute resting ECG only: reduces equipment cost and participant burden substantially, still captures SDNN, RMSSD, HF power, LF/HF for the primary hypothesis. Loses circadian HRV information but preserves core distributional comparison.

Drop the affective classifier validation component (Phase 2 IAPS paradigm) and focus solely on HRV distributional characterization: simpler design, faster IRB approval, no need for affective computing expertise or IAPS license. Answers whether the shift exists; defers the classifier bias question to a follow-up study.

Single-site design with 80 participants (40 stroke, 40 controls) to establish proof-of-concept before multi-site expansion: reduces coordination overhead and cost by ~50%, still adequately powered for d = 0.6.

Use wrist-worn consumer devices (Empatica E4, Polar H10) instead of clinical Holter monitors for the chronic outpatient group: reduces equipment cost and enables remote data collection, though signal quality is lower and requires validation against clinical ECG in a subset.
killer_risks: MIMIC-IV-ECG recording duration problem: MIMIC-IV-ECG contains 10-second diagnostic ECGs, not 5-minute recordings. Frequency-domain HRV (HF power, LF/HF ratio) requires minimum 2–5 minutes of stationary RR intervals. This makes the computational pilot's spectral HRV analysis unreliable or impossible from MIMIC-IV-ECG alone. Time-domain metrics (SDNN, RMSSD) from 10-second recordings are non-standard and not comparable to clinical 5-minute norms. This is a fundamental methodological constraint that must be addressed upfront.

NHANES HRV data limitations: NHANES HRV examination data (available in 2011–2014 cycles) uses a specific 2-minute resting ECG protocol with its own normative values. Self-reported stroke history in NHANES has low sensitivity and does not capture stroke timing (subacute vs. chronic) or severity. The NHANES proxy is weaker than the proposal implies.

Medication confounding: Beta-blockers and antihypertensives are nearly universal in post-stroke patients and profoundly suppress HRV. If the distributional shift is primarily medication-driven rather than neurological, the finding is clinically real but mechanistically different from autonomic dysregulation. Disentangling this requires large enough subgroups of medication-free or medication-naive patients, which may be impossible in stroke populations.

Cognitive and communication impairments in subacute stroke patients: Aphasia, neglect, and cognitive deficits may prevent reliable behavioral ratings of IAPS stimuli (the ground truth for classifier bias assessment). If ground truth is unreliable, the classifier bias index is uninterpretable. The study may need to exclude patients with significant aphasia, which biases the sample toward milder strokes.

Affective classifier access and reproducibility: Commercial affective HRV classifiers (Empatica SDK) may not be publicly documented, may change between software versions, and may not be independently replicable. If the classifier is a black box, the bias index cannot be decomposed or generalized. The study should pre-register the specific classifier version and algorithm.

Selection bias in rehabilitation recruitment: Patients enrolled in rehabilitation programs are systematically healthier and less severely affected than the full stroke population. The distributional shift may be underestimated relative to acute or severely affected patients.

Heterogeneity of stroke: Ischemic vs. hemorrhagic, cortical vs. subcortical, insular vs. non-insular lesions have very different autonomic profiles. With n=60 per subgroup, there is insufficient power to test lesion-location moderation (insular vs. non-insular) as a secondary analysis without inflating Type I error.

public_datasets: MIMIC_IV_ECG: MIMIC-IV-ECG (PhysioNet/BigQuery) — 800K+ 12-lead ECG waveforms linked to MIMIC-IV clinical data with ICD-10 codes. Stroke cohort extractable via I60, I61, I63 codes. CRITICAL CAVEAT: recordings are 10-second diagnostic ECGs, not 5-minute resting recordings. Time-domain HRV (SDNN, RMSSD) from 10-second segments is non-standard; frequency-domain HRV is unreliable. Useful for RR interval distribution comparison and time-domain proxies only. Age, sex, and comorbidity matching possible from linked clinical data.

NHANES: NHANES 2011–2014 HRV examination data — contains SDNN, RMSSD, HF power, LF/HF ratio from 2-minute resting ECG protocol, plus self-reported stroke history (MCQ160f variable), demographics, and medication use. Approximately 400–600 stroke-positive participants with HRV data available. Enables distributional comparison of HRV metrics between stroke and non-stroke community-dwelling adults. Limitations: self-reported stroke (no imaging confirmation), no stroke timing, no severity data, 2-minute protocol differs from clinical 5-minute standard.
data_availability.proxy_description: A two-part computational proxy is feasible before any patient recruitment. Part A (MIMIC-IV-ECG): Extract RR interval sequences from 10-second ECGs for ICD-10 stroke cases (I60, I61, I63) and age-sex-matched non-stroke controls. Compute time-domain HRV metrics (RMSSD, pNN50, SDNN approximation) from 10-second segments. Calculate Bhattacharyya distance, KL divergence, and Cohen's d between stroke and control distributions. Acknowledge frequency-domain limitations explicitly. Part B (NHANES): Download NHANES 2011–2014 HRV examination files (publicly available, no credentialing required beyond data use agreement). Merge with MCQ160f (stroke history), demographics, and medication variables. Compute distributional overlap metrics for SDNN, RMSSD, HF power, and LF/HF ratio between stroke-positive and stroke-negative participants, stratified by age and sex. Run Mann-Whitney U tests with Bonferroni correction. Both analyses executable in Python (neurokit2, scipy, pandas) within 2–4 weeks. Together they provide population-level evidence for or against the distributional shift hypothesis across two independent datasets with different recording protocols.
data_availability.proxy_limitations: The computational proxy cannot answer: (1) whether the shift is present specifically in subacute vs. chronic rehabilitation phases (MIMIC-IV captures acute hospitalization; NHANES captures community-dwelling survivors of unknown chronicity); (2) whether the shift biases real-time affective classifiers during emotional stimuli — this requires the IAPS paradigm with behavioral ground truth; (3) whether insular lesion location moderates the shift (no imaging data in MIMIC-IV-ECG or NHANES at the required granularity); (4) whether 24-hour ambulatory HRV shows the same pattern as resting laboratory recordings; (5) medication effects cannot be fully controlled in NHANES due to limited pharmacological detail. The proxy establishes whether the distributional shift exists at population level; only the full prospective study establishes its clinical and affective computing implications.

simulation_tasks.title: Lateralized Autonomic Asymmetry in Acute-to-Subacute Stroke: Right vs. Left Hemispheric Lesion Effects on HRV and Baroreflex Sensitivity
simulation_tasks.hypothesis_to_test: Right hemispheric stroke produces greater sympathetic hyperactivation (elevated LF/HF ratio, reduced baroreflex sensitivity) than left hemispheric stroke of matched volume, consistent with right-hemispheric predominance in cardiac sympathetic control, with the lateralization effect surviving adjustment for lesion volume and NIHSS severity.
simulation_tasks.method: Retrospective-prospective hybrid design. Phase 1 (Retrospective): Query MIMIC-IV-ECG for patients with acute ischemic stroke (I63) who have both ECG data and available imaging reports. Use NLP extraction (scispaCy) on radiology reports to classify lesions as right-hemispheric, left-hemispheric, bilateral, or brainstem/cerebellar. Extract HRV metrics from the first 24-hour ECG epoch post-admission. Phase 2 (Prospective): Recruit 80 subacute stroke patients (40 right-hemisphere, 40 left-hemisphere, confirmed by MRI DWI with lesion volume quantified via FSL or FreeSurfer lesion tools) at 2 stroke rehabilitation centers. Record 24-hour Holter ECG at weeks 2, 6, and 12 post-stroke. Measure baroreflex sensitivity (BRS) using the sequence method from continuous beat-to-beat blood pressure (Finapres or Task Force Monitor) and simultaneous ECG. Compute time-domain HRV (SDNN, RMSSD), frequency-domain HRV (LF, HF, LF/HF), and BRS. Use linear mixed models with hemisphere (right/left) × time interaction, covarying for lesion volume, NIHSS, age, sex, and autonomic medications.
simulation_tasks.simulation_description: MIMIC-IV-ECG retrospective analysis: (1) Extract all patients with ICD-10 I63.x codes who have ECG recordings within 48 hours of admission. (2) Apply scispaCy NLP to MIMIC-IV radiology notes to classify lesion laterality (right/left/bilateral/posterior fossa) with manual validation on a 10% random subsample to estimate NLP accuracy. (3) Compute time-domain HRV metrics (SDNN, RMSSD, mean RR, pNN50) from available ECG recordings. (4) Run linear regression: HRV ~ hemisphere + age + sex + severity surrogates (ICU admission, mechanical ventilation, vasopressor use) + medication flags (beta-blocker, antihypertensive). (5) Simultaneously stratify by stroke subtype (I60 SAH, I61 ICH, I63 ischemic) to address c1b. Report effect sizes and confidence intervals. If no lateralization signal detected in n>400, reconsider prospective investment.
simulation_tasks.simulation_dataset: MIMIC-IV-ECG via PhysioNet/BigQuery (ICD-10 I63.x cases with linked MIMIC-IV-Note radiology reports)

feasibility.experiment_title: Lateralized Autonomic Asymmetry in Acute-to-Subacute Stroke: Right vs. Left Hemispheric Lesion Effects on HRV and Baroreflex Sensitivity

required: 24-hour Holter ECG recorder (3-lead or 12-lead)
Continuous beat-to-beat blood pressure monitor (Finapres NOVA or Task Force Monitor)
3T MRI scanner with DWI capability for lesion segmentation
FSL or FreeSurfer neuroimaging software suite
HRV analysis software (Kubios HRV or custom Python/MATLAB pipeline)
Sequence method BRS analysis software

equipment.availability: Holter ECG and MRI are standard at stroke rehabilitation centers. Finapres/Task Force Monitor is less common but available at ~50-100 academic medical centers with autonomic labs. FSL/FreeSurfer are free software. BigQuery MIMIC-IV access requires PhysioNet credentialing (free, ~2 weeks). The bottleneck is co-locating continuous BP monitoring with stroke rehabilitation infrastructure.
equipment.cost_estimate: $180,000–$320,000 total for prospective arm (Holter equipment rental/purchase ~$20K, Finapres units ~$40K, MRI scan costs ~$60K for 80 patients x 3 timepoints if not covered by clinical care, personnel ~$120K over 2 years, biomarker assays ~$15K). Retrospective MIMIC arm: ~$5,000 (compute costs, personnel time).

required: Stroke neurologist with MRI lesion localization experience
Cardiac autonomic physiologist familiar with baroreflex sequence method
Neuroimaging analyst (FSL/FreeSurfer lesion segmentation)
HRV signal processing engineer
Clinical NLP developer (scispaCy, radiology report parsing)
Biostatistician with linear mixed models experience
Rehabilitation medicine physician for patient access and safety monitoring
IRB-experienced clinical research coordinator
expertise.rarity: The combination of stroke neurology + autonomic physiology + neuroimaging is rare. Roughly 15-25 academic centers worldwide have all three capabilities co-located. Individual expertise pools are larger but the intersection is the constraint. Groups at UCL, Mayo Clinic, Karolinska, and a handful of German stroke centers have published adjacent work.

sample.type: Adult patients with first-ever acute ischemic stroke confirmed by MRI DWI, classified as right-hemispheric or left-hemispheric (excluding bilateral and posterior fossa lesions), recruited at stroke rehabilitation centers during subacute phase (days 7-14 post-stroke)
sample.size: N=80 prospective (40 right, 40 left) provides ~80% power to detect a medium effect size (Cohen's d=0.65) for hemisphere × HRV interaction at alpha=0.05 in mixed models, assuming 15% attrition. This is likely underpowered for the insular cortex moderation analysis, which would require N=120-160 to detect interaction effects. The MIMIC retrospective arm may yield N=400-800 usable cases for HRV proxy analysis.
sample.ethical_concerns: Standard IRB approval required. Key concerns: (1) Capacity to consent in acute stroke patients with aphasia or cognitive impairment — requires surrogate consent protocols; (2) Continuous BP monitoring with Finapres is non-invasive but requires patient cooperation during subacute recovery; (3) Plasma catecholamine draws require venipuncture in a vulnerable population; (4) MIMIC-IV retrospective arm requires PhysioNet DUA but no additional IRB if using de-identified data. Overall: manageable but requires careful consent procedures and likely a DSMB for the prospective arm.

feasibility.timeline: Phase 1 (MIMIC retrospective): 4-6 months from credentialing to results. Phase 2 (prospective): 18-24 months recruitment + 3 months follow-up per patient + 6 months analysis = 30-36 months total. Full study from funding to publication: 3-4 years.
simplification_options: Run MIMIC-IV retrospective arm first as a standalone pilot (6 months, ~$10K) — if no signal in HRV lateralization in N=500+ patients, reconsider prospective investment
Drop plasma catecholamines to reduce invasiveness and cost (~$15K savings, simplifies IRB)
Reduce to 2 timepoints (week 2 and week 12) instead of 3 to cut 33% of follow-up burden

Use NHANES HRV data (SDNN, RMSSD, LF/HF available) with self-reported stroke (MCQ160f) as a population-level cross-sectional proxy — cannot lateralize but can establish HRV-stroke association magnitude
Limit to single-center with N=40 as a pilot feasibility study to establish effect size estimates before multi-center expansion
Replace Finapres continuous BP with oscillometric BRS estimation (less precise but widely available) to eliminate the specialized equipment bottleneck
killer_risks: Lesion heterogeneity: Right-hemisphere strokes are not anatomically uniform — MCA territory vs. watershed vs. lacunar infarcts have vastly different autonomic pathway involvement. N=40 per hemisphere may be insufficient to control for this, making the hemisphere × HRV interaction uninterpretable without stratification that the sample size cannot support.

Medication confounding: Post-stroke patients are heavily medicated with beta-blockers, ACE inhibitors, and antiarrhythmics that directly suppress HRV and BRS. Even with medication inventory as a covariate, differential prescribing by hemisphere (e.g., right-hemisphere patients with more cardiac complications receiving more beta-blockers) could mask or create spurious lateralization effects.

MIMIC-IV ECG limitation: MIMIC-IV-ECG records are 10-second diagnostic ECGs, not 24-hour Holter recordings. Frequency-domain HRV (LF, HF, LF/HF) requires minimum 5-minute recordings; 10-second ECGs yield only heart rate and limited time-domain metrics. The retrospective arm cannot test the primary frequency-domain hypothesis and may only provide weak HRV proxies.

NLP lateralization accuracy: scispaCy extraction of lesion laterality from radiology reports has unknown sensitivity/specificity in MIMIC-IV. Misclassification of hemisphere (e.g., bilateral lesions coded as unilateral, or watershed lesions with ambiguous laterality) will attenuate the effect toward null, potentially producing a false-negative result.

Attrition bias: Patients with the most severe right-hemisphere strokes (highest autonomic derangement) may be least able to complete 12-week follow-up due to mortality, medical complications, or inability to cooperate with Finapres monitoring. This survivorship bias would systematically underestimate the right-hemisphere autonomic effect.

Insular cortex moderation is underpowered: The most scientifically interesting question — whether insular involvement, not hemisphere per se, drives the effect — requires a 2x2 design (hemisphere × insular involvement) that needs N=160+ to detect interaction effects, making the N=80 prospective arm insufficient for this key dissociation.

public_datasets: MIMIC_IV_ECG: MIMIC-IV-ECG via PhysioNet/BigQuery — 800K+ 12-lead ECGs linked to MIMIC-IV clinical data with ICD-10 I63 stroke codes. Can extract time-domain HRV (SDNN, RMSSD from R-R intervals) from 10-second recordings as a proxy. Radiology reports accessible via MIMIC-IV-Note for NLP lateralization. Critical limitation: 10-second recordings preclude frequency-domain HRV and BRS computation. Estimated usable stroke cohort: 400-900 patients with both ECG and imaging reports.

NHANES: NHANES cycles 2011-2014 include resting HRV examination data (SDNN, RMSSD, LF power, HF power, LF/HF ratio from 2-minute ECG recordings) and self-reported stroke history (MCQ160f). Can test whether stroke survivors show different HRV profiles vs. controls at population scale. Cannot lateralize strokes. Provides population-level HRV-stroke effect size estimates to power the prospective study. N~200-400 stroke survivors across cycles.
data_availability.proxy_description: Two-stage computational proxy: (1) MIMIC-IV-ECG analysis: Extract all patients with ICD-10 I63.x codes who have ECG recordings within 48 hours of admission. Apply scispaCy NLP to MIMIC-IV radiology notes to classify lesion laterality (right/left/bilateral/posterior). Compute time-domain HRV metrics (SDNN, RMSSD, mean RR, pNN50) from available ECG recordings. Run linear regression: HRV ~ hemisphere + age + sex + NIHSS_proxy (e.g., ICU admission, mechanical ventilation as severity surrogates) + medication flags. (2) NHANES cross-sectional analysis: Compare HRV metrics (SDNN, RMSSD, LF/HF from examination data) between self-reported stroke survivors and matched controls, stratified by age, sex, and cardiovascular medication use. Estimate effect sizes for HRV depression post-stroke to inform prospective sample size calculations.
data_availability.proxy_limitations: The computational proxy cannot: (1) test frequency-domain HRV or LF/HF ratio with statistical validity from 10-second ECGs; (2) measure baroreflex sensitivity at all — BRS requires simultaneous continuous BP and ECG, unavailable in any public dataset; (3) lateralize strokes in NHANES (no imaging data); (4) test longitudinal recovery trajectories (MIMIC is cross-sectional at admission, NHANES is cross-sectional); (5) dissociate insular cortex involvement from hemisphere — the core scientific question. The proxy can only establish whether a gross HRV signal exists in administrative stroke data, not whether it is lateralized or mediated by insular involvement. Only the full prospective experiment with Holter + Finapres + MRI lesion segmentation can answer the primary hypothesis.

simulation_tasks.title: Longitudinal HRV Trajectory Mapping in Stroke Rehabilitation: Non-Monotonic Recovery and Within-Patient Drift Quantification
simulation_tasks.hypothesis_to_test: HRV recovery trajectories in stroke survivors across 6 months of rehabilitation are non-monotonic (exhibiting at least one inflection point), with within-patient HRV baseline drift exceeding the between-session variability of healthy controls by a factor of ≥2, rendering static healthy-population classifier baselines clinically inadequate across rehabilitation timescales.
simulation_tasks.method: Prospective longitudinal cohort study: 80 subacute stroke survivors (NIHSS 4–20 at enrollment, 2–4 weeks post-stroke) recruited from 2 inpatient rehabilitation units. Participants wear a medical-grade wearable ECG monitor (e.g., Holter patch, Zio XT or equivalent) continuously for the first 2 weeks of each measurement month, at months 1, 2, 3, and 6 post-stroke. Additionally, 40 age-sex-matched healthy controls wear the same monitor at months 1 and 6 (to quantify healthy-population between-occasion variability). Extract daily HRV metrics (SDNN, RMSSD, HF power, LF/HF) from each 24-hour epoch. Fit individual-level growth curve models (multilevel spline regression) to each patient's HRV trajectory. Test for non-monotonicity by comparing linear vs. quadratic vs. cubic spline fits using AIC. Quantify within-patient drift as the standard deviation of daily RMSSD across the 6-month period. Compare within-patient drift magnitude to between-session variability in healthy controls. Apply a static healthy-population-trained HRV affective classifier (trained on month-1 data) to month-6 data and measure classification accuracy degradation as a function of individual drift magnitude.
simulation_tasks.simulation_description: MIMIC-IV-ECG: Extract all stroke-admission patients (ICD-10 I60-I69) with 3+ serial ECG recordings during hospitalization. Compute RMSSD and SDNN from each 10-second recording (time-domain only; frequency-domain excluded). Fit individual-level growth curve models (linear vs. quadratic vs. cubic spline) to each patient's acute HRV trajectory across days 1-14. Compare AIC across model families. Compute within-patient RMSSD SD across available recordings and compare to age-matched non-stroke controls in the same database using Mann-Whitney U. Report proportion of patients showing non-monotonic trajectory shape and effect size for within-patient drift vs. between-patient variability. NHANES supplement: compare HRV metric variance between stroke-history and non-stroke groups across age strata as a cross-sectional drift magnitude proxy.
simulation_tasks.simulation_dataset: MIMIC-IV-ECG via PhysioNet/BigQuery (primary, serial ECGs during stroke hospitalization) + NHANES 2011-2014 HRV examination data (secondary, cross-sectional variance comparison)

feasibility.experiment_title: Longitudinal HRV Trajectory Mapping in Stroke Rehabilitation: Non-Monotonic Recovery and Within-Patient Drift Quantification

required: Medical-grade continuous ECG patch monitors (Zio XT or equivalent, ~120 units for 80 patients + 40 controls across 4 measurement windows)
Secure clinical data server for waveform storage (TB-scale)
HRV analysis software pipeline (Kubios, custom Python/R with neurokit2)
REDCap or equivalent clinical data management system
Statistical computing environment (R with lme4/nlme for multilevel spline models)
equipment.availability: Medical-grade Holter patches are commercially available and FDA-cleared. Zio XT (iRhythm) is widely used in clinical research. Data infrastructure is standard at academic medical centers. No exotic equipment required.
equipment.cost_estimate: $180,000–$320,000 total: patch monitors ~$150–$250/unit per 2-week wear × ~320 deployments = $48,000–$80,000; clinical coordination staff (2 FTE × 2 years) ~$120,000–$180,000; data infrastructure and analysis ~$20,000–$40,000; participant compensation ~$10,000–$20,000

required: Stroke rehabilitation medicine (physiatrist or neurologist PI)
HRV signal processing and longitudinal waveform analysis
Multilevel/mixed-effects growth curve modeling (biostatistician)
Affective computing and concept drift methodology
Clinical research coordination in inpatient rehabilitation settings
Neuropsychology for aphasia-compatible outcome assessment
expertise.rarity: Moderate rarity. Individual expertise domains are each common, but the combination — especially affective computing + stroke rehabilitation + longitudinal HRV — is uncommon. Realistically 15–30 research groups worldwide could assemble this team. Requires a rehabilitation hospital with research infrastructure and a collaborating biostatistician or computational neuroscientist.

sample.type: Subacute stroke survivors (NIHSS 4–20, 2–4 weeks post-stroke) from inpatient rehabilitation units; age-sex-matched healthy controls for drift benchmarking
sample.size: 80 stroke patients + 40 healthy controls. Justification: power analysis for detecting non-monotonicity in ≥60% of trajectories (vs. null of 30% under monotonic assumption) with 80% power requires ~65 patients; 80 accounts for ~20% attrition over 6 months (stroke mortality, withdrawal, device failure). 40 controls provides adequate precision for between-occasion SD estimation (±15% CI).
sample.ethical_concerns: IRB approval required. Key concerns: (1) capacity to consent in patients with aphasia or cognitive impairment — requires aphasia-compatible consent procedures and surrogate consent protocols; (2) continuous ECG monitoring raises data privacy concerns requiring secure storage; (3) skin irritation from prolonged patch wear in potentially fragile post-stroke skin; (4) incidental cardiac findings requiring clinical referral pathway. All manageable with standard IRB protocols at rehabilitation hospitals.

feasibility.timeline: 30–36 months from funding to primary results: 3–4 months IRB and site setup, 18 months enrollment (assuming ~4–5 patients/month across 2 sites), 6 months follow-up for last enrolled patient, 6 months data processing and analysis. Publication-ready results at ~36 months.
simplification_options: Reduce continuous monitoring to 72-hour windows (3 days) at each timepoint instead of 2-week continuous wear — reduces device cost and data volume by ~80% while still capturing daily HRV variability; validated in prior longitudinal HRV studies

Use consumer-grade wearables (Polar H10 chest strap or Garmin with validated HRV export) instead of medical-grade Holter patches — reduces cost by 60–70% but introduces device reliability concerns in clinical population
Reduce to 3 timepoints (months 1, 3, 6) instead of 4 — loses resolution on early trajectory shape but cuts participant burden and device costs by 25%
Single-site design with 50 patients — reduces statistical power but cuts coordination complexity substantially; adequate for detecting large effect sizes (drift ratio ≥3×)

Skip the affective classifier component and focus purely on trajectory characterization — removes the concept drift framing but makes the study a cleaner autonomic recovery paper publishable in rehabilitation journals
killer_risks: Attrition: stroke survivors have high 6-month mortality and morbidity; 20–30% dropout is realistic and could leave the study underpowered, particularly if dropouts are non-random (sicker patients with more abnormal HRV trajectories dropping out creates survivorship bias)

Device compliance: continuous 2-week patch wear in cognitively impaired or agitated post-stroke patients may be poor; missing data epochs will create irregular time series that complicate spline fitting

Medication confounding: autonomic medications (beta-blockers, antihypertensives, antidepressants) are commonly initiated or changed post-stroke and will independently alter HRV trajectories, making it difficult to attribute trajectory shape to neurological recovery vs. pharmacological effects

Heterogeneity of stroke type and location: ischemic vs. hemorrhagic, cortical vs. subcortical, right vs. left hemisphere strokes have different autonomic signatures; 80 patients may be insufficient to stratify meaningfully, and pooled trajectories may obscure subgroup patterns

The 'static classifier' test requires a pre-existing HRV affective classifier trained on healthy populations — if no validated classifier exists for the specific HRV features extracted, this component becomes circular (training and testing on the same study data)

Non-monotonicity detection via AIC comparison is sensitive to the number and placement of spline knots; researcher degrees of freedom in model specification could inflate false-positive rates for non-monotonicity claims without pre-registration

public_datasets: PhysioNet/MIMIC_IV_ECG: MIMIC-IV-ECG contains 800K+ 12-lead ECGs linked to MIMIC-IV clinical data with ICD-10 stroke codes (I60-I69). Serial ECGs during hospitalization (days 1–14) can be extracted for stroke patients to characterize acute-phase HRV trajectory shape. Limitation: 10-second recordings limit frequency-domain HRV; time-domain metrics (SDNN, RMSSD) are extractable. Can test whether non-monotonicity is present in the acute phase before committing to 6-month prospective study.

NHANES: Contains HRV examination data (SDNN, RMSSD, HF/LF power) and self-reported stroke history (MCQ160f) with demographics. Can be used to benchmark HRV levels in stroke-history vs. non-stroke participants and estimate between-occasion variability in the general population as a proxy for healthy-control drift benchmarking. Not longitudinal within-individual, but cross-sectional age-stratified comparisons are possible.
data_availability.proxy_description: Primary proxy using MIMIC-IV-ECG: Extract all stroke-admission patients (ICD-10 I60-I69) with ≥3 serial ECG recordings during hospitalization. Compute RMSSD and SDNN from each 10-second recording. Fit individual-level growth curve models (linear vs. quadratic) to each patient's acute HRV trajectory across days 1–14. Test AIC preference for non-linear fits. Compute within-patient RMSSD SD across available recordings and compare to age-matched non-stroke controls in the same database. Secondary proxy using NHANES: stratify participants by stroke history (MCQ160f), extract HRV metrics, and compare variance in HRV metrics between stroke-history and non-stroke groups across age strata as a cross-sectional approximation of drift magnitude. This two-dataset proxy can be executed computationally within 2–4 weeks.
data_availability.proxy_limitations: MIMIC-IV-ECG recordings are 10 seconds (not 24-hour Holter), making frequency-domain HRV (HF power, LF/HF) unreliable; only time-domain metrics are valid. The acute hospitalization window (days 1–14) does not capture the rehabilitation phase (months 1–6) where the hypothesis is most clinically relevant — non-monotonicity in the acute phase may not predict non-monotonicity across rehabilitation. NHANES is cross-sectional, so within-individual drift cannot be measured directly. Neither dataset contains the affective classifier component or functional outcome measures (FIM, NIHSS) needed to test clinical adequacy of static baselines. The full prospective study is irreplaceable for the rehabilitation-timescale and concept-drift claims.

protocols.title: Signal Space Overlap Between Insular Stroke Autonomic Activation and Emotional Arousal: A Within-Subject Dissociation Experiment
protocols.protocol_md:
# Protocol: Signal Space Overlap Between Insular Stroke Autonomic Activation and Emotional Arousal: A Within-Subject Dissociation Experiment

---

## Overview

Affective computing systems that infer emotional states from peripheral physiological signals—electrodermal activity (EDA) and heart rate variability (HRV)—implicitly assume that resting-state physiology is separable from emotionally aroused physiology in the feature space used for classification. This assumption may be systematically violated in patients with insular cortex stroke, because the insula is a primary cortical node in autonomic regulation. Insular damage may produce chronic autonomic dysregulation that mimics the physiological signature of emotional arousal, rendering affective classifiers fundamentally ambiguous in this population.

This experiment directly tests whether the resting-state EDA and HRV feature vectors of insular stroke patients occupy the same multivariate signal space as emotional arousal states in healthy individuals—a phenomenon we term *signal identity confound*. We quantify this overlap using a Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) trained on healthy-control emotional arousal data and Mahalanobis distance metrics, comparing three groups: insular stroke patients, non-insular stroke patients, and healthy controls. The study bridges insular cortex autonomic neuroscience and affective computing for the first time in a single experimental design.

Given the feasibility assessment rating of *difficult but possible*, this protocol adopts a simplified two-phase structure: a computational proxy phase using public datasets (DEAP, MIMIC-IV-ECG) to establish prior probability and refine the GMM reference space, followed by a prospective clinical study with a reduced measurement battery (EDA and HRV primary; facial EMG and plasma norepinephrine deferred to a follow-up study). The protocol is designed to be executable at a single high-volume academic stroke center.

---

## Design

**Study type:** Cross-sectional, three-group between-subjects comparison with within-session repeated measures (resting baseline, cognitive task, emotional arousal induction).

**Independent variables:**
- *Group* (between-subjects, 3 levels): (A) MRI-confirmed insular cortex stroke, (B) MRI-confirmed non-insular stroke matched for lesion volume, (C) age- and sex-matched healthy controls.
- *Session epoch* (within-subjects, 4 levels): resting baseline, neutral cognitive task (digit span), emotional film clip induction (low-arousal neutral, high-arousal positive, high-arousal negative), second resting baseline.
- *Emotion condition* (within-subjects, nested within film clip epoch, 3 levels): neutral, high-arousal positive, high-arousal negative.

**Primary dependent variables:**
- Mahalanobis distance from each participant's resting-state feature vector to the healthy-control high-arousal GMM centroid.
- Fraction of 30-second resting-state windows classified as "high arousal" by the healthy-control GMM (classification rate).

**Secondary dependent variables:**
- EDA features per epoch: skin conductance level (SCL, µS), skin conductance response (SCR) amplitude (µS), SCR frequency (events/min).
- HRV features per epoch: SDNN (ms), RMSSD (ms), LF power (ms²), HF power (ms²), LF/HF ratio.
- Self-reported arousal per epoch (Visual Analogue Scale, 0–100 mm, aphasia-adapted).
- Insular lesion volume (cm³) and laterality (left, right, bilateral) from clinical MRI.

**Controls and counterbalancing:**
- Film clip order is counterbalanced across participants using a Latin square design (neutral, positive high-arousal, negative high-arousal presented in one of six possible orders), with the constraint that the neutral clip always precedes the first high-arousal clip within each participant to avoid carryover arousal contamination. Order assignment is stratified by group to ensure balance.
- Testing sessions are conducted at the same time of day (09:00–13:00) for all participants to control for circadian variation in autonomic tone.
- Room temperature is maintained at 22 ± 1°C and ambient lighting is standardized (300 lux) to minimize thermoregulatory and luminance effects on EDA.
- EDA electrodes are placed on the non-dominant hand (or the unaffected hand in stroke patients) to standardize recording site. Laterality of recording relative to lesion side is recorded as a covariate.
- The experimenter leaves the room during physiological recording epochs to eliminate social facilitation effects on arousal.

---

## Participants

### Sample Size and Power Justification

The primary comparison is the proportion of resting-state windows classified as high arousal by the GMM, compared between Group A (insular stroke) and Group C (healthy controls). Based on the hypothesis that insular stroke patients will show a ≥3× higher classification rate (e.g., 45% vs. 15% of windows), a two-proportion z-test with α = 0.05 (two-tailed) and 80% power requires n = 22 per group. We target n = 30 per group (90 total) to provide a 36% buffer for dropout (estimated at 15–20% in stroke populations over a 90-minute protocol), to enable subgroup analyses by lesion laterality (minimum n = 10 per laterality subgroup), and to improve stability of Mahalanobis distance estimation in the multivariate feature space. For the secondary Mahalanobis distance comparison (continuous outcome), a two-sample t-test with the same α and power and an assumed effect size of d = 0.8 (large, consistent with the magnitude of autonomic dysregulation reported in insular stroke literature) requires n = 26 per group; n = 30 again provides adequate buffer.

Power calculations were performed using the `pwr` package in R (version 4.3.0). No correction for multiple comparisons is applied to the primary power calculation; corrections are applied at the analysis stage (see Analysis Plan).

### Inclusion Criteria

**Groups A and B (stroke patients):**
- Age 40–85 years.
- First-ever ischemic or hemorrhagic stroke confirmed by clinical MRI (DWI or FLAIR sequences) within the preceding 3–18 months (post-acute stable phase; ≥2 weeks post-stroke to allow initial autonomic reorganization, ≤18 months to minimize confounding from long-term neuroplastic reorganization).
- Group A: MRI-confirmed lesion involving the insular cortex (any subregion), verified by a board-certified neurologist using standardized lesion tracing (see Apparatus & Materials).
- Group B: MRI-confirmed lesion with no insular involvement, matched to Group A for total lesion volume (±20%) and hemisphere of primary lesion.
- Sufficient cognitive capacity to provide informed consent, assessed using the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA ≥ 18) or, for participants with aphasia, the Aphasia-Adapted Consent Procedure (see Ethical Considerations).
- Medically stable outpatient or inpatient rehabilitation status.

**Group C (healthy controls):**
- Age 40–85 years, matched to Groups A and B for age (±5 years) and sex.
- No history of stroke, transient ischemic attack, or other neurological disorder.
- MoCA ≥ 26.

**All groups:**
- Ability to sit comfortably for 45 minutes (with rest breaks).
- Sufficient vision to view film clips (corrected visual acuity acceptable).
- Willingness to provide written informed consent.

### Exclusion Criteria

**All groups:**
- Current use of medications with known major autonomic effects that cannot be safely withheld for 12 hours prior to testing: beta-blockers, anticholinergics, sympathomimetics, tricyclic antidepressants. Stable use of ACE inhibitors, statins, or anticoagulants is permitted.
- Active cardiac arrhythmia (atrial fibrillation, frequent ectopy) that would preclude valid HRV analysis.
- Diabetes mellitus with confirmed autonomic neuropathy (assessed by clinical history and, if uncertain, by absence of respiratory sinus arrhythmia on a 5-minute resting ECG).
