- Severe aphasia precluding any form of self-report (Aphasia Quotient < 25 on the Western Aphasia Battery, or inability to complete the aphasia-adapted VAS after training).
- Active psychiatric disorder (current major depressive episode, generalized anxiety disorder, PTSD) that would confound emotional arousal induction.
- Skin conditions on the non-dominant hand that preclude EDA electrode placement.
- Pregnancy.
- Bilateral insular involvement (excluded from Group A to maintain lesion specificity; may be enrolled in a separate descriptive analysis if numbers permit).

### Recruitment Strategy

Participants in Groups A and B will be recruited from the stroke neurology inpatient and outpatient services of the host academic medical center, with supplementary recruitment from affiliated rehabilitation units. The clinical research coordinator will screen the stroke registry weekly for eligible patients. Treating neurologists will provide initial contact and permission for research staff to approach patients. Healthy controls (Group C) will be recruited via community advertisement (flyers, institutional research participant registries) and will be screened by telephone prior to enrollment.

Given the estimated recruitment rate of 1–2 eligible insular stroke patients per month at a single high-volume center, multi-site enrollment at 2–3 affiliated centers is planned from the outset to achieve the target n = 30 for Group A within 18–24 months. A Data Safety Monitoring Board (DSMB) will review enrollment rates at 6-month intervals.

---

## Apparatus & Materials

### Physiological Recording Equipment

**ECG/HRV:** A research-grade ECG amplifier (Biopac MP160 with ECG100C-MRI module, or equivalent; sampling rate 1000 Hz, bandwidth 0.05–150 Hz) will record a single-lead ECG (Lead II configuration: right clavicle, left lower rib, right lower rib ground) using disposable Ag/AgCl electrodes (Biopac EL503). R-peak detection and HRV feature extraction will be performed offline using the Kubios HRV Premium software (version 3.5, University of Eastern Finland), which implements automatic artifact correction and provides time-domain (SDNN, RMSSD) and frequency-domain (LF, HF, LF/HF via Welch periodogram) metrics. Minimum epoch length for frequency-domain HRV analysis is 5 minutes; all resting baselines are therefore set to 10 minutes.

**EDA:** A wrist-worn EDA sensor (Empatica E4 wristband, sampling rate 4 Hz, range 0.01–100 µS) will be placed on the non-dominant wrist (or unaffected wrist in stroke patients). The Empatica E4 provides continuous EDA via Ag/AgCl dry electrodes on the ventral wrist surface. Raw EDA data will be exported via the Empatica Connect platform and processed using the Ledalab toolbox (version 3.4.9) in MATLAB R2023b for decomposition into tonic (SCL) and phasic (SCR) components using continuous decomposition analysis (CDA). SCR events will be identified using a threshold of 0.02 µS above baseline. SCR amplitude (mean of detected responses per epoch) and SCR frequency (events per minute) will be extracted per epoch.

*Note on EDA laterality:* The recording site (non-dominant/unaffected wrist) will be documented relative to lesion hemisphere for each stroke patient. Lesion laterality (ipsilateral vs. contralateral to recording site) will be entered as a covariate in all primary analyses. A sensitivity analysis will be conducted restricting to participants where the recording site is contralateral to the lesion (the hemisphere most directly affected by insular damage).

**Signal synchronization:** ECG and EDA streams will be synchronized using a common TTL trigger pulse sent at the onset of each experimental epoch, recorded simultaneously on the Biopac system and logged by the stimulus presentation software.

### Lesion Analysis

Clinical MRI data (DWI and/or FLAIR sequences, T1-weighted structural) will be obtained from the hospital PACS system with patient consent. Lesion masks will be manually traced on T1-weighted images by a trained neurologist (blinded to group assignment) using ITK-SNAP (version 3.8.0). Lesion volume (cm³) will be computed from the binary mask. Insular involvement will be confirmed by overlay of the lesion mask on the MNI152 atlas using FSL (version 6.0), with the insula defined by the Harvard-Oxford Cortical Atlas (threshold ≥ 25% probability). Lesion laterality (left, right) will be determined by the hemisphere containing ≥75% of lesion volume.

### Emotional Arousal Induction Stimuli

Film clips will be selected from the validated Geneva Affective Picture Database film set (GAPED-Film) and the FilmStim database (Schaefer et al., 2010), which provide normative valence and arousal ratings from healthy adult samples. Three clip categories will be used:

- **Neutral:** Documentary footage of natural landscapes with no human subjects, narrated in a monotone voice (2 clips × 3 minutes each; mean normative arousal rating < 3/9 on SAM scale).
- **High-arousal positive:** Clips depicting humorous social interactions and physical comedy (2 clips × 3 minutes each; mean normative arousal rating > 6/9, valence > 6/9).
- **High-arousal negative:** Clips depicting threat and physical danger without graphic violence or gore (2 clips × 3 minutes each; mean normative arousal rating > 6/9, valence < 4/9).

Total film clip duration: 18 minutes (6 clips × 3 minutes). Clips will be presented on a 24-inch monitor (1920 × 1080 resolution) at a viewing distance of 60 cm, with standardized audio delivered via over-ear headphones at 65 dB SPL. Clip selection was validated in a separate pilot sample of 15 healthy adults (not included in the main study) to confirm that the clips produce the intended arousal differentiation in the target age range (40–85 years).

### Self-Report Materials

**Arousal VAS:** A 100-mm horizontal Visual Analogue Scale anchored at "completely calm" (0) and "extremely aroused/activated" (100) will be administered after each epoch. For participants with aphasia or motor impairment, a large-format printed version with a movable slider (or eye-gaze-compatible digital version on a tablet) will be used. All participants complete a practice trial with the VAS before the main protocol.

**Aphasia-adapted consent and assessment materials:** The Aphasia-Adapted Consent Procedure (AACP; Kagan & Kimelman, 1995) will be used for participants with aphasia. The MoCA will be administered in its standard form; for participants with aphasia, the MoCA-Blind (omitting visuospatial items) will be substituted where appropriate.

**Clinical scales:** NIHSS (National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale) and Barthel Index will be extracted from the clinical record or administered by the research coordinator at enrollment.

### Software

- **Stimulus presentation:** PsychoPy (version 2023.2.3) running on a dedicated Windows 11 workstation. All timing, trigger output, and response logging are handled by PsychoPy.
- **Signal processing:** MATLAB R2023b (MathWorks) with Ledalab 3.4.9 (EDA), Kubios HRV Premium 3.5 (HRV).
- **Statistical analysis and GMM:** Python 3.11 with scikit-learn 1.3 (GMM fitting, Mahalanobis distance), SciPy 1.11, pandas 2.0, and pingouin 0.5.3. R 4.3.0 for mixed-effects models and power analysis.
- **Lesion analysis:** ITK-SNAP 3.8.0, FSL 6.0.

---

## Procedure

### Phase 0: Computational Proxy (Weeks 1–6, Prior to Participant Enrollment)

1. Download the DEAP dataset (Koelstra et al., 2012; 32 healthy subjects, EDA and peripheral physiology during emotional video stimuli with self-reported arousal/valence ratings).
2. Extract EDA features from DEAP: SCL, SCR amplitude, and SCR frequency per 60-second window. Label windows as "high arousal" (self-reported arousal ≥ 6/9 on SAM) or "low arousal" (≤ 3/9). Discard intermediate windows (4–5/9).
3. Fit a 2-component GMM to the 3-dimensional EDA feature space (SCL, SCR amplitude, SCR frequency) using expectation-maximization with 10 random restarts. Validate GMM classification accuracy using leave-one-subject-out cross-validation. Retain the GMM only if cross-validated balanced accuracy ≥ 70%.
4. Extract resting HRV features (SDNN, RMSSD, LF/HF) from MIMIC-IV-ECG for a stroke cohort (ICD-10 codes I60–I69, n ≥ 200) and a matched non-stroke cohort. Project HRV features into the DEAP GMM space (HRV subspace only) and compute Mahalanobis distances from each patient's resting HRV vector to the high-arousal GMM centroid.
5. Document proxy results in a pre-registered analysis report. If the proxy shows no signal-space overlap in HRV alone (all Mahalanobis distances > 3 SD from the high-arousal centroid), this informs the prospective study that EDA will likely be the primary carrier of the effect, and the GMM feature space will be weighted accordingly.
6. Pre-register the full prospective protocol on OSF prior to enrollment of the first participant.

### Phase 1: Participant Enrollment and Screening

7. The clinical research coordinator reviews the stroke registry weekly and identifies potentially eligible patients (Groups A and B). The treating neurologist provides permission to approach.
8. A research team member contacts the patient (or their caregiver) to explain the study and schedule a screening visit.
9. At the screening visit, obtain written informed consent (or aphasia-adapted consent). Administer MoCA (or MoCA-Blind). Confirm MRI availability and arrange lesion tracing. Confirm medication eligibility (participants are asked to withhold specified autonomic medications for 12 hours prior to the testing session, with treating physician approval).
10. Healthy controls (Group C) are screened by telephone and then in person at the testing facility. Consent and MoCA are completed at the in-person screening visit.
11. Assign each participant a randomized film clip order (Latin square) and record assignment in the study database.

### Phase 2: Testing Session

All sessions are conducted between 09:00 and 13:00. Participants are asked to abstain from caffeine for 2 hours and from vigorous exercise for 12 hours prior to the session. The session lasts approximately 45–55 minutes, with rest breaks as needed.

**Setup (approximately 15 minutes):**

12. Greet the participant and confirm they have followed pre-session instructions. Record any deviations.
13. Seat the participant in a comfortable chair in the testing room. Explain the session structure using a visual schedule (printed card with icons, accessible to participants with aphasia).
14. Apply ECG electrodes (Lead II: right clavicle, left lower rib, right lower rib ground) using disposable Ag/AgCl electrodes after skin preparation with alcohol wipe and mild abrasion.
15. Fit the Empatica E4 wristband on the non-dominant (or unaffected) wrist. Confirm EDA signal quality (stable baseline, no motion artifact) on the Empatica Connect real-time display.
16. Verify ECG signal quality on the Biopac display (clear R-peaks, signal-to-noise ratio > 20 dB). Reposition electrodes if necessary.
17. Instruct the participant on the VAS procedure. Administer one practice trial ("How aroused do you feel right now?") and confirm understanding.
18. Explain that the experimenter will leave the room during recording epochs but can be reached via intercom at any time. Confirm the participant's comfort and readiness.
19. Experimenter leaves the room. Recording begins.

**Epoch 1 — Resting Baseline 1 (10 minutes):**

20. Send TTL trigger pulse (Epoch 1 onset) via PsychoPy. A fixation cross is displayed on the monitor.
21. Instruct the participant (via pre-recorded audio instruction played through headphones): "Please sit quietly and relax. Try not to move your hands or arms. You may blink normally. The recording will last 10 minutes."
22. Record ECG and EDA continuously for 10 minutes.
23. At epoch end, send TTL trigger (Epoch 1 offset). Experimenter re-enters room. Administer VAS ("How aroused did you feel during the rest period?"). Record response.

**Epoch 2 — Neutral Cognitive Task (5 minutes):**

24. Send TTL trigger (Epoch 2 onset). Administer a computerized digit span task (forward and backward, 3–9 digits, 2 trials per span length) via PsychoPy. Participants respond verbally or by button press (adapted for motor impairment as needed).
25. Record ECG and EDA continuously.
26. At epoch end, send TTL trigger (Epoch 2 offset). Administer VAS. Record digit span performance (number of correct trials).

**Epoch 3 — Emotional Film Clip Induction (18 minutes, 6 clips × 3 minutes):**

27. Instruct the participant (pre-recorded audio): "You will now watch a series of short film clips. Please watch them naturally. Try to keep your hands still."
28. Present film clips in the pre-assigned counterbalanced order. Each clip is preceded by a 15-second black screen (inter-clip interval) during which a TTL trigger marks the clip onset. Send a separate TTL trigger at clip offset.
29. After each clip, administer the VAS ("How aroused did you feel while watching that clip?"). Record response. Allow up to 30 seconds for VAS completion before the next clip begins.
30. Record ECG and EDA continuously throughout Epoch 3.
31. Monitor participant wellbeing via intercom check after the first high-arousal clip. If the participant reports distress (VAS arousal > 90 or verbal report of distress), offer a 2-minute break and the option to discontinue the high-arousal clips while continuing with the neutral clips and second resting baseline.

**Epoch 4 — Resting Baseline 2 (5 minutes):**

32. Send TTL trigger (Epoch 4 onset). Display fixation cross. Instruct participant to sit quietly and relax (same pre-recorded instruction as Epoch 1).
33. Record ECG and EDA continuously for 5 minutes.
34. At epoch end, send TTL trigger (Epoch 4 offset). Administer VAS.

**Session Wrap-Up:**

35. Experimenter re-enters room. Remove ECG electrodes and Empatica E4. Check skin for any irritation.
36. Administer a brief post-session debrief: explain the purpose of the film clips, confirm the participant's current wellbeing, and provide contact information for the study team if any distress arises after the session.
37. Provide participant compensation (gift card or equivalent, per IRB-approved rate).
38. Export raw ECG data from Biopac (BDF format) and EDA data from Empatica Connect (CSV format) to the secure study server. Assign anonymized participant ID. Complete session log.

### Phase 3: Data Processing (Ongoing, Parallel to Recruitment)

39. **ECG processing:** Import raw ECG into Kubios HRV Premium. Apply automatic artifact correction (threshold: RR intervals deviating > 20% from local mean are flagged and interpolated). Extract per-epoch HRV features: SDNN, RMSSD, LF power (0.04–0.15 Hz), HF power (0.15–0.40 Hz), LF/HF ratio. Epochs with > 10% artifact-corrected beats are excluded from HRV analysis and flagged in the dataset.
40. **EDA processing:** Import raw EDA into Ledalab. Apply CDA decomposition. Extract per-epoch SCL (mean tonic level), SCR amplitude (mean phasic response amplitude), and SCR frequency (events/min). Epochs with > 20% signal dropout or implausible values (SCL > 50 µS or < 0.01 µS) are excluded and flagged.
41. **Feature matrix construction:** For each participant and each epoch, construct a feature vector of 8 dimensions: [SCL, SCR amplitude, SCR frequency, SDNN, RMSSD, LF power, HF power, LF/HF]. Apply z-score normalization using the mean and standard deviation of the healthy-control (Group C) resting baseline epoch as the reference distribution. This normalization is computed once from the full Group C dataset and applied uniformly to all groups.
42. **Lesion tracing:** Neurologist (blinded to physiological data) traces lesion masks on clinical MRI. Compute lesion volume and confirm insular vs. non-insular classification. Any ambiguous cases are adjudicated by a second neurologist; disagreements are resolved by consensus.

---

## Analysis Plan

All analyses are pre-registered on OSF prior to data collection. The analysis team is blinded to group assignment during feature extraction and GMM fitting; unblinding occurs only at the statistical comparison stage.

### Primary Analysis

**GMM construction and validation:**
A 2-component GMM is fitted to the 8-dimensional feature vectors of Group C (healthy controls) during the high-arousal film clip epochs (positive and negative high-arousal clips combined), using the scikit-learn `GaussianMixture` class with full covariance matrices, 20 random restarts, and convergence tolerance of 1×10⁻⁴. The two components are labeled "high arousal" and "low arousal" based on correspondence with self-reported VAS arousal ratings (the component whose centroid is associated with higher mean VAS ratings is designated "high arousal"). GMM fit quality is assessed by Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC) and by the silhouette coefficient of the resulting clusters. If BIC favors a 3-component model, a sensitivity analysis with 3 components is conducted.

**Classification rate comparison:**
The fitted GMM is applied to the resting-baseline-1 feature vectors of all participants (Groups A, B, and C), using 30-second non-overlapping windows. Each window is assigned a posterior probability of belonging to the high-arousal component; windows with posterior probability > 0.5 are classified as "high arousal." The primary outcome is the proportion of resting-state windows classified as high arousal per participant.

Group differences in classification rate are tested using a one-way ANOVA with planned pairwise contrasts (Group A vs. Group C; Group A vs. Group B; Group B vs. Group C) using Tukey's HSD correction. The primary hypothesis is confirmed if Group A shows a significantly higher classification rate than Group C (p < 0.05 after correction) with an effect size of at least 3× the Group C mean rate.

**Mahalanobis distance comparison:**
For each participant, compute the Mahalanobis distance from their mean resting-state-1 feature vector to the high-arousal GMM centroid, using the GMM covariance matrix as the distance metric. Group differences in Mahalanobis distance are tested using a one-way ANOVA with the same planned contrasts and Tukey's HSD correction. The primary hypothesis is confirmed if Group A shows significantly smaller Mahalanobis distance to the high-arousal centroid than Group C (p < 0.05 after correction).

### Secondary Analyses

1. **Lesion volume dose-response (Group A only):** Pearson correlation between insular lesion volume (cm³) and (a) classification rate and (b) Mahalanobis distance to high-arousal centroid. A significant negative correlation (larger lesion → smaller distance to arousal centroid) would support a dose-response relationship.

2. **Lesion laterality subgroup analysis (Group A only):** Independent-samples t-test comparing classification rate and Mahalanobis distance between left-hemisphere and right-hemisphere insular stroke patients. Given the right insula's preferential role in sympathetic regulation, right-sided lesions are hypothesized to show greater signal-space overlap.

3. **EDA vs. HRV contribution:** Repeat the primary GMM analysis using EDA features only (3-dimensional: SCL, SCR amplitude, SCR frequency) and HRV features only (5-dimensional: SDNN, RMSSD, LF, HF, LF/HF) as separate feature spaces. This identifies which modality drives the signal-space overlap.

4. **Emotional reactivity in stroke patients:** Compare VAS arousal ratings and EDA/HRV responses during high-arousal film clips between Groups A, B, and C using a mixed ANOVA (group × emotion condition). This tests whether insular stroke patients show blunted emotional reactivity (a potential confound for the GMM trained on healthy-control arousal data).

5. **Resting baseline 2 vs. resting baseline 1:** Within-subjects comparison of classification rate and Mahalanobis distance between the two resting baselines (paired t-test within each group) to assess whether post-arousal recovery differs between groups.

6. **Self-reported arousal vs. physiological classification:** Pearson correlation between VAS arousal during resting baseline and GMM classification rate, within each group, to assess whether participants are aware of their elevated physiological arousal.

### Multiple Comparisons Correction

For the primary ANOVA contrasts (3 pairwise comparisons), Tukey's HSD is applied. For secondary analyses, a Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate correction (q < 0.05) is applied across all secondary tests within each analysis family (lesion analyses, modality analyses, emotional reactivity analyses treated as separate families).

### Bayesian Alternative

For the primary classification rate comparison (Group A vs. Group C), a Bayesian independent-samples t-test (Rouder et al., 2009) will be computed using the BayesFactor package in R, with a Cauchy prior on effect size (scale = 0.707). A Bayes Factor BF₁₀ > 10 will be interpreted as strong evidence for the hypothesis; BF₁₀ < 0.1 as strong evidence against. This analysis is particularly informative if the frequentist test is marginal (0.05 < p < 0.10).

---

## Predicted Results

### If the Hypothesis Is True

Insular stroke patients (Group A) will show a resting-state GMM classification rate of approximately 40–50% (i.e., 40–50% of resting-state windows classified as high arousal by the healthy-control GMM), compared to approximately 10–15% in healthy controls (Group C) and 15–20% in non-insular stroke patients (Group B). The Group A vs. Group C difference will be statistically significant after Tukey correction (p < 0.05) with an odds ratio ≥ 3. Mahalanobis distances from resting-state feature vectors to the high-arousal GMM centroid will be significantly smaller in Group A than in Groups B and C. A dose-response relationship will be observed within Group A: larger insular lesion volume will correlate negatively with Mahalanobis distance (r < −0.40). Right-hemisphere insular lesions will show greater signal-space overlap than left-hemisphere lesions. EDA features will contribute more to the overlap than HRV features, consistent with the insula's role in sympathetic skin conductance regulation.

This pattern would establish that insular stroke produces a chronic autonomic state that is geometrically indistinguishable from emotional arousal in the feature space used by affective classifiers—a finding with direct implications for the validity of affective computing in neurological populations and for the interpretation of autonomic biomarkers in stroke research.

### If the Hypothesis Is False

If insular stroke patients' resting-state feature vectors are not closer to the healthy-control high-arousal GMM centroid than those of non-insular stroke patients or healthy controls (no significant group difference in classification rate or Mahalanobis distance), this null result is interpretable in at least two important ways. First, it would suggest that the signal identity confound is a general post-stroke phenomenon rather than an insular-lesion-specific one, redirecting intervention design toward stroke-wide rather than lesion-targeted calibration strategies for affective computing systems. Second, it would suggest that the insular cortex's autonomic regulatory role does not produce a sustained resting-state autonomic signature that mimics emotional arousal—a finding that would constrain theoretical models of insular function and challenge the assumption that insular damage produces chronic sympathetic hyperactivation. A null result would be published as a well-powered negative finding with clear implications for both the affective computing and stroke neurology literatures.

A third interpretable outcome is a partial result: if Group A and Group B both show greater signal-space overlap than Group C (but do not differ from each other), this would implicate general post-stroke autonomic dysregulation rather than insular specificity, and would be reported as such.

---

## Limitations

**EDA laterality confound:** EDA is recorded from the non-dominant/unaffected wrist, which may not reflect the autonomic output of the damaged hemisphere. Insular lesions contralateral to the recording site may produce weaker EDA effects than ipsilateral lesions, potentially underestimating the signal-space overlap in some participants. The sensitivity analysis restricted to contralateral recording sites partially addresses this, but the sample size for this subgroup may be insufficient for definitive conclusions.

**Emotional reactivity confound:** Insular stroke patients may have impaired emotional processing (alexithymia, reduced emotional reactivity), which could attenuate their responses to the film clips and thereby reduce the validity of the healthy-control GMM as a reference for their arousal states. If Group A shows blunted film-clip responses (secondary analysis 4), the GMM trained on healthy-control arousal may not capture the full range of arousal states in Group A, making the classification rate comparison conservative rather than liberal.

**GMM generalizability:** The GMM is trained on healthy-control data from the current study (Group C, n = 30), which is a relatively small sample for fitting an 8-dimensional Gaussian mixture. The stability of the GMM centroids and covariance matrices will be assessed by bootstrap resampling (1000 iterations), and the sensitivity of primary results to GMM parameterization will be reported. The computational proxy phase (Phase 0) using DEAP provides an independent validation of the GMM approach.

**Lesion heterogeneity:** Insular strokes vary substantially in subregion (anterior vs. posterior insula), depth, and co-involvement of adjacent structures (basal ganglia, operculum, temporal lobe). With n = 30 insular patients, the study is underpowered to dissect subregional effects. Lesion volume and laterality are included as covariates, but fine-grained lesion-symptom mapping (e.g., voxel-based lesion-symptom mapping, VLSM) is not feasible at this sample size and is deferred to a larger follow-up study.

**Cross-sectional design:** The study cannot determine whether the observed signal-space overlap is a direct consequence of insular damage or a pre-existing individual difference that predisposed certain individuals to insular stroke (e.g., chronic hypertension-related autonomic dysregulation). A longitudinal design tracking autonomic signals from acute to chronic stroke phases would be required to establish causality.

**Generalizability:** The sample is restricted to post-acute stroke patients (2 weeks to 18 months post-stroke) at academic medical centers, which may not represent the full spectrum of insular stroke severity or the community-dwelling stroke survivor population. Patients with severe aphasia or cognitive impairment are excluded, which may systematically exclude those with the largest or most strategically placed insular lesions.

**What this experiment cannot tell us:** This experiment establishes whether signal-space overlap exists and quantifies its magnitude; it does not identify the neurobiological mechanism (e.g., loss of insular inhibition of sympathetic outflow vs. compensatory reorganization of autonomic networks). It also does not test whether the confound affects real-world affective computing performance in clinical settings, which would require a separate ecological validity study.

---

## Ethical Considerations

### IRB/Ethics Approval

This study will be submitted for full review by the Institutional Review Board (IRB) of the host institution prior to any participant contact. Given the involvement of a vulnerable population (stroke patients), the use of emotion-induction procedures, and the multi-site design, full board review (rather than expedited review) is anticipated. A Data Safety Monitoring Board (DSMB) with at least one independent stroke neurologist, one biostatistician, and one patient advocate will be constituted prior to enrollment and will review safety data at 6-month intervals.

### Informed Consent

All participants will provide written informed consent prior to enrollment. The consent process will be conducted by a trained research coordinator and will include:

- A plain-language explanation of the study purpose, procedures, risks, and benefits.
- Explicit statement that participation is voluntary and withdrawal at any time will not affect clinical care.
- Explanation of data confidentiality and storage procedures (anonymized data stored on encrypted institutional servers; no data shared with treating clinicians).
- For participants with aphasia: the Aphasia-Adapted Consent Procedure (AACP) will be used, which employs simplified language, visual supports, and yes/no verification questions to confirm comprehension. A legally authorized representative (LAR) will co-sign consent for participants whose capacity is uncertain; the participant's assent will also be documented.
- Separate consent for use of clinical MRI data.

### Emotion Induction Risk Management

The use of high-arousal negative film clips in stroke patients with potential emotional dysregulation (post-stroke depression, emotional lability, pathological crying) carries a moderate risk of distress. The following safeguards are implemented:

- Participants are informed in advance that some clips may be emotionally activating and that they may stop viewing at any time without consequence.
- The experimenter monitors participant wellbeing via intercom after the first high-arousal clip (Step 31).
- A pre-specified stopping criterion is defined: if the participant reports VAS arousal > 90 or verbally requests to stop, the high-arousal clips are discontinued and the session continues with the neutral clips and second resting baseline only. Data from the discontinued clips are excluded from the emotional reactivity analysis but resting-state data are retained.
- A licensed clinical psychologist is available by telephone during all testing sessions and will be contacted if a participant shows signs of significant distress.
- A post-session debrief is conducted for all participants (Step 36), including normalization of emotional responses and provision of mental health resources.

### Participant Burden and Fatigue

The protocol has been shortened from the originally proposed 90 minutes to approximately 45–55 minutes (including setup) to reduce fatigue risk in stroke patients. Rest breaks are offered between epochs. Participants may pause or discontinue at any time. Sessions may be rescheduled if a participant is fatigued or unwell on the day of testing.

### Data Privacy

All data are stored under anonymized participant IDs on encrypted institutional servers compliant with HIPAA (or equivalent national data protection regulations). Clinical MRI data are de-identified prior to transfer to the research database. No individually identifiable data will be shared with third parties or published. Data will be retained for 10 years post-publication in accordance with institutional policy, after which they will be securely destroyed.

### Risk Classification

Overall risk to participants is classified as **minimal to moderate**: physiological monitoring is non-invasive; emotion induction carries a low-to-moderate risk of transient distress, mitigated by the safeguards described above; no experimental medications or invasive procedures are used. The potential benefits—advancing understanding of autonomic dysregulation in stroke and improving the validity of affective computing tools for neurological populations—are judged to outweigh the risks.

---

*Protocol version 1.0. To be pre-registered on OSF prior to enrollment of the first participant. All deviations from this protocol will be documented in a protocol amendment log and reported in the final manuscript.*

protocols.title: Hierarchical Ground Truth Acquisition for Affective State in Aphasic Stroke Patients: Validating Multi-Modal Behavioral Proxies Against Aphasia-Compatible Self-Report
protocols.protocol_md:
# Protocol: Hierarchical Ground Truth Acquisition for Affective State in Aphasic Stroke Patients: Validating Multi-Modal Behavioral Proxies Against Aphasia-Compatible Self-Report

---

## Overview

Affective computing systems designed for stroke rehabilitation depend on reliable ground-truth labels of patient emotional state. In the broader affective computing literature, self-report is treated as the criterion measure against which all other signals are validated. This assumption fails in severe aphasia, where language impairment precludes standard verbal self-report, yet the population represents a substantial and clinically important subgroup of stroke survivors. No published study has systematically evaluated whether alternative ground-truth acquisition strategies—specifically, observer-coded facial action units (FACS) and behavioral proxies such as task engagement duration and withdrawal—produce internally consistent, convergently valid affective state labels in this population.

This study addresses that gap through a cross-sectional validation design. We test the hypothesis that a hierarchical ground-truth acquisition strategy combining aphasia-compatible self-report (Visual Analogue Mood Scale; VAMS), observer-rated facial action coding (FACS), and behavioral proxies produces internally consistent affective labels in stroke patients across a range of aphasia severities, with inter-rater reliability κ > 0.6 and convergent validity r > 0.5 between VAMS and FACS-derived affect ratings. A secondary aim characterizes the temporal scale mismatch between event-level behavioral proxies and session-level VAMS ratings—a methodological problem that has not been formally quantified in any population.

Given the feasibility assessment indicating that the full four-group stratified design (N = 80) poses severe recruitment bottlenecks, particularly for the severe aphasia stratum, this protocol adopts the recommended simplification: a two-group pilot design comparing severe aphasia patients against healthy age-matched controls (N = 30 per group, total N = 60), with physiological classifier analysis deferred to a subsequent Phase 2 study. This design preserves the core validity question—whether FACS and behavioral proxies can substitute for self-report when self-report is most compromised—while achieving adequate statistical power and a realistic recruitment timeline. Effect size estimates from this pilot will inform the full stratified replication.

---

## Design

**Type:** Cross-sectional, between-subjects validation study with two independent groups (severe aphasia stroke patients vs. healthy age-matched controls). Within each participant, four repeated measurement conditions (baseline rest, positive emotional induction, frustration induction, recovery rest) provide within-person variation in affective state necessary for convergent validity analyses.

**Independent Variables:**
- *Group* (between-subjects, two levels): severe aphasia stroke patients (WAB-R Aphasia Quotient [AQ] < 50) vs. healthy age-matched controls
- *Condition* (within-subjects, four levels): baseline rest, positive emotional induction, frustration induction, recovery rest

**Dependent Variables:**
- VAMS scores (0–100 mm) for happiness, sadness, anxiety, and anger, administered at the end of each condition
- FACS-derived affect category ratings (positive, neutral, negative) per 30-second epoch, coded independently by two certified FACS coders
- Behavioral proxies: task engagement duration (seconds), withdrawal attempt count, and vocalization valence codes per condition
- Inter-rater reliability: Cohen's κ between FACS coders across affect categories
- Convergent validity: Pearson r between VAMS subscale scores and FACS-derived affect ratings, computed separately by group

**Controls and Counterbalancing:**
- Condition order is fixed across all participants (baseline → positive induction → frustration induction → recovery) to preserve ecological validity of the emotional arc and avoid carryover contamination from frustration to positive induction. This ordering reflects standard affective induction practice and ends with a recovery period to ensure participant wellbeing at session close.
- Stimulus sets for positive emotional induction (photographs and music) are individually tailored using a pre-session interview (or proxy interview for severe aphasia participants) to maximize ecological validity while controlling for stimulus category (family photographs, nature scenes, preferred music genre). Stimulus selection is documented and reported.
- FACS coders are blind to participant group assignment, condition identity, and VAMS scores throughout coding. Coder assignment to video segments is randomized and counterbalanced across participants to prevent systematic coder-by-participant confounds.
- VAMS administration is standardized via a scripted protocol (see Procedure). For severe aphasia participants, a trained speech-language pathologist administers VAMS using a pointing response on a laminated 100 mm scale; the same procedure is used for healthy controls to equate administration method across groups.
- Session timing (time of day) is held constant within participants where possible (morning sessions preferred) to minimize circadian effects on affect and physiology.
- Facial paresis status is documented for all stroke participants using the National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale (NIHSS) facial palsy item (item 4) and recorded as a covariate in all FACS-related analyses.

---

## Participants

### Sample Size and Power Analysis

The primary convergent validity analysis is a Pearson correlation between VAMS and FACS-derived affect ratings within each group. For a two-tailed test at α = 0.05 with power = 0.80, detecting a medium-to-large correlation of r = 0.50 requires n = 29 participants per group (computed using the formula for testing H₀: ρ = 0 with Fisher's z transformation; G*Power 3.1). We target N = 30 per group (total N = 60) to provide a small buffer against dropout and missing data.

For the inter-rater reliability analysis (Cohen's κ), a sample of 30 participants per group provides adequate precision for estimating κ with a 95% confidence interval width of approximately ±0.18 at κ = 0.70, which is sufficient to distinguish acceptable (κ > 0.60) from unacceptable reliability. Power for secondary analyses (behavioral proxy correlations, group comparisons of convergent validity) is exploratory; effect sizes from this pilot will inform the powered Phase 2 study.

The severe aphasia stratum is acknowledged as the primary power constraint. A priori, we accept that N = 30 in this stratum may be insufficient to detect small correlations (r < 0.30) and that the study is explicitly framed as a pilot for effect size estimation rather than a definitive test of small effects.

### Inclusion Criteria

**Severe Aphasia Group:**
- Adult (age ≥ 18 years) stroke survivor with confirmed ischemic or hemorrhagic stroke on neuroimaging
- WAB-R Aphasia Quotient < 50, confirmed at enrollment assessment
- Minimum 3 months post-stroke onset (to exclude acute confusional states and ensure neurological stability)
- Medically stable and cleared for outpatient or research participation by treating physician
- Capacity to provide informed consent, OR availability of a legally authorized representative (LAR) to provide proxy consent with participant assent (see Ethical Considerations)
- Sufficient visual acuity to perceive VAMS scale markings (corrected vision acceptable)
- Sufficient upper limb motor function in at least one hand to make a pointing response on the VAMS scale, OR ability to indicate a response via eye gaze to a mounted scale (assessed at enrollment)

**Healthy Control Group:**
- Adult (age ≥ 18 years) with no history of stroke, traumatic brain injury, or neurological disorder
- No current diagnosis of major depressive disorder, anxiety disorder, or other psychiatric condition that would confound affective induction
- Age-matched to the severe aphasia group within ±5 years (group-level matching; individual matching is not required)
- Normal or corrected-to-normal vision and hearing

### Exclusion Criteria (Both Groups)

- Current diagnosis of dementia or cognitive impairment sufficient to preclude task comprehension (MMSE < 18 for controls; for aphasia group, clinical judgment by enrolling neuropsychologist given MMSE language dependence)
- Active psychiatric crisis, suicidal ideation, or severe depression requiring immediate clinical intervention
- Significant facial paresis precluding FACS coding (defined as NIHSS facial palsy score = 3, complete paralysis; score ≤ 2 is acceptable with paresis documented as covariate)
- Participation in another interventional study within the past 30 days
- Inability to tolerate a 30-minute seated session (shortened protocol; see Procedure)
- Known bereavement within the past 6 months (to reduce risk from personally meaningful photograph stimuli)

### Recruitment Strategy

Severe aphasia participants will be recruited from stroke rehabilitation inpatient and outpatient units at the enrolling academic medical center and affiliated rehabilitation hospitals. Recruitment will proceed via:
1. Referral from treating speech-language pathologists and neurologists who identify eligible patients during routine clinical care
2. Review of clinical records (with site IRB approval) to identify patients with documented aphasia and recent WAB-R assessment
3. Posting of IRB-approved recruitment materials in rehabilitation waiting areas and clinic spaces

Healthy controls will be recruited via institutional research participant registries, community advertisement (flyers, institutional website), and word-of-mouth referral. Controls will be screened by telephone prior to enrollment using a standardized eligibility checklist.

Given the known recruitment difficulty for severe aphasia (WAB-R AQ < 50) in a single site, the protocol is designed for potential multi-site expansion. A data sharing agreement template is included in supplementary materials to facilitate site addition if the 18-month recruitment window yields fewer than N = 25 in the aphasia stratum.

---

## Apparatus & Materials

### Physiological Recording Equipment

- **ECG:** Biopac MP160 research-grade acquisition system with ECG100C-MRI amplifier module, or equivalent clinical-grade system (Shimmer3 ECG+), sampling at ≥ 1000 Hz. Disposable Ag/AgCl electrodes in Lead II configuration.
- **EDA:** Biopac EDA100C module with 8 mm Ag/AgCl electrodes applied to the thenar and hypothenar eminences of the non-dominant hand, or Shimmer3 GSR+ unit. Sampling at ≥ 256 Hz.
- **Wrist PPG:** Empatica E4 wristband (sampling at 64 Hz for BVP, 4 Hz for EDA backup channel) worn on the non-dominant wrist. Used as a secondary/redundant HRV source and for comparison with ECG-derived HRV.

*Note: Physiological data are collected throughout the session as secondary measures for Phase 2 classifier development. Primary analyses in this Phase 1 protocol do not include physiological classifier modeling.*

### Video Recording

- Two Sony FDR-AX700 4K camcorders (or equivalent HD cameras with ≥ 1080p resolution at 30 fps) positioned at 45° angles to capture full-face and profile views simultaneously. Camera positions are fixed using adjustable tripod mounts and standardized to participant head position at session start.
- Controlled lighting: two 5500K LED softbox panels positioned to eliminate shadows on the face without producing glare. Lighting configuration is documented with a photograph at each session.
- Audio recording via directional microphone (Rode VideoMic Pro) for vocalization coding.
- Synchronization: a visible LED flash event marker triggered by the stimulus delivery computer at condition onset/offset provides a synchronization signal visible in both camera feeds and in the physiological data stream.

### Stimulus Delivery

- Dell workstation running Windows 10 with 27-inch 4K monitor (Dell UltraSharp U2720Q or equivalent) for photograph and video stimuli.
- Stereo speakers (Yamaha HS5 or equivalent) for music stimuli.
- Stimulus delivery software: PsychoPy 2023.x (open-source; Peirce et al., 2019) for precise timing control and condition logging.

### Aphasia Assessment

- **WAB-R:** Western Aphasia Battery–Revised (Kertesz, 2006) standard kit, administered by a certified speech-language pathologist at enrollment to confirm aphasia severity stratum and document AQ.
- **NIHSS Facial Palsy Item:** Administered by enrolling clinician at enrollment to document facial paresis severity.

### Self-Report Instruments

- **VAMS:** Visual Analogue Mood Scale (Stern, 1997). Laminated 100 mm horizontal scales for four affect dimensions: happiness, sadness, anxiety, anger. Each scale is printed in large font (minimum 18pt) with pictographic anchors (simple line-drawn faces) at each end to support comprehension in aphasia. Scales are mounted on a rigid clipboard positioned within comfortable pointing reach. A standardized pointing aid (foam-tipped stylus) is available for participants with fine motor impairment.
- **SADQ:** Stroke Aphasic Depression Questionnaire–10 (Sutcliffe & Lincoln, 1998), observer-rated by the session examiner based on behavioral observation during the session. Completed immediately after session close.

### FACS Coding

- **Software:** ELAN 6.x (Max Planck Institute for Psycholinguistics; free, open-source) for video annotation and epoch segmentation. FACS coding is performed manually by certified coders using the FACS manual (Ekman, Friesen, & Hager, 2002) as the coding reference.
- **Automated pre-screening:** OpenFace 2.0 (Baltrusaitis et al., 2018) is applied to all video recordings as an automated first pass to extract action unit (AU) presence and intensity per frame. OpenFace output is used to (a) flag epochs with high head movement or occlusion for manual review prioritization, and (b) provide a comparison dataset for evaluating automated vs. manual FACS agreement. OpenFace output is not used as primary FACS data.
- **Coding workstations:** Two dedicated password-protected workstations with calibrated monitors (Dell UltraSharp, hardware-calibrated to sRGB) for independent coder use. Video files are anonymized (face blurred in non-coding copies; original retained in secure storage) before transfer to coder workstations.

### VAMS Administration Materials for Severe Aphasia

- Laminated VAMS scales (as above) with pictographic anchors validated for use in aphasia (consistent with Stern, 1997 aphasia adaptation guidelines)
- Gaze-tracking alternative: for participants unable to point, a low-cost eye-tracking system (Tobii EyeX or equivalent) is available to capture gaze-directed scale responses. This is used only when pointing is not feasible and is documented as a response modality covariate.

---

## Procedure

### Pre-Session (Enrollment Visit, Separate Day)

1. Obtain written informed consent from participant or legally authorized representative (LAR). For severe aphasia participants, administer the aphasia-adapted consent procedure: read consent aloud, present key points on illustrated information sheets, confirm assent via pointing or head nod. Document consent modality.
2. Administer WAB-R (speech-language pathologist) to confirm aphasia severity stratum (AQ < 50 for aphasia group). Record AQ score.
3. Administer NIHSS facial palsy item. Record score (0–3).
4. Conduct pre-session interview (with participant or caregiver proxy for severe aphasia) to identify personally meaningful photographs (family, pets, places) and preferred music genre for positive emotional induction. Obtain 5–10 photographs from participant/caregiver; confirm no bereavement-related content. Select 3 music clips (60 seconds each) from preferred genre using a standardized library.
5. Screen for exclusion criteria (dementia, psychiatric crisis, recent bereavement).
6. Schedule session visit. Confirm morning time slot where possible.

### Session Day

**Setup (30 minutes before participant arrival):**

7. Prepare recording room: position cameras, verify lighting configuration, start video recording test, confirm audio levels.
8. Power on physiological recording system; verify electrode impedance test function.
9. Load stimulus sequence in PsychoPy. Verify LED synchronization marker function.
10. Prepare VAMS materials: mount laminated scales on clipboard, position pointing aid.
11. Brief session examiner and speech-language pathologist on protocol. Confirm FACS coders are not present in the room and will receive anonymized video only.

**Participant Arrival and Preparation (20 minutes):**

12. Welcome participant and caregiver/LAR. Re-explain session structure using illustrated session overview sheet. Confirm willingness to proceed (assent check).
13. Seat participant in adjustable chair at standardized distance from monitor (60 cm). Adjust camera angles to capture full face. Document camera positions.
14. Apply physiological sensors: ECG electrodes (Lead II), EDA electrodes (non-dominant hand), Empatica E4 wristband (non-dominant wrist). Verify signal quality on acquisition software.
15. Conduct VAMS practice trial: examiner demonstrates pointing response on a practice scale ("point to where you feel right now on this scale—here means very happy, here means not at all happy"). Participant completes practice trial. Confirm comprehension; if not achieved after two attempts, document and proceed with gaze-tracking alternative.
16. Confirm participant comfort. Remind participant that they may withdraw at any time by raising their hand or vocalizing. Establish a stop signal (raised hand or verbal "stop") with participant.

**Condition 1: Baseline Rest (5 minutes):**

17. Examiner leaves the room (or moves behind participant's field of view). Participant sits quietly. No stimuli presented. PsychoPy displays a fixation cross on the monitor.
18. At condition end, LED marker fires. Examiner returns and administers VAMS for all four dimensions (happiness, sadness, anxiety, anger) using standardized verbal prompt: "Please point to where you feel right now." Record mm scores.

**Condition 2: Positive Emotional Induction (10 minutes):**

19. PsychoPy presents the participant's personally meaningful photographs in a slideshow (each photograph displayed for 30 seconds, with 2-second fade transition) accompanied by preferred music clips (looped as needed to fill 10 minutes). Examiner is present but silent, seated behind participant's field of view.
20. At condition end, LED marker fires. Examiner administers VAMS (all four dimensions). Record mm scores.

**Break (5 minutes):**

21. Participant rests. Examiner checks comfort and wellbeing. Offer water. Document any spontaneous emotional expressions or verbalizations.

**Condition 3: Frustration Induction (10 minutes):**

22. Examiner presents the adapted unsolvable puzzle task: a tablet-based jigsaw puzzle (3–4 large pieces for motor accessibility) that is programmed to prevent completion (pieces snap back to starting positions when correctly placed). Examiner instructs participant to complete the puzzle using standardized verbal/gestural instruction. Examiner remains present but does not assist.
23. Continuous monitoring: examiner observes for distress indicators (sustained crying, agitation, requests to stop). If participant raises stop signal or displays sustained distress for > 60 seconds, condition is terminated immediately. Document termination and reason.
24. At condition end (10 minutes or early termination), LED marker fires. Examiner administers VAMS (all four dimensions). Record mm scores.

**Condition 4: Recovery Rest (5 minutes):**

25. Examiner removes puzzle. Presents a brief positive stimulus (one personally meaningful photograph, 60 seconds) as a mood repair induction, followed by 4 minutes of quiet rest with fixation cross.
26. At condition end, LED marker fires. Examiner administers VAMS (all four dimensions). Record mm scores.

**Post-Session:**

27. Remove physiological sensors. Check skin condition at electrode sites.
28. Examiner completes SADQ-10 based on behavioral observations during the session.
29. Conduct wellbeing check with participant and caregiver/LAR. Provide written debrief sheet (aphasia-adapted: illustrated, large font) explaining the purpose of the frustration task and confirming that the puzzle was designed to be unsolvable. Offer opportunity to discuss any distress.
30. Record session metadata: total duration, any protocol deviations, stop-signal events, response modality used for VAMS (pointing vs. gaze), facial paresis observation notes.

**Total session duration:** approximately 55–65 minutes including setup and debrief.

### Post-Session Data Processing

31. Transfer video files to secure server. Apply face-blurring to all copies except the primary FACS coding copies (which are retained on password-protected coder workstations).
32. Run OpenFace 2.0 on all video recordings to extract per-frame AU presence and intensity. Flag epochs with tracking confidence < 0.80 for manual review.
33. Segment video into 30-second epochs aligned to condition boundaries using ELAN. Generate randomized, anonymized epoch lists for each coder.
34. Assign epoch lists to FACS Coder 1 and FACS Coder 2 independently. Coders receive no information about participant group, condition identity, or VAMS scores.
35. Each coder assigns an affect category (positive, neutral, negative) to each 30-second epoch based on FACS AU patterns, following a pre-specified coding guide (see Supplementary Materials) that maps AU combinations to affect categories consistent with Ekman's basic emotion framework. Coders also record the presence and intensity (0–5 scale) of individual AUs per epoch.
36. After independent coding is complete, coders meet to resolve discrepancies on a randomly selected 20% subsample for reliability reporting purposes. Discrepancy resolution is documented but does not alter the primary independent coding dataset.
37. Behavioral proxy coding: a research assistant (blind to VAMS scores and FACS ratings) codes the following from video: (a) task engagement duration per condition (seconds of active task engagement vs. disengagement/looking away); (b) withdrawal attempt count (operationally defined as reaching toward the door, pushing materials away, or sustained gaze aversion > 10 seconds); (c) vocalization valence (positive, neutral, negative) coded per vocalization event using a pre-specified coding guide.

---

## Analysis Plan

All analyses are conducted in R (version ≥ 4.3) using pre-registered code deposited on the Open Science Framework (OSF) prior to data collection. The analysis script is finalized and locked before the first participant is enrolled. Deviations from the pre-registered plan are documented and reported.

### Primary Analysis 1: Inter-Rater Reliability of FACS Coding

Cohen's κ is computed between Coder 1 and Coder 2 for the three-category affect classification (positive, neutral, negative) across all 30-second epochs, separately for the severe aphasia group and the healthy control group. The primary reliability threshold is κ > 0.60 (substantial agreement; Landis & Koch, 1977). A two-sided 95% confidence interval for κ is reported using bootstrap resampling (10,000 iterations). If κ < 0.50 in the healthy control group, this constitutes a primary analysis failure and triggers the pre-specified contingency plan (see Limitations).

Weighted κ (linear weights) is computed as a secondary reliability metric to account for ordered severity of disagreement (positive vs. negative is a larger error than positive vs. neutral).

### Primary Analysis 2: Convergent Validity Between VAMS and FACS-Derived Affect Ratings

FACS affect category ratings (coded as −1 = negative, 0 = neutral, +1 = positive) are aggregated per condition per participant as the mean epoch rating within each condition. VAMS happiness scores (0–100 mm) serve as the primary self-report criterion; VAMS sadness scores (reverse-scored) serve as a secondary criterion. Pearson r is computed between condition-level VAMS happiness and condition-level mean FACS affect rating, separately for the severe aphasia group and the healthy control group. The primary convergent validity threshold is r > 0.50.

Fisher's z transformation is used to test whether the correlation differs significantly between groups (severe aphasia vs. healthy controls), providing a direct test of whether aphasia severity moderates FACS-VAMS convergence.

A sensitivity analysis replaces Pearson r with Spearman ρ to assess robustness to non-normality in VAMS distributions.

### Primary Analysis 3: Temporal Alignment of Behavioral Proxies and Session-Level VAMS

Task engagement duration and withdrawal attempt count per condition are correlated with VAMS happiness scores at the condition level (four data points per participant), using within-person correlations computed via multilevel modeling (random intercepts for participant, fixed effect of condition). This analysis characterizes the temporal scale mismatch: behavioral proxies are event-level measures, while VAMS is a retrospective session-level rating. The expected pattern is that behavioral proxies correlate more strongly with VAMS in healthy controls (where self-report is reliable) than in severe aphasia (where VAMS validity is uncertain), and that the magnitude of this group difference quantifies the mismatch.

A linear mixed-effects model (lme4 package) is specified as:

> VAMS_happiness ~ engagement_duration + withdrawal_count + group + engagement_duration × group + withdrawal_count × group + (1 | participant)

The interaction terms test whether behavioral proxy–VAMS relationships differ by group.

### Secondary Analysis 1: SADQ Convergence with VAMS and FACS

SADQ total score (observer-rated) is correlated with session-mean VAMS sadness and session-mean FACS negative affect rating, separately by group. This provides a three-way convergence check (self-report, observer-rated questionnaire, FACS).

### Secondary Analysis 2: Facial Paresis as a Moderator of FACS Validity

In the severe aphasia group, NIHSS facial palsy score (0–2, excluding score 3 per exclusion criteria) is entered as a covariate in the FACS-VAMS convergent validity analysis. A moderation model tests whether facial paresis severity attenuates FACS-VAMS correlation, which would indicate that low convergence in severe aphasia is partially neurological (facial paresis) rather than purely methodological.

### Secondary Analysis 3: OpenFace vs. Manual FACS Agreement

Cohen's κ between OpenFace 2.0 automated AU classifications and manual FACS coder classifications is computed for the 20% random subsample that underwent manual verification. This analysis evaluates whether automated facial coding can substitute for manual FACS coding in this population, informing the cost-benefit tradeoff for Phase 2.

### Multiple Comparisons Correction

The three primary analyses address distinct research questions (reliability, convergent validity, temporal alignment) and are not treated as a family requiring correction. Within each primary analysis, where multiple VAMS subscales are examined (happiness, sadness, anxiety, anger), Bonferroni correction is applied (α = 0.05/4 = 0.0125 per subscale test).

### Bayesian Alternative

For Primary Analysis 2 (convergent validity), a Bayesian correlation analysis is conducted using the BayesFactor package (Morey & Rouder, 2018) with a default Jeffreys-Zellner-Siow prior. Bayes factors (BF₁₀) are reported alongside frequentist results to quantify evidence for the null hypothesis (r ≈ 0) in the severe aphasia group, where low convergence may reflect either genuine invalidity of FACS or insufficient statistical power. BF₁₀ > 3 is interpreted as moderate evidence for the alternative; BF₁₀ < 1/3 as moderate evidence for the null.

---

## Predicted Results

### If the Hypothesis Is TRUE

Inter-rater FACS reliability will exceed κ = 0.70 in the healthy control group and κ = 0.60 in the severe aphasia group, demonstrating that FACS coding is sufficiently reliable even for neurologically atypical facial expressions. FACS-VAMS convergent validity will reach r > 0.60 in healthy controls and r > 0.40 in severe aphasia, indicating that FACS-derived affect ratings capture meaningful variance in affective state even when self-report is compromised. Behavioral proxies (task engagement duration, withdrawal attempts) will correlate with VAMS at r > 0.50 in healthy controls but decline to r < 0.30 in severe aphasia, formally quantifying the temporal scale mismatch. This pattern would establish that: (a) FACS is a viable ground-truth acquisition strategy for affective computing in aphasia, (b) behavioral proxies introduce systematic temporal mismatch that must be addressed in label construction, and (c) a hierarchical strategy combining FACS with behavioral proxies is preferable to either alone. These findings would directly enable the development of validated affective computing datasets for stroke rehabilitation.

### If the Hypothesis Is FALSE

Two distinct failure modes are informative:

*Failure Mode A:* FACS-VAMS convergent validity r < 0.30 even in the healthy control group, or inter-rater κ < 0.50 in healthy controls. This would indicate that FACS coding is not a valid substitute for self-report even in neurologically intact stroke patients—a finding that challenges the feasibility of FACS-based ground truth acquisition in any stroke population, regardless of aphasia. This result would redirect the field toward purely physiological or caregiver-report approaches and would constitute a significant negative finding warranting publication as a methodological cautionary report.

*Failure Mode B:* FACS-VAMS convergence is adequate in healthy controls (r > 0.50) but fails in severe aphasia (r < 0.20), with facial paresis not accounting for the difference. This would indicate that FACS validity degrades specifically in severe aphasia beyond what neurological confounds explain—potentially reflecting reduced facial expressivity, emotional blunting, or fundamental differences in affective processing post-stroke. This finding would be equally publishable as it would establish empirical boundaries on FACS applicability and motivate the development of aphasia-specific facial coding norms.

In all scenarios, the temporal alignment analysis provides novel quantitative characterization of the behavioral proxy–self-report mismatch problem, which has not been formally reported in any population and constitutes an independent publishable contribution regardless of the convergent validity outcome.

---

## Limitations

**Recruitment bottleneck for severe aphasia:** Patients with WAB-R AQ < 50 who are medically stable, consented, and able to tolerate a 30-minute session represent a small fraction of any single rehabilitation site's caseload. If N = 25 in the aphasia stratum is not achieved within 18 months, the study will be underpowered for detecting correlations below r = 0.50. This is acknowledged a priori; the study is explicitly framed as a pilot for effect size estimation.

**Facial paresis confound:** Approximately 30% of stroke survivors exhibit unilateral facial weakness that will systematically distort FACS coding by reducing the expressivity of affected facial regions. Although facial paresis is documented and included as a covariate, it cannot be fully controlled. Low FACS-VAMS convergence in the aphasia group may reflect neurological facial motor impairment rather than FACS invalidity per se. The study cannot fully disentangle these explanations.

**VAMS validity in severe aphasia is itself unvalidated:** Using VAMS as the criterion measure in severe aphasia assumes that pointing responses on a visual analogue scale reliably reflect internal affective state in this population. This assumption is not fully established. The study is therefore testing convergence between two measures of uncertain validity in the severe aphasia group, and low convergence cannot be unambiguously attributed to FACS invalidity versus VAMS invalidity. This circularity is a fundamental limitation of any validation study in populations where no gold standard exists.

**Temporal scale mismatch is partially confounded by design:** The frustration induction (Condition 3) is the only condition designed to produce negative affect; VAMS is administered retrospectively at condition end. If affective state fluctuates within a condition, the retrospective VAMS rating may not represent the mean affective state captured by FACS epoch coding. This mismatch is the phenomenon of interest but also limits causal interpretation.

**Single-site design:** Recruitment from a single rehabilitation center limits generalizability across stroke etiologies, demographic compositions, and clinical care contexts. Phase 2 replication across multiple sites is required before findings can be generalized.

**Emotional induction efficacy in severe aphasia:** Patients with severe aphasia may not engage sufficiently with photograph and music stimuli to produce detectable affective responses, resulting in floor/ceiling effects in FACS ratings and VAMS scores that make convergent validity uninterpretable. Induction success will be evaluated descriptively (condition-level VAMS change scores) and reported as a manipulation check.

**What this experiment cannot tell us:** This study cannot determine whether FACS-derived affect labels are ecologically valid (i.e., whether they reflect the affective states that matter clinically for rehabilitation outcomes). It cannot establish the optimal temporal resolution for affective state labeling in aphasia. It cannot evaluate whether the hierarchical ground-truth strategy generalizes to naturalistic (non-laboratory) settings. These questions require longitudinal ecological validity studies beyond the scope of this protocol.

---

## Ethical Considerations

### IRB/Ethics Approval

This study involves a vulnerable population (stroke patients with severe aphasia, who may have impaired decision-making capacity) and includes an emotional induction procedure with potential for psychological distress. Full IRB review (not expedited) is required prior to any recruitment or data collection. The protocol will be submitted to the Institutional Review Board of the enrolling academic medical center. For any multi-site expansion, a reliance agreement or single IRB (sIRB) arrangement will be established.

### Informed Consent

For participants with severe aphasia, standard written informed consent may not be achievable due to language comprehension impairment. The following tiered consent procedure is implemented:

1. **Capacity assessment:** The enrolling speech-language pathologist assesses the participant's capacity to understand the study purpose, procedures, risks, and right to withdraw, using an aphasia-adapted capacity assessment tool (illustrated, yes/no response format). Capacity assessment is documented.
2. **Proxy consent:** For participants who lack capacity to provide independent informed consent, written consent is obtained from a legally authorized representative (LAR; typically a family member or legal guardian) following the jurisdiction's applicable proxy consent regulations.
3. **Participant assent:** Regardless of capacity status, participant assent is obtained using an aphasia-adapted assent form (illustrated, large font, pointing response). Assent is re-confirmed at the start of each session. Withdrawal of assent at any point results in immediate session termination without penalty.
4. **Healthy controls:** Standard written informed consent is obtained.

All consent and assent forms are available in aphasia-adapted format (plain language, pictographic support, large font, ≤ 8th grade reading level equivalent).

### Risk Mitigation

**Frustration induction:** The unsolvable puzzle task carries a risk of psychological distress, particularly in participants with pre-existing post-stroke depression or anxiety. The following safeguards are implemented: (a) participants with active suicidal ideation or severe depression are excluded at screening; (b) the session examiner monitors continuously for distress indicators and applies pre-specified stopping rules (sustained crying > 60 seconds, agitation, withdrawal signal); (c) the recovery condition (Condition 4) includes a positive mood repair stimulus; (d) a licensed clinical psychologist or social worker is available by telephone during all sessions for consultation; (e) participants are debriefed immediately after the session with an explanation that the puzzle was designed to be unsolvable.

**Personally meaningful photographs:** Photographs of family members carry a risk of triggering grief responses, particularly in participants who have experienced bereavement. Bereavement within 6 months is an exclusion criterion. Stimulus selection is reviewed by the enrolling clinician before use.

**Video recording:** Video recordings of identifiable participants are stored on encrypted, password-protected servers with access restricted to the research team. Face-blurred copies are used for all analyses not requiring FACS coding. Original recordings are retained for the minimum period required by institutional data retention policy (typically 7 years) and then securely destroyed. Participants are informed of video recording in the consent process and may withdraw consent for video use at any time.

**Physiological monitoring:** ECG, EDA, and PPG recording carries minimal risk (skin irritation from electrodes). Electrode sites are inspected before and after application. Participants with known skin sensitivity to adhesive electrodes are accommodated with hypoallergenic alternatives.

**Participant burden:** The total session duration (approximately 55–65 minutes including setup) is designed to be tolerable for severe aphasia patients. Sessions may be shortened to 30 minutes (eliminating the frustration induction) if the participant shows signs of fatigue at any point, with this documented as a protocol deviation.

### Data Protection

All data are stored in compliance with HIPAA (US) or applicable national data protection regulations. Participant identifiers are replaced with study codes at data entry. The linkage file connecting study codes to participant identifiers is stored separately from research data on an encrypted server accessible only to the principal investigator and IRB-designated personnel. Video recordings are subject to the additional protections described above.

contradictions.description: The two runs of sim_stroke_hrv_laterality (loop 0 and loop 1) report slightly different primary beta values for the right-hemisphere effect on LF/HF ratio: 0.725 (loop 0) vs. 1.092 (loop 1), with different sample sizes (403 vs. 420).
contradictions.suggested_resolution: Both runs use synthetic data generated with random seeds. The difference in beta estimates (0.725 vs. 1.092) and sample sizes (403 vs. 420) reflects stochastic variation in synthetic data generation across pipeline loops, not a replication failure. Both estimates are directionally consistent and both are statistically significant. However, this variability across synthetic runs underscores that the effect size estimates are not stable empirical measurements — they are artifacts of the simulation parameterization.

surprises.why_surprising: The supporting results (sim_stroke_hrv_laterality) address a laterality sub-claim (c2: right vs. left hemisphere differences within stroke patients) that is downstream of and logically dependent on c1. The core thesis — that stroke patients as a group differ from healthy controls — was never evaluated. The pipeline's summary statistic of '2 supporting' is therefore misleading: the two supporting results address a different claim (c2) using synthetic data, while the foundational claim (c1) and the directly tested sub-claim (c1b) remain completely unevaluated. A thesis about classifier bias in stroke rehabilitation cannot be assessed without first establishing the distributional shift relative to healthy norms.
surprises.significance: This means the core thesis is currently without any empirical support or refutation. The apparent 'supporting' results are for a laterality effect within stroke patients — a scientifically interesting finding in its own right, but not the same as demonstrating that stroke patients differ from healthy-population norms in a way that would bias affective classifiers.

surprises.description: The sim_stroke_hrv_laterality simulations produced large effect sizes (Cohen's d = 0.69 for LF/HF, 0.64 for SDNN, 0.50 for RMSSD) that would, if real, substantially exceed the c1 pass threshold of Cohen's d > 0.3. However, these are within-stroke comparisons (right vs. left hemisphere), not stroke vs. healthy controls.
surprises.why_surprising: The magnitude of the laterality effect within stroke patients is large enough that, if stroke patients as a group show even a fraction of this deviation from healthy norms, c1 would likely pass. But this inference cannot be made from the available data — it requires the untested healthy-control comparison.
surprises.significance: The synthetic laterality data are calibrated to published literature values (Colivicchi 2004, Naver 1996, Sykora 2008), which do report reduced HRV in stroke patients relative to controls. This suggests the published literature likely supports c1, but the current analysis did not access or analyze that literature directly, and no quantitative literature synthesis was provided.

interpreted_findings.strongest_result: The strongest result in the dataset is the adjusted OLS regression from sim_stroke_hrv_laterality (loop 1): beta = 1.092 (95% CI: 0.793–1.390) for right vs. left hemisphere on LF/HF ratio, with Cohen's d = 0.693 for the unadjusted comparison. This is internally consistent across two synthetic runs and directionally aligns with published literature on hemispheric lateralization of cardiac autonomic control. However, its strength is severely limited by the fact that it is entirely synthetic data calibrated to the literature it purports to test — it cannot be treated as independent empirical evidence. It addresses c2 (laterality), not c1 (stroke vs. healthy controls) or c1b (ischemic vs. hemorrhagic), which are the claims actually under evaluation here.
interpreted_findings.weakest_link: The weakest link is the complete failure to obtain any real data for c1 — the foundational claim of the thesis. Both NHANES simulation attempts (sim_c1, loops 0 and 1) failed at file download due to format errors, producing zero observations, zero test statistics, and zero distributional metrics. Without c1, the thesis has no empirical grounding: the claim that stroke patients show HRV distributions shifted relative to healthy-population norms — the prerequisite for any downstream claim about classifier bias — is entirely unverified by this analysis. The entire evidential structure of the thesis rests on a foundation that was never tested.

breakthrough.raw_response:
No direct prior art exists for this specific connection. The pieces exist separately — interoceptive inference models (Allen 2022, Seth 2016), insular stroke and HRV (Oppenheimer 1996, Colivicchi 2005), and affective computing domain adaptation (Zhao 2021, Chen 2020) — but nobody has connected them into a unified framework.
